papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.
authors: Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu, Ziqi Huang, Tianqi Liu, Mingze Sun, Ziyi Wang, Zhongang Cai, Hanming Deng, Quan Wang, Lei Yang, Lewei Lu, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Dahua Lin, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Problem: Fixed visual encoders may discard action-critical details such as local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes.
Method: Tokenizes images with lightweight patch convolutions and jointly processes visual tokens with language across the backbone.
Action generation uses a flow-matching expert conditioned on visual representations from multiple depths.
Controlled comparisons find native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts; scaling alone does not close the gap.
Layer-wise probing and evaluations under distribution shifts indicate that useful control signals often emerge before the final visual layer.

Figure 2: NEO-VLA: pixels in, continuous actions out. Previous and current multi-view observations preserve their aspect ratios within a fixed token budget and enter patch embedder shared across time and views. The visual path uses no vision transformer, autoencoder, or vector-quantised codebook. Shared MLPs embed camera intrinsics and rotations, while state MLPs embed previous and current robot states. These tokens join a structured prompt describing control frequency, embodiment, frame reference, and task instruction. A separate, narrow, randomly initialised action expert jointly attends to cached prefix keys and values from selected backbone layers and its own action-token keys and values. Its suffix embeddings combine projected noisy actions and flow time τ with additive step, frame, and identity embeddings. Both arm blocks and the body block share temporal rotary offsets 0–29, with identity embeddings distinguishing the blocks. Trained by flow matching, the expert predicts a velocity field that covers both arm and body action chunks.

Figure 1: Three VLA designs: encoder-based vs. encoder-free backbones, and discrete vs. continuous actions. (a) A separate visual encoder converts pixels into image features, which are consumed by the language backbone together with text tokens; actions are generated as discrete tokens. (b) The same encoder-based visual interface is retained, while a separate action head predicts continuous actions conditioned on the backbone. (c) NEO-VLA removes the separately pretrained visual encoder: a lightweight patch embedder maps pixels directly into the backbone token space, while text tokens enter the backbone jointly. A narrow action expert then reads cached keys and values from selected backbone layers and predicts a flow-matching velocity field.

papers.title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: NEO-VLA improves vision-language-action control by letting action policies access evolving, instruction-conditioned visual representations instead of relying on a fixed visual encoder output.

papers.abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.
authors: Mattia Greiche, Reihaneh Rabbany, Maximilian Puelma Touzel
bullets: Motivated by LLM agents’ behavioral brittleness under meaning-preserving prompt variations, which challenges social-simulation validation.
Defines controlled context enrichment through four prompt types: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding.
Introduces selective robustness: invariance to meaning-preserving prompt changes alongside directional responses to decision-relevant changes in the social environment.
Demonstrates the framework in a Prisoner’s Dilemma-like game, identifying distinct behavioral effects of different enrichment strategies.
Finds that enrichment effects and behavioral patterns vary across the two tested models.

papers.abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.
authors: Fei Lin, Tengchao Zhang, Ziyang Gong, Xiaotong Yu, Bohan Zhang, Yifan Zhou, Qihao Yang, Ji Dai, Dong Li, Yining Jiang, Qinghua Ni, Jun Huang, Qiang Zhang, Yue Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Yonglin Tian, Fei-Yue Wang, Xue Yang

Includes 1,000 manually created and reviewed question-answer samples spanning 11 image and video task types.
Evaluates affordance grounding, trajectory planning, apparatus and state recognition, safety, setup, operation, and temporal reasoning.
Benchmarks 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied multimodal language models in an offline, single-turn setting.
Finds a gap between coarse video procedure following and fine-grained action grounding, feasible trajectories, laboratory recognition, safety judgment, and step ordering.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.
authors: Siyuan Hu, Abulikemu Abuduweili, Yue Meng, Shipeng Liu, Quentin Leboutet, Chen Chen, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun
bullets: Addresses the lack of large-scale paired data mapping visual and language inputs to humanoid joint commands.
Synthesizes training data across 1,000 procedurally generated homes, scaling with compute rather than human teleoperation.
Learns skills such as navigation, sitting, crouching, crawling, door traversal, and box pushing, then composes them for longer tasks.
Transfers to six unmapped real-world environments without real-home training, achieving 91% success across 360 trials.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Synthetic data generation and training pipeline. (A) Each task is decomposed into segments defined by text prompts and keyframe poses. After sampling target asset locations and routing navigation waypoints, a conditional diffusion model synthesizes motion segments from these constraints, stitching them into a continuous whole-body trajectory. (B) This generated trajectory and its associated assets are embedded into procedurally generated scenes, ensuring collision-free placement. (C) A simulator replays the kinematic motion to render egocentric vision from the robot’s head-mounted cameras. Visual domain randomization is applied to maximize appearance diversity. (D) The resulting corpus is used for training the autonomy stack, via imitation learning for the motion generator and via reinforcement learning for the motion tracker.

Fig. 6: Motion tracker onboard inference architecture. On the Jetson Orin NX, the tracker runs at 50Hz and fuses three onboard streams: (top left) raw stereo IR frames from the RealSense D435i (emitter off) are mapped by LiteAnyStereo [45] (TensorRT FP16) to a clean 48×84 egocentric depth image and encoded by a 2D CNN; (bottom left) a 30-step proprioceptive history together with the next 30 plan frames is encoded by a 1D temporal CNN; and (center) both feature vectors are concatenated with the current proprioceptive state and 5-frame motion plan lookahead and passed through a SimBa residual MLP [49] to output 29 target joint positions for the low-level PD controller.

Fig. 2: Onboard autonomy stack. (A) A VLM (∼0.5 Hz) processes a natural-language request and egocentric visual input (top left) and outputs a sequence of subtasks. (B) The motion generator (∼3 Hz) maps each subtask and the corresponding egocentric RGB frames into a 5 s whole-body motion plan. (C) The motion tracker (50Hz) executes the motion plan, grounding the trajectory into the physical world using egocentric depth (bottom left) and proprioception.

Fig. 5: Episodes of the six skills. Top: training frames from the egocentric fisheye camera (1280×800). Bottom: a typical episode of each skill on the same time axis (blue triangles are full-body keyframes), where only SIT chains several KIMODO calls.

Fig. 4: Procedural rooms and scene baking. Top: path-traced training rooms from INFINIGEN. Bottom: a held-out view of a dense living room rendered from the bake in three engines, where the mean absolute error relative to path tracing is 4.2 (Blender), 4.5 (MuJoCo) and 4.7 (Isaac Sim) grey levels and mostly lies in the light pool of the lamp on the floor and at object edges (error map: white is 0, dark blue is 32 grey levels or more).

Fig. 10: Real-world generalization across people, tables, and seats. Each tile is one frame from a separate real-world run. (a) GO-TO toward different people in different rooms. (b) CRAWL under two tables (outdoors and indoors) and CROUCH under three desks of different heights. (c) SIT on a black armchair, a white armchair, two sofas and a corner sofa.

Fig. 7: Communication graph. The generator pulls the robot state (get state) and the not-yet-executed reference (get trim) from the tracker and sends each new motion plan (put plan). The orchestrator sends the current subtask to the generator (subtask) and receives the egocentric frame (obs) and the generator’s motion status (gen status). The web GUI subscribes to state, obs, subtask, and plan.

Fig. 9: Real-world rollouts, one per skill. Each row is one single-task run on the physical robot, filmed by an external camera. The row header is the subtask prompt given to the motion generator. The five frames are spaced through the run, and the time in each frame is measured from the first frame of its row.

Fig. 8: Onboard compute and sensing. A Mac mini M4 Pro in the rear enclosure runs the orchestrator (∼ 0.5Hz) and the motion generator (∼ 3Hz). The robot’s Jetson Orin NX runs the motion tracker in a 50Hz real-time loop. The OAK-1W supplies the 120◦ RGB the generator reasons over; the RealSense D435i supplies the 55◦ depth the tracker reacts to. All modules run onboard, with external network calls used only when querying an optional cloud VLM for orchestration.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces HALO, a system for generating vision-language-motion data for humanoids and achieving zero-shot transfer to real-world tasks, advancing generalist humanoid autonomy.
papers.title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
papers.tldr: HALO generates large-scale simulated vision-language-motion data to train humanoids that transfer zero-shot to real-world homes and solve long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.
authors: Michal Korniak, Marco Bagatella, Ralf R\"omer, Michal Nauman, Yarden As, Pranav Vignesh, Manan Agarwal, Leander Diaz-Bone, Piotr Zalewski, Miko{\l}aj Czarnecki, Lenart Treven, Shashwat Saxena, Sreyas Venkataraman, Sarvesh Patil, Zhiyuan Zhou, Daniel Marta, Oier Mees, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah, Carmelo Sferrazza, Bhavya Sukhija, Angela P. Schoellig, Andreas Krause, Max Simchowitz, Andrew Wagenmaker

Introduces structured evaluations for multi-task, online improvement of generalist robot policies.

papers.abstract: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
authors: Yiwen Chen, Qiqi Hou, Jisoo Jeong, Yinhao Zhu, Huaizu Jiang, Amir Said
bullets: JEPA-style latent dynamics can preserve episode-specific static content while discarding manipulation-relevant state changes, harming control.
Randomized backgrounds expose this failure: planning degrades even when the underlying manipulation task is unchanged.
The method contrasts predicted latent transitions with same-episode candidate observations, using optical-flow similarity as soft supervision.
Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, it promotes within-episode state distinctions and motion-related similarities.
Planning success improves from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, with comparable performance on four other benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Static collapse and our solution. (A) We train JEPA world models end-to-end on OGBench-Cube (Cube) and a variant with randomized backgrounds (Cube-RB). In Cube-RB, one background image is sampled per episode and held fixed throughout it. Only distant pixels (depth ≥ 1.0m) are replaced, so the robot, cube, and dynamics are unchanged and only task-irrelevant background variation is added. (B) t-SNE visualizations of the encoder embeddings, where each point is one input frame and each color one episode. On Cube-RB, LeWorldModel (LeWM; Maes et al., 2026) maps distinct states within each episode to tightly clustered latents, whereas our motionguided contrastive regularization preserves within-episode state variation. (C) Planning success of LeWM, Planning with Latent Dynamics Models (PLDM; Sobal et al., 2026), and our method. LeWM and our method perform similarly on Cube, but LeWM’s success drops on Cube-RB and is low on LIBERO-Object. Our method achieves the highest success of the three in all settings.

Figure 2: Motion-guided contrastive learning. The world model encodes the current observation xt and predicts ẑt+1. The true next observation xpos = xt+1 provides the positive sample, while other frames from the same episode provide negative candidates xm and xn. All observations share the same encoder. Image-space: Optical flow is computed from xt to each candidate. Comparing these fields with the positive flow assigns higher target similarity to candidates with similar motion (xm) than to those with different motion (xn). Latent-space: Angles illustrate cosine similarities between the predicted transition ẑt+1 − zt and candidate transitions zj − zt. Our motion-guided contrastive loss matches the resulting latent similarity distribution to the motion-derived target distribution through cross-entropy. The prediction loss aligns ẑt+1 with zpos. The grippers in the sample frames are highlighted for illustration purposes only.

Figure 3: Latent-space decoding on Cube, Cube-RB, and LIBERO-Object. Compared to LeWM, reconstructions from our frozen latents more clearly preserve the robot and manipulated objects on the challenging Cube-RB and LIBERO-Object datasets. Check our video demo for more comparisons.

papers.abstract: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.
authors: Chibueze Praise Onyenweaku, Toyibat Adele, Sikirulahi Opeyemi Abdulkareem, Obed Honour Eje
bullets: Apparent pedestrian height remains relatively stable under occlusion, while monocular depth shifts toward the nearer occluding surface.
The method uses only the ordering of these cues, avoiding focal-length, body-height, and depth-scale calibration when depth errors are approximately a gain.
It requires no training or occlusion annotations and can check the depth-model assumption without labels.
It detects heavy occlusion with AUC 0.909 on KITTI, 0.819 in synthetic CARLA scenes, and remains effective within fixed distance ranges.
Several tested architectural approaches did not generalize beyond training distributions, highlighting the value of annotation-free signals.

papers.abstract: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.
authors: Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Uksang Yoo, Xinyue Zhu, Meadow Shen, Jaimyn Drake, Eugen Solowjow, Lionel Gulich, Alexander Millane, Rafael Cathomen, Tuur Stuyck, Sangeeta Subramanian, Yichao Pan, Bruce McGowan, Michael Benedict, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu, Spencer Huang, Ken Goldberg

Provides standardized variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and 33 reusable skills with human-authored programmatic solutions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
authors: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
bullets: Addresses the latency of summarizing growing agent histories while preserving important information.
Uses a small fine-tuned drafter to propose structured summary slots in parallel.
A target model verifies each proposed line, repairs rejected content, and guides subsequent drafting.
Reports 2.04–5.63× speedups on AppWorld and τ³ with two target models, plus an 8.68× median speedup in a Hermes user study.
Downstream quality shows model- and task-dependent trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.
bullets: Studies self-repair for simulated robot manipulation using repeated program generation after scene resets.
A fixed lookup selects feedback templates from failure labels and API variants, while a frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-7B generates retries.
On 252 initial failures, template feedback recovered 85.3% within five retries versus 68.3% for resampling, with the gap persisting under equal token budgets.
Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance achieved similar recovery estimates, with no detected benefit from matching coarse failure labels.
Template feedback reduced recovery on a rim-grasp nut-insertion task, highlighting the need for task-compatible baselines.

papers.tldr: Retry success in code-as-policy agents may come largely from resampling and task guidance rather than failure-specific feedback.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at https://pranjal2041.github.io/vtr
bullets: Targets the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of visual tokens accumulating across long interaction histories.
Jointly trains a vision-language model with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that selects action-relevant, nonredundant image-region tokens.
Uses an adaptive loss to minimize token count while limiting performance degradation.
Matches the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video-game action prediction using 2.5–5.8× fewer visual tokens.
Reduces inference cost by up to 3.3× and prefilling time by up to 2.9×; outperforms resolution reduction and other token-dropping baselines on OSWorld.

It drops the regions that did not change, and also drops the circled part of the video, which changed but is not relevant to the task.

Figure 6: VTR adapts how many visual tokens it keeps to each domain and game. Percentage of visual tokens kept by each method on desktop tasks and on video games grouped by how much of the screen changes between consecutive frames.

Figure 7: VTR keeps only the regions that the agent needs. The previous observation (top) and the current observation with the regions that VTR drops dimmed (bottom), in three video games and a desktop application.

Figure 3: Training in VTR. Joint training: We train πθ and the router together with the crossentropy (CE) loss on the kept tokens, and also train the router to keep fewer tokens with L = Ltok + λLdeg. The full and blind models see all tokens and only the anchors, and are used only during training. Measuring degradation: We compare the losses of the three models to measure how much the full history helps (in) and how much dropping tokens hurts (dn). Adaptive weight λ: We increase λ when the share of this help that πθ loses, r̄, exceeds the small tolerance r⋆, so that the router keeps more tokens, and decrease it otherwise.

papers.tldr: Visual Token Routing sparsifies screenshot representations for computer-use agents, preserving action performance while substantially reducing visual-token and inference costs.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections. They are trained largely on single-session object captures whose images vary in viewpoint while the object and its environment remain nearly fixed. Public photo archives contain a different form of multi-view data. They hold found photos of the same object or design: photos taken independently by many people across years, environments, cameras, and sometimes physical units. In this work, we introduce Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We reconstruct each object to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. We categorize the objects into three regimes: objects fixed at one site, objects that move between sites, and designs shared by many physical units. Evaluating recent feedforward reconstruction models on Trainspotting shows that they fail most severely in the last two regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting significantly improves camera pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects. We observe similar improvements on the independent NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, which contains photos of each object in different environments. Performance on conventional benchmarks remains largely unchanged.
bullets: The dataset contains 12,068 objects and 311,886 Wikimedia Commons photos collected across people, years, environments, cameras, and physical instances.
It reconstructs camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks, while categorizing objects by whether they stay at one site, move between sites, or represent shared designs.
Recent feedforward models struggle most with objects that move or have multiple physical units.
Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting improves pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects and also improves performance on the NAVI benchmark.
Conventional benchmark performance remains largely unchanged after fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA$^{I}$, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA$^{W}$) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: https://github.com/YingyingYan1/DGP.
authors: Yingying Yan, Jiaqi Tang, Wei Wei, Qianzhou Wang, Lei Zhang, Jianmin Chen, Yuyang Xia, Botong Geng, Jinjian Wu, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Addresses the limitation of injecting a fixed visual representation into all LLM layers.
Creates all-to-all ViT–LLM connections, with each LLM layer learning dynamic gates over visual layers.
Built on LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP consistently improves the 7B baseline across reported benchmarks.
Outperforms prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks.
Routing analyses show that different LLM layers select different visual granularities, providing interpretability.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of DGP. (A) At every LLM layer, the Dynamic Gated Pathways module routes over all ViT layers conditioned on the current language-layer state, aggregates the selected visual features, and injects them back into the LLM hidden states through a gated residual connection— establishing all-to-all cross-layer connections between ViT and LLM. (B) Inside the module, ViT layer summaries serve as keys/values and the language-layer state as the query; a shared cross-attention followed by a layer-specific routing MLP produces the per-layer routing weights. Weight Matrix(m) denotes the routing weights of LLM layer m over all ViT layers.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamic gated pathways for MLLM layer connections; improves multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Where to Connect? Boosting MLLMs via Dynamic Gated Pathways across ALL ViT and LLM Layers
papers.tldr: DGP improves MLLMs by dynamically routing visual features from every ViT layer to each LLM layer according to its semantic needs.

papers.abstract: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.
bullets: The work addresses the cost of characterizing stochastic answer variation, which normally requires many autoregressive rollouts.
Context–answer metamodels map context activation sequences to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations.
Four metamodel families achieve high-fidelity forecasts, with distribution models also capturing rollout variability.
Performance scales with training data, generalizes zero-shot across datasets, and preserves behavior-predictive information.
Forecasts can transfer across models: Qwen2.5 context activations predict answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes metamodels to forecast LLM answer activations from context, suggesting a mechanism for predicting future behavior and retaining predictive signal.
papers.title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
papers.tldr: Context activations can forecast the content-related activation patterns and variability of an LLM’s future answers before generation begins.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
authors: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
bullets: Targets looped Transformer limitations: loop-dependent memory growth, coarse compute control, and fixed post-training loop counts.
Loops decoder layers after the first, using global memory written once per token and publishing each token’s KV entry only on its first visit.
Independent layer loops provide budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token; one model supports all budgets without a router.
With sufficient looping, LooM improves language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity over a same-data single-pass baseline while keeping cache size unchanged.
Training-budget distributions determine what additional depth provides; the approach supports deployment-time depth selection.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Loop-invariant memory in LooM. Every visit re-reads global memory (left), but only a layer’s first visit publishes the token’s local KV entry (right); publishing arrows are drawn for the 21-call path only. (b) D2, standing for any of D2–D6: a later token reads one local entry per earlier token however often the layer ran, so the cache (after a 128-token prompt) is the same on every path. papers.selection_reason: Novel looped transformer architecture that keeps cache size constant, improving long-context perplexity and efficiency.
papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.tldr: LooM enables flexible, memory-efficient looping in causal encoder-decoder language models, allowing deployment-time depth adjustment without increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.
authors: Juncheng Ma, Jiaxin Li, Jiankai Tu, Bo Liang, Guodong Lv, Yufan Deng, Junzhe Tang, Liangzhu Yang, Chen Bian, Zicong Cao, Baohao Zhu, Jianxin Bi, Tengfei Yan, Yinyuan Zhang, Kewei Zhang, Xinglong Chen, Kaiqi Chen, Duomin Wang, Xiaotian Tang, Liang Tan, Li Li, Yuan Xu, Haosen Yang, Yuqi Wang, Jingfei Xia, Songyan Huang, Zhiyang Dou, Zhen Dong, Enze Xie, Tat-Seng Chua, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Curates egocentric human video with dense hand-motion and language annotations for scalable robot-learning pretraining.
Finds a log-linear relationship between human-video pretraining hours and downstream robot success in closed-loop simulation.
HumanWAM-Vanilla, pretrained only on human video, achieves strong RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo performance after robot post-training.
Joint human–robot pretraining with goal conditioning improves zero-shot generalization, reaching 84.60% on RoboTwin Clean2Random.
Releases the corpus, curation and training pipelines, model checkpoints, inference code, and evaluation suites.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.
authors: Yihong Luo, Tianyu Pang, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Addresses quality loss and unreliable student-score estimation in few-step distillation.

Unifies score, Fisher-based, and moment matching while motivating new training objectives.
Uses trajectory distribution matching with online transition-aware velocity learning and dual-form supervision.
Achieves state-of-the-art four-step text-to-image and text-to-video results, including scaling to the 33B MiniMax-H3 model.

papers.abstract: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.
bullets: Raw integer-grid serialization obscures spatial structure and causes excessive exploratory actions.
A zero-parameter, linear-time perception engine builds object inventories, tracks changes over time, distinguishes invariants from hypotheses, and annotates frames.
Combined with code-as-action execution, grounded perception improved the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 and reduced token use by 89.4%.
Geometric invariants generalized perfectly on 23 held-out games, while single-frame affordance guesses were unreliable, motivating active verification.
On the public set, briefing improved single-pass efficiency from 59.4% to 63.5%; the system scored 16.53 on the hidden evaluation within nine hours.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.

bullets: Introduces UMBench, a benchmark covering traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning.

papers.abstract: Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.

papers.abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.
authors: Yequan Bie, Dengyang Jiang, Zhixuan Chen, Xiaozhuan Liang, Haoxuan Che, Quande Liu, Xi Chen, Hao Chen
bullets: Introduces Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, requiring models to render events, infer their consequences, and reveal plausible outcomes later—even off-screen.
Uses a vision-language “world brain” to track evolving state and reason about transitions, paired with a segment-autoregressive video renderer.
Provides EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency.
Experiments report improved event-conditioned causal evolution while preserving visual quality and consistency.
Targets limitations of existing diffusion video models, which often produce visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent scenes.

papers.abstract: Scene Graph Anticipation (SGA) predicts object relationships in future video frames. Continuous-time SGA models evolve each subject-object pair with an independent Neural ODE, so relationships sharing an entity cannot influence one another during integration, and nothing prevents mutually exclusive predictions, such as "sitting on" and "standing on", for the same pair. We introduce CoupledSGA, which links such relationships through a Relationship Interaction Graph with graph attention inside the ODE vector field, and adds a Structural Consistency Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{SC}$) based on a matrix of mutually exclusive predicates. Developing CoupledSGA revealed a limitation of the evaluation protocol. With-Constraint evaluation keeps one predicate per group for each subject-object pair, so its R@K and mR@K cannot capture the within-group violations targeted by $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$: we prove they are unchanged whenever each group's winning predicate and its score are held fixed. We further show that the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ depends on predicate scores rather than ground-truth labels: for two-predicate rules it amplifies the ordering the model already holds, and when all scores in a group are equal it suppresses predicates in more exclusion rules more strongly, explaining why the penalty can lower recall while improving consistency. On Action Genome, activating $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ after two warm-up epochs reduces R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% while lowering the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07% (matched-budget R@20: 40.48% CoupledSGA vs. 44.78% SceneSayerODE). CoupledSGA is a testbed, not a state-of-the-art claim: With-Constraint recall captures the cost of enforcing structural consistency but not the improvement. We recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate for methods that constrain predicate co-activation.
authors: Zeno Nongmaithem, Anushttha Srivastava, Anshit Sinha, Apoorv Sisodia, Suman Chowdhury, Prerana Mukherjee, Rajesh P. Barnwal
bullets: Independent Neural ODEs in continuous-time SGA cannot model interactions among relationships sharing an entity and may produce mutually exclusive predicates together.
CoupledSGA adds graph-attention coupling through a Relationship Interaction Graph and a Structural Consistency Loss based on mutually exclusive predicates.
The authors prove With-Constraint R@K and mR@K cannot reflect within-group violations when each group’s winning predicate and score remain fixed.
On Action Genome, the consistency loss reduces contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07%, but R@20 falls from 42.21% to 35.18%; matched-budget R@20 is 40.48% versus 44.78% for SceneSayerODE.
The paper recommends reporting No-Constraint results with contradiction rates; CoupledSGA is presented as a testbed rather than a state-of-the-art method.

papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting recurring shell-output structure alongside execution-specific content without running commands.
Provides reusable output templates with sentinels; the model autoregressively generates only the missing gaps.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
authors: Shuai Dong, Kanghui Tian, Linghan Chen, Wenqi Shao, Hongrui Wu, Haowen Hou, Yongfu Zhu, Xuehui Wang, Ziyue Wang, Wenpu Liu, Weichu Xie, Yuqi Xu, Congcong Wang, Kaiwen Tuo, Caoyuan Ma, Taiqiang Wu, Ji Zhao, Wenzheng Chang, Dianyi Wang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei, Yu Qiao, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Streaming video models must repeatedly choose whether to respond or keep observing, but trajectory-level credit can reinforce redundancy or suppress useful follow-ups.
TurnWise computes turn-level group-relative advantages from silence-completed prefix scores and each decision’s remaining return.
Turn-mean policy optimization gives response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of token output length.
The framework requires neither a learned critic nor additional rollouts.
Experiments report improved performance over prior RL methods for streaming video understanding.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.
bullets: Organizes recent research into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications.
Highlights human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing as cross-cutting perspectives, supported by a system-level architecture, comparative tables, and case analyses.

Finds that human-data value depends on kinematic, visual, and contact alignment—not recording volume alone—and that foundation policies cannot eliminate embodiment-specific force, latency, and contact constraints.
Argues that task completion alone does not demonstrate physical correctness or deployment readiness.

Identifies limited evidence for zero-shot transfer across morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization; proposes reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
authors: Zohreh Abbasi Liasi, Batoul Hammoud, Anas Madkoor, Ehsaneddin Asgari
bullets: Evaluates 43 models across six languages using 450 controlled multiple-choice questions covering 30 Wikidata relations.
Tests five Bloom-inspired reasoning levels and three knowledge conditions: factual, counterfactual, and neutralized.

Difficulty rankings are largely consistent across languages, suggesting shared cross-lingual structure in relational reasoning difficulty.

Items are then evaluated in six languages under two multilingual settings. The 43 models comprise 41 open-weight models from seven model families, analyzed as eight model series because Qwen2.5 Base and Qwen2.5 Instruct are treated separately, plus two Gemini models.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.
authors: Muhammad Danish Waseem, Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan
bullets: Evaluates seven inference-optimization families across seven VLAs and four GPU families, from H100 to Jetson Thor.
Analyzes the roles of CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency in determining optimization gains.
Shows that optimization benefits and interactions depend on the model, hardware, and deployed execution mode.
Introduces VLA-Triage, guidelines for selecting and stacking optimizations under latency budgets.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.
authors: Pranay Samineni, Adam Thorpe, John Chubick, Anand Balakrishnan, Christian Ellis, Swarat Chaudhuri, Ufuk Topcu
bullets: Targets the challenge of deciding when a UGV needs aerial assistance and what map information the UAV should collect.
Evaluates how uncertain map layers affect the UGV’s current MPPI rollouts, then selects the most useful aerial measurement.
Fuses the returned aerial information and replans the UGV trajectory.
In 180 simulation trials, achieved 98.9% goal attainment and reduced mean UAV flight time by 87.7% versus continuous greedy mapping.
Field experiments over approximately 2 km demonstrated uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

papers.abstract: Online reasoning video segmentation (Online RVS) requires a model to segment query-referred objects as a video streams in, using only the frames observed so far. Existing formulations largely assume a fixed target set throughout the video, overlooking a fundamental property of streaming reasoning: as new events occur, the objects that satisfy a query may change over time. To address this, we propose a new task, Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation (GRVS), where the target set depends on query-relevant events accumulated over the observed video history. As new evidence accumulates, the target set can evolve from empty to one or multiple objects, requiring a model to continuously maintain target validity while localizing the valid objects currently in view. To evaluate GRVS, we build Isekai, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 videos and 197 queries across 11 temporal query families, with 12,569 scoring points whose target sets are causally annotated over time. We further propose Sekai, an online framework with two complementary components: an Event Memory Reasoner (EMR) that maintains query-relevant events and evolving target states in structured memory, and a Memory-Grounded Decoder (MGD) that identifies valid targets from this memory and localizes them in the current frame. Experiments show that Sekai significantly outperforms existing online RVS methods, achieving 50.33 J&F and improving over the strongest baseline by 3.2 points. Code, example annotations, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zenastangbi/Sekai.
authors: Zhengtao Liu, Jinrong Xu, Shiu-Hong Kao, Huixin Sun, Yicong Li
bullets: Problem: Existing online video segmentation assumes a fixed target set, while streaming events can change which objects satisfy a query.
Method: The Event Memory Reasoner maintains query-relevant events and target states; the Memory-Grounded Decoder selects and segments valid objects in each current frame.
Benchmark: Isekai contains 60 videos, 197 queries, 11 temporal query families, and causally annotated target states across 12,569 scoring points.
Result: Sekai achieves 50.33 J&F, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.2 points.
Scope: The task focuses on online, causal reasoning where target sets may evolve from empty to one or multiple objects.

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors capture multiple aspects of physical interaction within a single image stream, including contact appearance, geometry, indentation depth, and tangential deformation. However, existing visuo-tactile policies often directly process tactile observations as images, making it difficult to determine which physical cues contribute to policy learning. This paper presents a controlled real-robot study that compares physically interpretable tactile signals using the LeRobot platform, enhanced with our visuo-tactile perception system. From the same tactile stream, we derive tactile RGB images, normal/depth maps, and marker-flow fields, representing contact appearance, geometry, and tangential deformation, respectively. Using identical task demonstrations and the same policy backbone, we evaluate the individual and combined contributions of these tactile cues. We further compare tactile encoders and visuo-tactile fusion strategies. Evaluation across 720 real-robot trials yields four key findings: (1) tactile perception substantially improves the overall success rate from 57.8% to 78.9%, although its contribution varies across task stages; (2) marker flow is the most effective individual cue, achieving a success rate of 74.4% and playing a particularly important role in regulating established contact; (3) cue-factorized encoding consistently improves performance, highlighting that different physical cues require tailored processing techniques; and (4) although the effectiveness of tactile fusion is task-dependent, cross-attention offers a lightweight solution with performance comparable to that of pretrained tactile encoders.
authors: Xuhao Qin, Xiyan Huang, Haoyu Dong, Xi Zhang, Chenxi Xiao
bullets: The study isolates contact appearance, geometry/depth, and tangential deformation from the same tactile stream.
Across 720 real-robot trials, adding tactile perception raised success from 57.8% to 78.9%.
Marker flow was the strongest individual cue, reaching 74.4% success and helping regulate established contact.
Cue-factorized encoders consistently improved performance, suggesting different physical cues need tailored processing.
Cross-attention provided a lightweight fusion strategy with performance comparable to pretrained tactile encoders, though fusion effectiveness was task-dependent.
