papers.abstract: Portrait video relighting aims to modify the illumination of a portrait video while preserving photorealism and temporal stability. The task becomes particularly challenging under dynamic lighting, where illumination direction, intensity, and color vary over time. To tackle this problem, we introduce FlashRelight, a novel two-stage framework for dynamic portrait video relighting. FlashRelight first suppresses the source illumination through delighting, and then synthesizes the target dynamic lighting on an illumination-neutral portrait video. FlashRelight supports three complementary control modalities: envmap sequences for explicit frame-level lighting control, dynamic lighting text for semantic illumination editing, and lighting reference videos for visual lighting transfer. Training follows a low-cost hybrid strategy that combines static one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, covering both controlled illumination variation and realistic portrait motion. Extensive experiments show that FlashRelight achieves temporally coherent and photorealistic dynamic relighting while enabling flexible cross-video lighting transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/vivoCameraResearch/FlashRelight
authors: Jiahui Sheng, Le Li, Limin Lin, Jiahao Li, Wansen Feng, Hong Gu, Shuhan Chen, Xiaorun Li, Rui Hu
bullets: Addresses dynamic lighting changes in portrait videos while preserving appearance and temporal consistency.

Experiments demonstrate coherent, photorealistic relighting and flexible cross-video lighting transfer.

papers.abstract: Existing traffic signal control methods typically rely on structured traffic states produced by dedicated perception pipelines. Emerging visual approaches often use idealized simulator images and convert them into intermediate representations before control, limiting their ability to directly exploit roadside visual observations. To bridge both the visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps, we introduce SynTra-V and Traffic-VL. SynTra-V converts physics-based traffic simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery across diverse road topologies and sensing conditions, and automatic semantic auditing checks that control-critical geometry, vehicle movements, and lane semantics match the simulator state. Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that directly maps synchronized multi-view images and natural-language phase descriptions to signal decisions without intermediate structured states. Building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning framework, Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder via offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V and freezes it during online visual stepwise trajectory policy optimization in closed-loop simulation. Experiments show that Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 while outperforming image-based controllers and general-purpose vision-language models, including Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluations on unseen topologies, degraded sensing conditions, real surveillance footage, and a three-week deployment across ten intersections further demonstrate robust visual generalization and effective constrained online control.

bullets: Addresses the limitations of structured-state pipelines and idealized simulator imagery in visual traffic signal control.

Tests cover unseen road topologies, degraded sensing, real surveillance footage, and three weeks of deployment across ten intersections.

papers.abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single model. Existing post-training methods either use understanding as a fixed teacher to improve generation, or rely on ground-truth trajectories to supervise both understanding and generation. Prism instead derives bidirectional supervision from self-generated interleaved rollouts, constructing training targets according to the reliability of their text and image chains. We propose Prism, a bidirectional self-teaching post-training method for UMMs. Like a prism decomposing mixed light, Prism decouples a coupled interleaved trajectory into a text chain and an image chain, assesses the reliability of each chain, and constructs a corresponding training target from their reliability states. Experiments on both SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL show that Prism improves both understanding and generation. On the generation side, GenEval improves from 85.8 to 89.2 (+3.4), and DPG improves from 86.1 to 87.3 (+1.2) on SenseNova-U1. On the understanding side, the total MME score improves from 2282.6 to 2311.6, and MMVP improves from 58.0 to 62.0. Consistent improvements are observed on BAGEL. These results highlight that Prism enables coordinated improvements in generation and understanding by constructing reliability-guided self-training targets from self-generated trajectories, without relying on an external verifier or externally annotated corrected trajectories during target construction.
authors: Peng Zhang, Qian Chen, Xianyin Zhang, Yimin Tian, Ruite Fei, Dongyi Lv, Lifan Guo, Chi Zhang, Shuai Liu

Constructs bidirectional training targets based on the reliability states of the two chains, without external verifiers or corrected annotations.
Improves both generation and understanding on SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL; on SenseNova-U1, GenEval rises from 85.8 to 89.2 and MME from 2282.6 to 2311.6.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models enable dense monocular reconstruction without requiring camera calibration, but independently reconstructed submaps can accumulate scale drift, and even a valid revisit can yield an inconsistent cross-submap measurement. We extend VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with fixed-root scale anchoring and short-sequence-assisted direct loop connections. SALAD selects an image pair between the initial submap and each eligible new submap; joint VGGT inference then uses learned implicit semantic-geometric cues to supply a scale-only anchor while preserving the original overlap chain. For loop closure, neighboring image pairs support a consistency check and translation-scale alignment. Each accepted candidate contributes one robust Sim(3) factor between existing center-frame nodes, without an auxiliary loop submap. A 17-sequence comparison lowers mean Sim(3) ATE on nine TUM sequences from 0.1018 to 0.0451 m relative to the VGGT-SLAM 2.0 baseline. Anchoring improves all seven no-loop module ablations. On three Clio scenes, a fixed-loop comparison favors the direct connection pipeline over the tested auxiliary-submap pipeline. A separate candidate audit exposes additional rejections of visually overlapping pairs by the short-sequence check. These comparisons distinguish the gains from long-range scale anchoring and loop connection choices from the limitations of candidate verification.
authors: Ziyi Jin, Kangjin Yu, Beichen Wang, Can Jiang, Zhongpu Xia, Jie Xu
bullets: Addresses scale drift across independently reconstructed submaps and inconsistent measurements during revisits.
Uses fixed-root scale anchoring: selected cross-submap image pairs provide a scale-only constraint through joint VGGT inference while preserving overlap chains.
Uses neighboring image pairs to verify loop consistency and align translation scale, adding robust Sim(3) factors without an auxiliary loop submap.
On nine TUM sequences, mean Sim(3) ATE decreases from 0.1018 m to 0.0451 m versus VGGT-SLAM 2.0; anchoring helps all seven no-loop ablations.
Candidate verification can reject visually overlapping pairs, indicating a scope or limitation of the short-sequence consistency check.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained action understanding requires vision-language models to ground what an agent does, how it acts, and why it acts in spatio-temporal evidence. However, richer supervision can backfire: fine-tuned models may generate detailed action descriptions grounded in static scenes and salient objects rather than motion, a failure we call Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH). To mitigate EGAH, we propose Staged Attention Rectification and Reinforcement (STARR), an action-centric video-text alignment framework that breaks scene-action shortcuts through Action-Environment Dissociation and reinforces action-focused grounding with an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization. We further construct FineActionR&R, combining temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points over its base model and achieves 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench. Qualitative comparisons further indicate more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.
authors: Zhiliang Zhu, Jiazheng Huang, Dawei Zhao
bullets: Fine-grained vision-language models can hallucinate actions from static scenes and salient objects, termed Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH).
STARR uses Action-Environment Dissociation to break scene-action shortcuts and an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization to reinforce action-focused grounding.
FineActionR&R combines temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data.
Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points and reaches 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench.
Qualitative results suggest more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.

(b) Attention Consistency Reinforcement: GRPO optimizes a reward encouraging stable attention on key action-relevant visual tokens throughout generation.

Figure 1: Illustration of Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination. (a) VLM often generate accurate environment descriptions but incorrect action ones. (b) When environmental information is explicitly described in fine-grained action description tasks, it can easily trigger hallucinated actions unrelated to the actual video content.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D object detection offers a low-cost route to 3D perception, but it remains fundamentally ill-posed, since depth must be inferred from a single view. Recent transformer-based detectors learn geometry purely from image features and 3D box annotations, lacking the high-level semantic priors that vision-language models (VLMs) acquire from large-scale pretraining. VLMs offer such priors, but deploying one directly as a detector is impractical due to its heavy inference cost. We propose MonoLaDN, a language-guided denoising framework that transfers the geometric reasoning of a VLM into a monocular 3D detector while keeping the deployed model purely vision-based. During training, a frozen VLM produces structured reasoning about each object's occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle from the image and its ground-truth boxes. We encode this reasoning into queries, perturb them with noise, and train the detector to reconstruct the clean reasoning. Reconstructing the corrupted reasoning forces the detector's depth-guided features to internalize the VLM's geometric priors, so this knowledge remains available even after the reasoning path is discarded at inference, adding no latency or parameters to the deployed model. Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes show that MonoLaDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detectors and generalizes well to new domains.
authors: Kiet Dang Vu, Cao Le Minh Khoa, Nguyen Viet Tri Pham, An Nguyen Gia, Tam Le Thuc Ho, Duc Dung Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed depth estimation problem in monocular 3D detection.
Uses a frozen VLM during training to reason about object occlusion, depth, dimensions, and angles.
Encodes and noise-perturbs this reasoning, training the detector to reconstruct the clean version and absorb geometric priors.
Discards the reasoning pathway at inference, so the deployed detector remains purely vision-based with no added latency or parameters.
Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art detectors and strong cross-domain generalization.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of MonoLaDN. During training, a 3D Reasoning Generation stage queries a frozen VLM with the image and ground-truth 3D boxes to produce structured reasoning about each object’s occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle. A text encoder and noise injector turn this reasoning into perturbed queries, decoded jointly with the N learnable object queries under a Language-Guided Mask and trained to reconstruct the clean attributes, alongside the detection loss. At inference, the reasoning path is discarded, leaving a purely vision-based detector with no added cost.

Fig. 1: Comparison of paradigms for monocular 3D detection. (a) VLM-based methods carry rich semantic and geometric priors but are too costly for real-time inference. (b) Traditional vision-only detectors are efficient yet lack such priors, learning geometry only from image features and box annotations. (c) Our MonoLaDN injects VLM-derived 3D reasoning into a depth-guided detector during training, so it gains these priors while keeping a vision-only, efficient model at inference.

Fig. 5: Qualitative results on KITTI val set. (a) MonoDETR [45]. (b) MonoDGP [26]. (c) MonoLaDN (Ours). For each image set, the top row presents the camera-view visualization, while the bottom row offers the corresponding bird’s-eye view. Ground-truth bounding boxes are rendered in green, and predictions are shown in order: red, yellow, blue. We also circle some objects to highlight the difference between other state-of-the-art methods and our method.

Fig. 5: Additional qualitative results on KITTI val set. (a) MonoDETR [45]. (b) MonoDGP [26]. (c) MonoLaDN (Ours). Ground-truth bounding boxes are rendered in green, and predictions are shown in order: red, yellow, blue. Fig. 4: Object reconstruction heads. Each attribute output Êa is decoded into the box component it reasons about. The occlusion output Êocc has no box target of its own and is broadcast as shared visibility context (dashed) to the dimension, depth, and angle heads. When a head takes more than one embedding, the inputs are averaged before the head; the 2D center head uses the mean of all four outputs. The reconstructed components are supervised by the same 2D and 3D objectives as the detection loss.

Fig. 3: 3D Reasoning Generation. The object-centric visual input and a geometryto-language mapping are fed to a frozen VLM. The mapping discretizes each attribute into an ordinal label: depth by distance binning, angle by viewpoint sectoring, dimension by shape-archetype matching, and occlusion by combining truncation and occlusion flags. The VLM then produces structured reasoning per attribute.

Fig. 2: Decoder self-attention under the Language-Guided Mask on the KITTI val set. Each row is one scene. The left column shows the image with all projected ground-truth 3D boxes (the target object in orange, others in green) and the generated reasoning for its four attributes. The right column shows the decoder self-attention matrix over the W = 4M + N queries, ordered as the 4M reasoning queries followed by the N = 50 learnable queries; the red lines separate the two groups and the thin gray lines delimit the four-attribute block of each object.

Fig. 1: Deformable cross-attention of the reasoning queries on the KITTI val set. Each row is one object, and the four columns show the occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle reasoning queries. For each query, we accumulate its deformable sampling locations at the final decoder layer, weighted by the corresponding attention weights, into a Gaussian heatmap overlaid on the image (red high, blue low). The target object is marked in green, and the generated reasoning for each attribute is shown beneath its column.

Fig. 3: Designs of the language-guided attention mask. Black entries are blocked and white entries are permitted. The leakage-prevention mask Alp stops the learnable queries from attending to any reasoning query. The separated-reasoning mask Asr lets each reasoning query attend to all reasoning queries of the same object and to those of the same attribute across objects. The attribute-isolated mask Aai is a stricter variant that additionally blocks different attributes of the same object from attending to each other.

Fig. 4: Strategies for forming the perturbed queries. All three start from the ground-truth 3D boxes and end with perturbed queries, but inject noise at different stages. BBox perturbation perturbs the boxes before the VLM, so the reasoning is generated from corrupted geometry. Reasoning perturbation generates clean reasoning and then applies text augmentation to the reasoning text before encoding. Embedding perturbation (ours) encodes the clean reasoning and injects learned noise in the embedding space.

papers.abstract: Adversarial training enables one- and few-step image and video generation, but conventional adversarial losses supervise critic values without directly specifying the gradients used to update the generator. We present NEXTGAN, which trains a scalar critic by regressing its input gradient onto displacements between independently paired reference and generated features at interpolated locations in frozen representation spaces. For a fixed generator, this regression is equivalent to an adversarial objective with a gradient-energy penalty, while the generator retains the standard potential-based GAN update. The same objective adapts pre-trained image and video generators with up to 14B parameters, without auxiliary losses, online teacher scores, or trajectories. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, NEXTGAN achieves one-step FIDs of 2.87 with pixel-space JiT-B and 1.54 with latent-space DiT-XL/1; its adversarial form further reaches 1.36. For text-to-video generation, a single trained Wan2.1-1.3B model supports one-, two-, and four-step sampling, achieving the highest VBench total scores among the compared 1.3B methods at one and two steps. At two steps, NEXTGAN scores 83.13, exceeding rCM and AnyFlow by 1.25 and 0.47 points, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/LINs-lab/NextGAN.git.
authors: Xinhao Lou, Dongye Xie, Peng Sun, Chenyi Zhuang, Kaicheng Yu, Tao Lin
bullets: Addresses the gap between conventional critic-value supervision and the generator gradients it produces.
Regresses critic gradients toward displacements between paired reference and generated features in frozen representation spaces.
Retains standard potential-based GAN updates and adapts generators up to 14B parameters without auxiliary losses, online teacher scores, or trajectories.
Achieves strong one-step ImageNet image-generation FIDs and leading VBench scores among compared 1.3B text-to-video methods at one and two steps.
Supports one-, two-, and four-step sampling with a single trained video model.

papers.abstract: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench
authors: Dohyun Kim, Junyong Lhim, Kwanyong Park
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering multimodal personalized reasoning across 12 sub-tasks and real-world challenges.
Supports interpretable analysis of representative model errors.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.
authors: Yuxi Hu, Wenhao Dong, Jun Zhang, Friedrich Fraundorfer
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed anchor representations and growing multi-view support sequences.
Routes spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers using coverage-cycled evidence routing.
Retains all decoder-facing anchor queries while reducing support-side fusion cost through pre-projection routing and joint context packing.
Achieves up to 26.12× faster cross-view fusion and 1.43× end-to-end acceleration without retraining.
Maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion on long input sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CrossPressor. We keep the original ZPressor [25] pipeline unchanged, including anchor selection, anchor–support grouping, the anchor-query pathway, and the downstream prediction modules. One representative anchor–support group is expanded to compare the fusion stage. The original dense fusion (top) uses all support features as K/V evidence for cross-attention, whereas CrossPressor (bottom) preserves the full anchor-query pathway and routes only the support-side features before K/V projection. For cluster stride sc, the sc × sc grid enumerates the s2c possible spatial sampling offsets. We index the offset assigned to support view v at fusion layer ℓ by pℓc,v = (rc(v) + κℓ) mod s2c , where rc(v) is the support-view rank and κ is the layer-wise increment. Moving across support views advances the sampling pattern by one offset, while moving across fusion layers advances it by κ, distributing the retained spatial evidence across both dimensions. The selected support features are gathered and packed into a compact sequence before the original K/V projection and cross-attention, producing the same updated-anchor interface for the unchanged downstream prediction pipeline.

Figure 1. Representation–fusion mismatch and CrossPressor. ZPressor [25] bounds the decoder-facing representation by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps. As more context views are assigned to these anchors, the dense support features used to construct each anchor continue to grow. CrossPressor keeps the anchor representation unchanged while routing a bounded support sequence across cameras and spatial locations, with spatial sampling offsets varied across fusion layers. Gray tokens denote dense support evidence, while green tokens indicate routed evidence from different support views.

Figure 3. Runtime scaling on MVSplat–ZPressor. As the number of context views increases, dense cross-view fusion becomes progressively more expensive, whereas CrossPressor remains nearly flat. The resulting end-to-end speedup reaches 1.43× at 256 views.

papers.abstract: The performance of large language model (LLM) agents depends on both the underlying model and the harness that governs interaction with tools and the environment. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. We introduce HarnessFlow, a framework for optimizing complete executable harnesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, with the model and task environment held fixed. HarnessFlow organizes candidates and their evaluation histories in a refinement tree, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based policy to balance exploitation and exploration. A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized harnesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incurring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.

bullets: Targets the largely manual design of tool- and environment-interaction harnesses while keeping the model and task environment fixed.
Maintains a refinement tree of candidate harnesses and evaluation histories, balancing exploration and exploitation with MCTS.
A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and reusable mechanisms.
With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, it achieves the highest mean test scores across six agentic, coding, and web-interaction benchmarks.
The optimized harnesses average 69.48%, improving over initial harnesses and Meta-Harness, while costing less per task than hand-engineered baselines.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal remote sensing image retrieval (RS-CMIR) requires representations that are simultaneously modality-invariant and semantically discriminative, despite the profound physical gap between heterogeneous sensors such as Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and multispectral imagery. Recent JEPA-based Predictive self-supervised approaches such as X-JEPA formulate cross-modal alignment as a deterministic latent forecasting task, implicitly assuming uniform patch predictability and leaving cross-modal distributional alignment unaddressed. We propose CAPE-JEPA, a probabilistic cross-modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture with three contributions: (i) a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor outputting per-patch parameters (mu, sigma^2) conditioned on opposite-modality context, trained via negative log-likelihood to model inherent cross-sensor prediction uncertainty; (ii) adversarial distributional regularization combining unimodal isotropic Gaussian regularization with a novel cross-modal adversarial variant that aligns modality distributions via worst-case Epps-Pulley characteristic function tests without explicit sample pairing; and (iii) in-training contrastive learning with attention-pooled heads for scene-level discriminative grounding. Evaluated on BigEarthNet-14K (BEN-14K) and fMoW across SAR, multispectral, and RGB modalities, CAPE-JEPA surpasses X-JEPA by up to 13.74 points on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, outperforming all baselines including SkySense and CROMA across both unimodal and cross-modal directions while using fewer parameters (407.30M vs. 432.72M).
bullets: Targets the modality gap between SAR, multispectral, and RGB imagery while preserving semantic discrimination.
Uses a cross-attentional Gaussian predictor that estimates per-patch mean and variance and is trained with negative log-likelihood.
Applies unimodal and cross-modal adversarial distribution regularization using Epps–Pulley characteristic-function tests without requiring paired samples.
Adds attention-pooled contrastive learning for scene-level grounding.
Evaluated on BEN-14K and fMoW, it reports gains of up to 13.74 points over X-JEPA on BEN-14K and 15.59 points on fMoW, with fewer parameters.

papers.tldr: CAPE-JEPA improves cross-modal remote-sensing image retrieval by modeling prediction uncertainty, aligning sensor distributions adversarially, and learning scene-level contrastive representations.

papers.abstract: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.
bullets: Provides 4B, 9B, and 27B decision models targeting 27 European languages.
Uses low-rank adapters and pointer heads trained on frozen open-weight base models.
On 11 held-out sources spanning 9 task groups and 27 languages, the 27B model achieves 87.5% accuracy with pooled expected calibration error of 0.016.
Calibration differences are driven more by task than language; knowledge tasks are overconfident, while acceptability judgments are underconfident.
Cross-language reach largely follows the base model: languages outside its documented coverage score substantially lower, and Zuse trails Jev and Kev on English public suites.

papers.abstract: Inspired by the coordination of global motion and local shape adaptation in snakes, elephant trunks, and octopus arms, we propose a unified planning and control framework for mobile continuum robots in cluttered and confined environments. Existing approaches often address high-level path planning and local motion control separately, limiting coordinated base-arm motion, kinematic consistency, and collision avoidance. Our framework integrates long-horizon trajectory planning with real-time geometric refinement under kinematic and environmental constraints. The global layer combines A* search with minimum-jerk planning to generate smooth reference trajectories. The local layer uses a geometry-consistent inverse kinematics solver and Riemannian optimization to coordinate mobile-base motion and continuum deformation while avoiding obstacles. We evaluate the framework through simulated pipe-traversal tasks with multiple baseline planners and real-world experiments involving navigation among dense obstacles and manipulation in confined spaces. Results demonstrate improved motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability, supporting coordinated whole-body motion of mobile continuum robots in constrained environments.
authors: Duo Tang, Ping Deng, Sophie Armanini, Yajing Shen, Toshio Fukuda, Cosimo Della Santina, Peng Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitations of separately planned base motion and local arm control, which can cause kinematic inconsistency and poor obstacle avoidance.
Combines A* search with minimum-jerk planning for smooth, long-horizon reference trajectories.
Uses geometry-consistent inverse kinematics and Riemannian optimization for real-time coordination of mobile-base motion and continuum deformation.
Evaluated in simulated pipe traversal and real-world dense-obstacle and confined-space manipulation tasks.
Reports improved motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability compared with multiple baseline planners.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models have often scored below text-only baselines in the BabyLM Challenge (Klerings et al., 2024; Takmaz et al., 2025). We test whether additional recurrent computation helps close this gap. Recurrence increases computation by reusing layers without adding parameters or training data. Using a single implementation, we compare standard and looped Transformers under a 100M-word budget, with three seeds per main condition. Each image is represented by one feature vector from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, used as a prefix token. Caption words count toward the budget, so multimodal training also changes the language data. In a pre-registered text-only comparison, a 12-layer stack repeated four times exceeds a standard 48-layer Transformer by 5.4 BLiMP percentage points at matched inference compute. However, multimodal training lowers BLiMP accuracy by about 3.8 points in both architectures, with no clear mitigation from recurrence. An exploratory loop-side no-image control, trained with the multimodal language data and batching schedule, scores 5.7 points below the text-only baseline. Adding the visual prefix raises accuracy by 1.85 points on average, but this contrast is uncertain with three seeds. These results suggest that changes in language data and its presentation are a major source of the drop. Diagnostic tests show that the models use visual information; its contribution to grammatical generalization remains uncertain under this single-vector interface.
authors: Daichi Hotta, Yohei Kobashi, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo

A matched no-image control suggests that altered language data and batching, rather than visual input alone, drive much of the multimodal drop.
Visual prefixes improve accuracy by 1.85 points on average in the exploratory comparison, but this result is uncertain with three seeds.
Diagnostic tests confirm visual information is used, while its role in grammatical generalization remains unclear with the single-vector interface.

papers.abstract: Ensuring safety in advanced robot control methods such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Reinforcement Learning remains an open challenge. A common approach relies on control-invariant sets, yet their exact computation for nonlinear systems is generally intractable, and numerical approximations compromise theoretical guarantees. In this work, we show that safety does not need to rely exclusively on control invariance. We introduce novel classes of safe sets, each broader than classical control-invariant sets, and analyze corresponding MPC schemes that guarantee recursive feasibility by constraining different nodes of the prediction horizon rather than only the terminal state. Furthermore, when the safe set is an inner approximation of a suitable control-invariant set, our methods can ensure safety through a safe-abort strategy, even in the absence of recursive feasibility. We validate our approaches in extensive simulations on a 6-joint robot manipulator, showing fewer constraint violations than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable tracking performance and computational efficiency. Hardware experiments further demonstrate the practicality of our schemes for real-world robotic applications.
authors: Gianni Lunardi, Elias Fontanari, Matteo Saveriano, Andrea Del Prete
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of computing exact control-invariant sets for nonlinear robots without weakening safety guarantees.
Introduces safe sets broader than classical control-invariant sets and constrains multiple prediction-horizon nodes instead of only the terminal state.
Provides recursive-feasibility guarantees and a safe-abort strategy when recursive feasibility cannot be maintained.

papers.abstract: Object detection research remains constrained by high annotation costs and the closed-set assumptions of supervised models, limiting scalability to novel categories. We present a target-dataset annotation-free object detection framework that eliminates the need for human labeling on the target dataset by leveraging the complementary strengths of pretrained foundation models, including segmentation and vision-language systems, combined with a self-refining training loop. To further reduce reliance on expensive LVLM queries, we introduce a landmark-based clustering mechanism that amortizes labeling across image clusters, improving label consistency while lowering computational cost. Our method autonomously generates segmentation proposals, assigns semantic labels through multimodal reasoning, and iteratively improves both localization and classification using a lightweight open-set detector. This modular pipeline enables adaptation to completely unseen object classes and domains without any human-provided target-dataset annotations, while maintaining compatibility with existing detection architectures. Evaluations on COCO, LVIS, ODinW-35, and Roboflow-100 demonstrate substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art open-vocabulary and long-tail detection methods, achieving 60.8 AP on COCO and 47.4 AP on LVIS under zero-shot settings. Beyond strong benchmark results, our approach provides a scalable foundation for real-world detection systems in unknown environments, where annotation is infeasible.

Reports 60.8 AP on COCO and 47.4 AP on LVIS in zero-shot settings, with evaluations across four benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.

papers.abstract: We present the Rohbau3D-Semantics dataset, which adds dense semantic and instance-level labels to laser scans of the previously released Rohbau3D domain data from shell construction sites. The dataset comprises 504 point cloud scenes from 14 survey sites, each captured with a terrestrial laser scanner and stored in a scanner-centered local coordinate system. Unlike point clouds sampled from reconstructed meshes or synthetic building models, the data preserve the characteristic properties of real laser scanning, including non-uniform sampling, measurement artifacts, reflections, and fine geometric detail. Combined with manual labels, expert oversight during pointwise annotation, and full-scene review, this yields a high-quality benchmark for semantic scene understanding in complex built environments. The dataset includes 17 class labels of building components and one background class, along with instance annotations for object-level analysis. In addition to the 3D point clouds, the release also provides scripts for deriving geometrically aligned panoramic and cube-map representations of color, LiDAR reflection intensity, depth, surface normals, semantic labels, and instance labels from the 3D arrays. We describe the acquisition pipeline, annotation protocol, quality-control process, and panorama-generation procedure, and provide benchmark splits and baseline experiments for semantic segmentation. By combining precise terrestrial laser scans, dense annotations, and a wide variety of shell-construction scenes, Rohbau3D-Semantics bridges the gap among synthetic indoor datasets, mesh-derived benchmarks, and smaller construction-specific resources. The dataset is intended to support research on 3D scene understanding, construction-site analytics, and multimodal scene analysis in the built environment. Access and download the full dataset via https://github.com/RauchLukas/rohbau3d

papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities. Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.
bullets: Targets low-resource Assamese challenges including tokenization inefficiency, unstable generation, and interference from related languages.
Uses an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary, Hybrid LoRA continual pre-training, and supervised fine-tuning on balanced multi-domain data.

Reports a 0.7488 BPB score on FLORES-200, a 96.7% overall RAG score, and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) integrate visual inputs with textual and parametric knowledge, allowing sensitive information to be accessed through cross-modal associations during reasoning. This raises privacy concerns when a visual input should no longer provide access to such information. Machine unlearning can remove this influence without retraining the model from scratch. However, multimodal unlearning methods mainly target samples, concepts, or knowledge content, without separating the knowledge from the cross-modal association through which it is accessed. In reasoning models, target information may disappear from the final answer while remaining in intermediate reasoning, or be replaced by incorrect substitute knowledge. We therefore study cross-modal association unlearning, where the forget target is a designated visual-to-knowledge association: the model should suppress target-bearing behavior under the designated visual context while preserving access to the same knowledge in permitted contexts. We propose Visual-Keyed Counterfactual Rebinding (VKCR), a parameter-efficient framework for cross-modal association editing. VKCR first localizes the edit to a compact association-conditioned parameter subspace. It then reduces support for the designated target at task outputs and counterfactually rebinds the affected reasoning behavior by discouraging target-bearing or unsupported continuations while favoring valid non-sensitive alternatives. We further introduce CLEAR-R and MLLMU-R to evaluate target leakage, hallucinated reassociation, reasoning preservation, and modality-specific utility. Experiments show that VKCR substantially reduces image-conditioned target leakage and hallucinated reassociation, including across heterogeneous task formulations, while preserving non-sensitive visual reasoning and permitted text-only knowledge.
authors: Xinghao Li, Chenchen Tan, Youyang Qu, Shujie Cui, Xingliang Yuan, Cunjian Chen, Chi Liu, Longxiang Gao

Introduces CLEAR-R and MLLMU-R to assess leakage, hallucinated reassociation, reasoning preservation, and modality-specific utility.
Experiments show reduced image-conditioned leakage and hallucinated reassociation while preserving visual reasoning and text-only access to permitted knowledge.

papers.abstract: Existing reasoning segmentation frameworks typically employ multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with broad world knowledge to extract semantics in a human-like manner and generate corresponding segmentation masks. Nevertheless, these frameworks lack the necessary scene-specific awareness. This paper introduces driving scene reasoning segmentation (DSRS), a scene-specific task that requires models to interpret implicit instructions, infer spatial relations, detect potential risks, handle challenging conditions, and comprehend underlying traffic rules, ultimately generating accurate segmentation masks. Meanwhile, we establish a benchmark dataset to facilitate future research on the DSRS task. To pioneer this task, we propose DSRS-Net, a novel architecture with advanced reasoning segmentation capability for automated driving. Specifically, DSRS-Net seamlessly infuses geometric features for deeper reasoning segmentation, without compromising the original multimodal fusion mechanism. This strategy effectively mitigates the modality representation mismatch in MLLMs caused by RGB-only pretraining, while enhancing the integration of geometric, contextual, and linguistic features. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of DSRS-Net in both driving scene reasoning segmentation and other language-driven segmentation tasks across various public datasets. The source code and dataset will be released upon publication.

papers.abstract: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points. NER thus enables partial transfer from text to video, while more reliable grounding will likely require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.
authors: Divyanshu Mishra, Sabine Sternig, Rakshith Shetty, Erhan Gundogdu
bullets: Motivation: avoid costly paired video-text data and precise temporal annotations by training solely on textual video descriptions.

LLM2CLIP transfers better than CLIP, achieving 61.54 vs. 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid.
Nearest Entity Replacement maps each frame to nearby text-entity embeddings, improving mtIoU to 14.45 on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights.
Scope: transfer remains partial, indicating that better-aligned text and visual encoders are needed for reliable grounding.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models. On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.
authors: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Saeid Shokoufa, Seyedarmin Azizi, Arya Fayyazi, Souvik Kundu, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Reducing active experts can weaken refusal behavior even when standard accuracy declines only slightly.
The safety degradation mainly occurs during prompt processing and the first few generated tokens.
SafeStart uses all experts initially, then switches to a reduced expert set via a fused vLLM kernel.
On one RTX A6000, retaining about two-thirds of selected experts yields 15–28% faster offline decoding at batch size 8.
SafeStart retains at least 85% of the speedup and limits harmful-compliance increases to 0.6–2.6 points on held-out requests.

papers.title: SafeStart: Mitigating the Overlooked Safety Cost of Active Expert Reduction in MoE LLM Serving
papers.tldr: SafeStart preserves most of the speed gains from reducing active MoE experts while substantially restoring harmful-request refusal by using all experts during prompt processing and the first eight generated tokens.

papers.abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) can segment objects from text prompts and track them across video, but its memory and computation costs make deployment difficult. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by using fewer bits. However, a quantized model can select the wrong object or lose track of its target across frames. We call this prompt-alignment drift. Controlled tests show that perturbing low-variance feature directions strongly affects target selection. We propose Semantics-Preserving Quantization (SPQ), which gives more calibration weight to concept-sensitive parameters, preserves residual features, and corrects the mean error in video memory. Fixed text concepts guide calibration without task annotations. All three components operate offline and add no inference operators. With a W4A8 image encoder, SPQ improves RefCOCO Pr@0.5 from 42.1 to 72.5 over PTQ4SAM while retaining 54.8 COCO mask AP. Experiments on LVIS, RefCOCO variants, and SA-V show consistent gains. A CLIP study also shows improved image-text retrieval.
authors: Xi Xiao, Yunbei Zhang, Lin Zhao, Janet Wang, Xinru Jiang, Yanshu Li, Chenrui Ma, Pan Wang, Tianyang Wang, Xiao Wang
bullets: PTQ can cause prompt-alignment drift, leading to wrong object selection or lost targets across video frames.
SPQ prioritizes concept-sensitive parameters, preserves residual features, and corrects mean error in video memory.
Fixed text concepts guide offline calibration without task annotations; no additional inference operators are required.
With a W4A8 image encoder, SPQ raises RefCOCO Pr@0.5 from 42.1 to 72.5 over PTQ4SAM while retaining 54.8 COCO mask AP.
Consistent gains are reported on LVIS, RefCOCO variants, SA-V, and CLIP image-text retrieval.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity 3D geometry generation requires maintaining global structural coherence alongside fine-grained surface details. While recent coarse-to-fine frameworks leverage Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to condition local queries, we reveal a critical training-inference resolution discrepancy: coordinate guidance and geometric supervision are aligned during training, whereas inference decodes high-resolution geometry from coarse spatial coordinates. This mismatch introduces a severe distribution shift that degrades fine details. To overcome this, we propose Resolution-Decoupled Training (RDT), which anchors RoPE guidance at 512 resolution while supervising geometry at 1536, enabling robust detail extrapolation. Additionally, to eliminate high-resolution data bottlenecks, we present Dual3D-300K, a large-scale paired dataset comprising 300K watertight 3D point clouds explicitly aligned across 512 and 1536 resolutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RDT substantially improves sharp geometric regions, while Dual3D-300K offers a scalable benchmark for high-resolution 3D generation.
authors: Jiale Zhang, Yang Liu, Chengyang Li, Jin Yuan, Qianxi Jia, Taicheng Huang
bullets: Identifies a training–inference resolution discrepancy that causes distribution shift and loss of fine surface details.
Uses Resolution-Decoupled Training (RDT): RoPE guidance at 512 resolution with geometry supervision at 1536 resolution.
Introduces Dual3D-300K, a paired dataset of 300K watertight point clouds aligned across 512 and 1536 resolutions.
Experiments show improved generation of sharp geometric regions and provide a scalable benchmark for high-resolution 3D generation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed RDT-3D framework. Training (Left): RDT-3D decouples spatial guidance from geometric supervision. Coarse point clouds (5123) provide spatial query locations injected into the DiT via ROPE, while fine point clouds (15363) are encoded into high-resolution GT shape latents for diffusion training. Inference (Right): Spatial queries sampled from a coarse mesh guide the trained DiT to generate fine shape latents, which are subsequently decoded into a high-fidelity 3D mesh via Marching Cubes.
Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison with state-of-the-art methods. Compared to existing approaches, our method captures significantly finer geometric details and produces sharper surface reconstructions.
Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison for ablation study. RDT recovers sharper edges and thinner structures.
Fig. 2: Visual cases in Dual3D-300K. Higher resolution (1536) captures significantly finer geometric details and sharper surfacecompared to the base resolution (512). (Best viewed when zoomed in.)

papers.title: RDT-3D: Resolution-Decoupled Training for High-Fidelity 3D Geometry Generation
papers.tldr: RDT-3D addresses resolution mismatch in coarse-to-fine 3D generation by training coarse spatial guidance with high-resolution geometric supervision.

papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.
authors: Jo\~ao Eduardo Batista, Emil Vatai, Mohamed Wahib
bullets: Targets full-attention layers that remain costly at long contexts in hybrid models.
Combines a recent-token sliding window, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of salient context tokens.
Uses per-layer multi-objective search to select the window size and token budget without changing weights.
Across six models and 21 long-context datasets, configurations preserve baseline accuracy.
Provides up to 2.22× faster decoding at 256k tokens, depending on the model.

papers.abstract: Static and incomplete parametric knowledge limits the performance of multimodal large language models on novel-knowledge and knowledge-intensive tasks, especially those requiring multi-hop evidence acquisition. Existing multimodal agentic search methods often fix visual evidence at the input or a predefined trajectory position, making it difficult for agents to select search modalities as their information needs evolve and to handle complex real-world queries. We define this capability as autonomous cross-modal search: an agent chooses among direct reasoning, text-to-text search, text-to-image search, and reverse-image search, actively introduces visual evidence when appropriate, and switches between and integrates modalities across multiple hops. We propose ModalSearch-Pipeline, a scalable procedure for constructing an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph. It samples paths with diverse depths and modality compositions and uses backward question construction to obscure entity names and image targets that would expose reasoning shortcuts while retaining necessary disambiguating clues, yielding text-only, image-initialized, and arbitrarily interleaved multi-hop problems. We train the ModalSearcher Agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and construct ModalSearch-Bench. Experiments show that ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.

Trains ModalSearcher with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, alongside ModalSearch-Bench.
ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B across five multimodal QA benchmarks, with consistent gains on active visual-search benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Embodied video world models predict scene changes caused by robot actions, yet generated object responses may remain inconsistent with task intent and contact dynamics. Critical responses in embodied scenes often concentrate in local regions and specific time intervals. Inspired by chain-of-thought reasoning, we introduce ReactWorld, an embodied video generation model guided by structured interaction anticipation. In the generation backbone's feature space, an interaction response field predictor anticipates how the interaction will unfold, explicitly describing participant roles, future motion response intensity, and local motion changes. A response feedback adapter forms increments to object features from the difference between the object branch's outputs with predicted and zeroed local dynamics inputs. It also converts predicted displacements into positional biases for temporal attention. These two mechanisms guide object feature updates and information retrieval across frames, respectively. Through interaction anticipation and generative feedback, ReactWorld achieves an average score of 77.51 on RBench, outperforming PhysisForcing by 3.29 points with improvements in all nine categories. On EZS-Bench, it achieves a Domain score of 86.98 and an average score of 81.87.
authors: Hanwei Liu, Huijia Zhang, Hanzhang Wang, Guangyu Liu, Hanbei Zhan, Linjie Hu, Bin Xiao, Xuan Zhou, Dong Zhang

Scores 77.51 on RBench, 3.29 points above PhysisForcing, with gains across all nine categories.
Achieves an 86.98 Domain score and 81.87 average score on EZS-Bench.

papers.abstract: Manipulating visually identical objects with different physical properties requires adapting actions based on information acquired through interaction. We address the problem of learning from demonstrations how to adapt manipulation actions, such as regrasping and changing contact locations, based on physical-property information acquired during interaction. To this end, we propose a learning-from-demonstration method that learns latent representations of physical properties needed to predict object responses and conditions a policy on online estimates of these representations. A dynamics model and object-specific latent representations are jointly learned from demonstrations that include behaviors adapting to the objects' physical properties, and the learned representations are then used to condition an imitation policy. During execution, the dynamics model and policy weights remain fixed, while the latent representation is updated based on the discrepancy between predicted and actual observations, allowing interaction with the object to inform action generation. Real-world and simulation experiments with objects whose centers of mass differ suggest that online adaptation through latent representations of physical properties can improve task success rates. However, in simulation, success rates on center-of-mass locations absent from the demonstrations remained around 30%, indicating limited adaptation to unseen physical properties. Project page: https://isri-aist.github.io/latent-dynamics-project-page/
authors: Kotaro Kajitsuka, Masaki Murooka, Fumio Kanehiro
bullets: Targets visually identical objects whose differing physical properties require actions such as regrasping or changing contact locations.

papers.abstract: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.

Experiments find that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle with scam-versus-advertisement discrimination, while ScamCourt reduces false positives and resists misleading arguments.
The work targets more reliable and interpretable web scam video detection; its scope is defined by the benchmark’s annotated mechanisms and categories.

papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it also introduces a practical risk: the model may spend so much of its output budget reasoning that it never produces usable code. We study this behaviour in relatively small open-weight reasoning models, framing it as reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, we measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls can mitigate overflow. Our results show that the value of reasoning is highly conditional. Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks, but becomes common on harder code-generation benchmarks and for particular model families: on several model--benchmark pairs, more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k-token budget while still reasoning. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Disabling reasoning can therefore be competitive for overflow-prone models, simply because it ensures that an answer is produced. At the same time, reasoning remains valuable for stronger models on harder algorithmic and code-understanding tasks. Finally, prompt steering can substantially reduce overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions provide more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models. These findings suggest that explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation, rather than an always-on capability.
authors: Lukas Twist, Helen Yannakoudakis, Jie M. Zhang
bullets: The study evaluates seven small open-weight reasoning models across six code-generation benchmark settings using a fixed 32k-token output budget.
Reasoning-trace overflow is uncommon on simpler function-level tasks but frequent for some models on harder benchmarks, often involving repetitive loops.
Reasoning provides conditional benefits: disabling it can be competitive for overflow-prone models, while stronger models still benefit on difficult algorithmic and code-understanding tasks.
Prompt steering sometimes reduces overflow, whereas budgeted transitions offer more direct control and can improve performance and token efficiency.
The findings support treating explicit reasoning as a controllable resource rather than an always-on capability.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision models provide strong general-purpose representations, but in Domain-Incremental Learning (DIL), where the input distribution changes sequentially, adapting to new domains often degrades performance on previously learned ones. We observe that forgetting is not uniform across domains and classes and is not explained by training order alone. This motivates us to track each past domain-class concept individually. We use representation drift, defined as the deviation of a past concept's current representation from a fixed anchor, as a measurable surrogate for forgetting risk. The measured drift then serves two complementary roles. A consolidation loss assigns stronger preservation to high-drift pairs, while prototype construction down-weights highly drifted domains to reduce their influence on the class reference. Preservation is thus allocated by measured drift rather than assumed importance. To obtain this signal during training without storing past raw data, we repurpose a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). For each domain-class pair, we store only a compact context summary in the backbone feature space and rerun it through the learned context-to-target relation to measure its drift from the fixed anchor. Across DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50, and CDDB-Hard, our method sustains a strong accuracy-forgetting balance on every benchmark, using substantially less training memory than accuracy-competitive methods and the smallest storage among compared methods.
authors: Hyunmin Kong, Gyutae Oh, Jitae Shin
bullets: Tracks representation drift for each previously seen domain-class concept as a surrogate for forgetting risk.
Uses drift to weight consolidation more heavily for at-risk concepts and down-weight unreliable domains during prototype construction.
Employs a JEPA-based mechanism with compact feature-space context summaries, avoiding storage of past raw data.
Evaluated on DomainNet, Office-Home, CORe50, and CDDB-Hard, with strong accuracy–forgetting balance and low training memory/storage versus compared methods.

papers.abstract: In this study, we focus on service robots that retrieve and transport everyday objects based on free-form instructions that may refer to visual features and scene text. This is challenging because it requires a multimodal understanding of the visual features and spatial relationships of objects, as well as scene text embedded in the environment. To address this, we propose Scene Text-Aware multimodal Retrieval for Everyday objects (STARE), which leverages visual and textual cues in response to free-form instructions. STARE introduces Crosslingual Visual Prompt to enhance scene text interpretation, and models the complex relationships between named entities in the instructions and their corresponding objects. We evaluate STARE using two novel benchmarks, GoGetIt and TextCaps-test, both of which consist of real-world indoor/outdoor images and instructions involving object manipulation and navigation. The results show that STARE outperforms all baseline methods on standard multimodal retrieval metrics. Furthermore, in physical experiments conducted under a zero-shot transfer setting, STARE achieves an overall success rate of 80%. Our project page and code are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

papers.abstract: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, with progress driven largely by scaling model size and omni training data. We ask whether a model needs to hear the audio directly at all, and present SleuthVLM, an agent harness built on a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech will be transcribed into text, and the VLM will sleuth the video on its own without any predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, SleuthVLM achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it also tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8%}; with an open-source 27B VLM, it beats all open-source omni models. We draw three findings: SleuthVLM beats a model that glances; hearing is not the bottleneck, agentic ability is; omni understanding needs better agentic ability, not just more omni data for modality alignment. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding. Omni understanding needs better agents, not just bigger models that hear.
authors: Peiran Wu, Fangfei Gou, Zhaoxi Mu, Changhao Zhang, Jian Liu, Weiqiang Wang, Yuntao Wang, Yuanchun Shi, Junxiao Shen

Achieves 75.0% average accuracy across four omni benchmarks and 77.8% on Video-MME-v2, as reported in the abstract.
With an open-source 27B VLM, outperforms all open-source omni models evaluated.
Concludes that improving agentic reasoning may be more valuable than simply scaling omni data or model size.

papers.abstract: Embodied and edge systems increasingly rely on vision-language models (VLMs) to support heterogeneous skills, yet deploying a separate task adapter for each skill while retaining a high-precision backbone creates substantial memory and management costs. We present UniCompress, a deployment-oriented framework that converts multi-task expertise into one compact, adapter-free model. Starting from a consolidated BF16 Qwen3-VL-4B teacher, UniCompress constructs an asymmetric INT2 student using GPTQ initialization and teacher-guided quantization recovery. The approach jointly quantizes and recovers the projection weights in the vision encoder and language backbone, enabling aggressive compression of the complete vision-language model while preserving its multi-task behavior. We evaluate UniCompress on four heterogeneous embodied tasks: posture recognition, household-safety understanding, multimodal dialogue routing, and mobile-GUI action prediction. UniCompress reduces the approximate weight storage from 8.9 GB in BF16 to 2.1 GB in INT2, corresponding to a reduction of approximately 76%. It improves the INT2 macro task score by 34.3 percentage points over GPTQ-INT2 while remaining within 0.9 points of the consolidated BF16 teacher. These results demonstrate the potential of teacher-guided joint vision-language INT2 recovery for deploying a single multi-skill VLM on resource-constrained embodied platforms.
authors: Mingkang Liu, Peipei Jiao, Weiming Meng, Tianyuan Liu, Lichen Pang, Junyan Li
bullets: Addresses the memory and management overhead of maintaining separate LoRA adapters for heterogeneous embodied skills.

Jointly quantizes and recovers projection weights across the vision encoder and language backbone.
Evaluated on posture recognition, household-safety understanding, multimodal dialogue routing, and mobile-GUI action prediction.
Reduces approximate weight storage from 8.9 GB to 2.1 GB and stays within 0.9 macro-score points of the BF16 teacher, outperforming GPTQ-INT2 by 34.3 points.

papers.abstract: Existing audio-visual segmentation methods mainly predict sound-related regions or category masks and often fail to identify the sounding instance when multiple same-class candidates coexist. Recent audio-visual instance segmentation methods address instance-level prediction but rely largely on motion and cross-frame association, which may become unreliable under sparse observations or inconspicuous motion. To this end, we introduce binaural audio, whose interaural differences encode source-direction information, to provide spatial constraints for distinguishing the sounding instance among same-class visual candidates. We propose Binaural Sounding Instance Disambiguation for Audio-Visual Segmentation (BiSID-AVS), which progressively refines category-level candidate responses into a mask of the true sounding instance. BiSID-AVS first grounds category-consistent candidate regions through audio prompting, then projects binaural cues into an image-plane spatial response map, and finally refines the true sounding instance through dual-level spatial conditioning at the feature and decoder levels. Experiments on the binaurally extended AVS-Synthetic benchmark and Habitat-AVS dataset for robotic indoor perception show that BiSID-AVS achieves the best performance on the multi-candidate subsets, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points, respectively, while substantially reducing false activation on non-sounding same-class regions.
authors: Haoze Ma, Yidi Li, Yu Ma, Pengyuan Zhao, Yi Shi, Bin Ren, Yanwen Guo, Dimitrios Kanoulas
bullets: Targets a key weakness of audio-visual segmentation: confusing which instance is producing the sound.
Uses interaural differences in binaural audio to infer sound-source direction and constrain visual selection.
Progressively refines category-level candidates through audio prompting, image-plane spatial mapping, and dual-level spatial conditioning.
Achieves the best multi-candidate performance on AVS-Synthetic and Habitat-AVS, improving instance-level mIoU by 35.19 and 41.21 percentage points.
Reduces false activation on non-sounding regions of the same class; the method is evaluated particularly for sparse or inconspicuous-motion scenarios.

papers.abstract: While single-image 3D texture generation has advanced significantly, conditioning texture synthesis on multi-view reference images remains largely under-explored, despite its necessity for resolving surface ambiguity in unobserved regions. In this paper, we propose RouTex, a novel multi-reference 3D texture generation framework based on in-context Diffusion Transformers (DiT). Our key insight is that native 3D Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) inherently possesses spatial addressing capabilities. We introduce Positional Routing (PR) to reprogram 3D RoPE along spatial and semantic dimensions, establishing explicit reference-to-view correspondence without introducing additional parameters. To execute this routing efficiently, Dual-Granularity Attention (DGA) combines per-view local attention for fine texture fidelity with global joint attention over deduplicated references for cross-view consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RouTex achieves new state-of-the-art performance in multi-reference 3D texture generation.

bullets: Addresses ambiguity in unseen surfaces that single-image texture generation cannot resolve.

Uses Dual-Granularity Attention: local per-view attention for texture detail and global attention for cross-view consistency.
Experiments show state-of-the-art performance in multi-reference 3D texture generation.
