papers.abstract: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Madina Abdusalomzoda, Nasimjon Rajabov, Akhrorkhon Ikromov, Komron Giyosiev, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
bullets: LoRA adaptation reduced Tajik text loss across 0.6B–8B models, but comprehension gains were absent or unreliable.
On Belebele, 1.7B and 8B adapters were unchanged, the 4B model fell 3.7 points, and the 0.6B increase likely reflected answer-letter bias.
At 8B, continued pretraining on roughly 375M raw Tajik tokens improved Belebele by 9.9 points.
The final e3 model improved Tajik Belebele by 11.4 points over Qwen3-8B, while English MMLU declined by 1.2 points.
The study documents scope and reproducibility issues, including undocumented data branches and an invalid 4-bit release.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models allow users to explore generated environments through camera navigation. Continuous hand motion provides a fine-grained action channel for interacting with the people and objects encountered during exploration. We present Touch\'{e}World, a framework that integrates gesture-driven interaction into a camera-controlled video world model. Given an initial image and a scene-description prompt, the model generates video conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand controls. We construct joint camera--hand training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos through annotation completion, consistency-based filtering, and temporal alignment. Building on a pretrained camera-controlled world model, we combine spatial hand-skeleton conditioning with numerical hand-motion features through parameter-efficient adaptation. Causal adaptation and few-step distillation support chunk-level online generation, allowing users to update their controls based on generated visual feedback. We further introduce Touch\'{e}Bench to evaluate hand-motion following, camera--hand coordination, online interaction, and object response. Together, these components establish a framework for studying continuous exploration and hand-driven interaction within generative worlds.
authors: Jiaao Yu, Yanjian Zhang, Haoyang Jiang, Guillaume Wisniewski, Nadi Tomeh, Shijie Jia
bullets: Addresses the need for fine-grained hand interaction beyond camera-only navigation in video world models.
Generates video from an initial image and scene prompt conditioned on temporally aligned camera and hand motion.
Builds joint training data from heterogeneous egocentric videos using annotation completion, consistency filtering, and temporal alignment.
Adapts a pretrained camera-controlled world model with hand-skeleton and numerical motion features using parameter-efficient methods.
Introduces chunk-level online generation and TouchéBench for evaluating hand following, camera–hand coordination, online interaction, and object response.

papers.abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
authors: Sen Yang, Jiaduo Lin, Zehong Huang, Wen Liu
bullets: Maintains an append-only per-user memory that updates preferences and forgets outdated facts.
Uses a coding agent to propose harness patches from failure traces and a second-model critic to screen them for gaming.

Outperforms reported memory systems on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S across two backbones, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently been extended to handle multiple input images, but this extension dramatically increases the visual token budget, making visual-token pruning not merely an efficiency option but a practical necessity. Existing visual-token pruning methods, primarily designed for the single-image setting, rely on attention-derived saliency signals to estimate per-token importance. However, this attention-centric design transfers poorly to the multi-image regime: it causes substantial performance degradation on multi-image benchmarks, suffers from strong positional bias, and loses discriminative attention signals as the number of input images increases. To test whether attention-selected tokens are truly important for multi-image reasoning, we conduct two complementary causal probes Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion, which measure token importance by restoring individual tokens to a zeroed visual sequence or removing them from the full sequence. Attention-based pruners provide only marginal gains over random selection, showing that attention is a weak proxy for visual-token importance in multi-image reasoning. Motivated by this gap, we propose Relation and Information Aware Pruning (RI-Prune), a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector for multi-image visual token pruning. RI-Prune scores each visual token using a z-normalized combination of three signals computed from projector outputs: query relevance, cross-image correspondence with compact per-image prototypes, and intra image representativeness. By integrating these signals, RI-Prune performs balanced per-image Top-K selection to preserve information across input images. Across multiple multi-image benchmarks and three LVLM backbones, RI-Prune achieves a stronger trade-off between token reduction and task performance than prior pruning methods, particularly under aggressive token budgets.
authors: Dongjin Lee, Eunju Lee, Jinhee Jang, Yoonji Lee, Youngbin Kim
bullets: Multi-image inputs greatly increase visual-token budgets, making pruning necessary for practical LVLM inference.
Attention-based pruning transfers poorly to multi-image reasoning due to positional bias and weakening attention signals as image count grows.
Causal Leave-One-In and Leave-One-Deletion probes show attention-selected tokens are only marginally better than random selections.
RI-Prune is a training-free, attention-free pre-decoder selector using three z-normalized projector-output signals.
Balanced per-image Top-K selection preserves information across images and yields a better token-reduction/task-performance trade-off, especially at aggressive budgets.

(c) CLS-based saliency selects tokens with weaker query alignment than query-driven attention, suggesting that CLS attention is less effective at preserving question-relevant visual evidence.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a novel, training-free visual token pruning method specifically designed for multi-image LVLMs. It addresses the limitations of attention-based pruning in multi-image settings by incorporating cross-image correspondence and intra-image representativeness, directly contributing to efficiency in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: RI-Prune: Relation and Information Aware Visual Token Pruning for Multi-Image Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: RI-Prune improves multi-image LVLM efficiency by selecting visual tokens using relevance, cross-image relations, and within-image representativeness instead of attention alone.

papers.abstract: Underwater spatial reasoning depends on object boundaries and geometric cues that are obscured by scattering, color distortion, and low visibility. Existing underwater resources capture these cues through images, annotations, and depth maps, but provide fragmented supervision for vision-language models. We present a spatial data engine that connects visual appearance with object-level geometry through enhancement, 2D and geometry-assisted question generation, and expert filtering. It produces 4.27M QA pairs across five capability groups. We use this corpus to train USI-Brain and introduce an Underwater Prior-guided Rectifier (UPR) that applies gated corrections to visual features. USI-Bench evaluates the resulting capabilities with 6,525 held-out QA pairs. On its 15 task metrics, USI-Brain and USI-Brain + UPR improve over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct by 5.76 and 7.63 points on average, respectively, using signed differences on 100-point scales. Ablations show that geometry-assisted supervision improves depth and ordering by 4.8 and 6.1 points with UPR disabled, while UPR adds 18.0 points in scene description under matched training data. Both variants use raw images at evaluation. Across NautData, UWBench, and MarineEval, USI-Brain achieves the best or joint-best score on 28 of 32 metrics. Model weights and USI-Bench will be released at https://github.com/SKY-Zhu-91/USI-Brain.
authors: Zhiliang Zhu, Zhiqiang Zhao, Xie'an Jiang, Yingxin Lai, Kangye Zheng, Dawei Zhao
bullets: Underwater scattering, color distortion, and low visibility obscure object boundaries and geometric cues needed for spatial reasoning.
A spatial data engine generates and filters 4.27M QA pairs covering five capability groups, including geometry-assisted supervision.

On USI-Bench, USI-Brain and USI-Brain + UPR improve over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct by 5.76 and 7.63 average points across 15 metrics.
Across three external benchmarks, USI-Brain obtains the best or joint-best result on 28 of 32 metrics; evaluation uses raw images.

papers.abstract: When a language model chooses a number between 1 and 30, every integer in the range is valid, yet the model can favor particular answers. We use numerical choice to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1. After the edit ends, selective cache and attention-output replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs jointly produces similar immediate readout contributions; both interventions restore 17 but have different final log-odds effects on 7 versus 5. Holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs at their values from the edited run without either replacement reduces this effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch. Prompt tests also separate influence from answer changes: one held-out prompt retains influence without switching, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; there, joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap between the two reader effects while the answer remains 17. These results use numerical choice as a controlled case for studying persistent state and conditional downstream processing; they do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.
bullets: Uses choices between 1 and 30 as a controlled setting where every answer is valid.
Combines perturbation probing, gradient attribution, activation edits, and selective cache/attention-output replacements.
In a Qwen3-4B case, an intervention changes the final answer from 17 to 15 even though both runs initially emit 1.
Similar local attention contributions can lead to different final effects because later MLP computation alters their influence.
Results across additional contexts show persistent influence does not always cause an answer switch; the study does not establish the origin or full circuit of numerical preference.

papers.title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
papers.tldr: A causal study of numerical choices shows that answer preferences can persist across tokens and be reshaped by later computation, without identifying a complete underlying circuit.

papers.abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.
bullets: Synthetic training causes knowledge loss across generations, with rare knowledge disappearing first.
A cultural-evolution model predicts retention under mixtures of synthetic and fresh data, from simple language models to pretrained transformers.
As the world changes faster, self-copying lineages require more fresh data; fixed pretrained knowledge is comparatively insulated.
When models influence what people write, fresh-data supply becomes endogenous: greater reliance on model text requires more independent learning.
Plausibility filters worsen collapse, whereas fact-checking and relearning can preserve new information.

papers.selection_reason: Applies cultural evolution theory (Rogers' paradox) to explain and predict model collapse in LLMs, analyzing the endogeneity of training data supply.
papers.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
papers.tldr: Model collapse is a version of Rogers’ paradox: copying model outputs saves effort but erodes rare and current knowledge unless people keep generating and checking fresh information.

papers.abstract: A 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction inherits arbitrary units from structure-from-motion, so it cannot be measured or used to place AR content until someone supplies a scale. Both standard recipes are fragile on real captures: on five indoor scenes with tape-measured ceilings, a quantile floor-to-ceiling heuristic errs by 27% and metric-depth alignment by 35-71% across three networks. We present METRIC-GS, a selective scale estimator for real indoor photographs: it reads the scale off the reconstruction's own semantic content and, just as importantly, refuses when the evidence is thin. A frozen 2D teacher labels Gaussians by visibility-aware voting; instance-level size priors for architectural and furniture classes (doors, tables, the floor-to-ceiling gap) are fused by a robust maximum-likelihood step; and an inlier-mass test turns thin evidence into an explicit abstention that doubles as a router to a heavyweight metric model. On 47 ScanNet++ scenes with laser ground truth, with a configuration frozen before public evaluation, the estimator alone cuts the heuristic's mean error from 21.1% to 16.6% (9.3% on the 28 scenes it acts on) at ~11 s per scene. MASt3R remains the more accurate standalone estimator (9.9%), but routing only our refusals to it matches running it everywhere with 60% fewer invocations; this selective hybrid is the configuration we advocate. Visibility-aware voting raises the scenes the estimator can act on from 16 to 28 at unchanged deployed accuracy. Applied unchanged to 13 phone and drone captures of our own, on which MASt3R fails its own registration gate 12 times, the system improves all five captures it acts on and degrades none. We also report that a current feed-forward metric model scores 2.3% on a benchmark inside its training mixture and 28-35% on captures it has never seen: a published metric-scale number is a best case, not a deployment estimate.
bullets: Addresses the arbitrary scale of structure-from-motion reconstructions, which limits measurement and AR placement.
Uses visibility-aware semantic voting, architectural and furniture size priors, robust maximum-likelihood fusion, and an inlier-mass abstention test.
On 47 ScanNet++ scenes, reduces mean heuristic scale error from 21.1% to 16.6% overall and 9.3% on scenes where it acts, at about 11 seconds per scene.
Routing only abstentions to MASt3R matches running MASt3R everywhere while invoking it 60% less often.
Visibility-aware voting increases actionable scenes from 16 to 28; results also show strong variation in metric-model performance across seen and unseen captures.

papers.selection_reason: Metric-scale estimation for 3D Gaussian splatting is a 3D vision method for recovering real-world geometry from reconstructed scenes.
papers.title: METRIC-GS: Selective Metric-Scale Estimation for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: METRIC-GS estimates metric scale directly from semantic content in 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructions and abstains when evidence is insufficient, enabling efficient routing to a stronger metric model.

papers.abstract: High-content multi-channel imaging, from Cell Painting assays to remote sensing, is central to modern scientific pipelines. Because these channels are highly heterogeneous and experimental configurations frequently evolve, a practical vision backbone must be fundamentally channel-agnostic. Current channel-adaptive vision transformers rely on global self-attention with learnable channel embeddings, which can be computed only for previously known channels. Attempts to overcome this limitation of new channels either discard the embeddings, losing channel identity, or process each channel independently, thereby eliminating critical cross-channel interactions. To address this, we introduce ChanSFormer, an efficient Vision Transformer that replaces rigid embeddings with disentangled spatial-channel attention and individual channel CLS tokens. This architecture natively preserves both distinct channel identities and cross-channel information flow. Furthermore, the individual channel class token design unlocks more informative feature representations for self-supervised learning and enables representation-based channel sampling while remaining channel-agnostic. We evaluate ChanSFormer on two biology multi-channel datasets, CHAMMI, JUMP-CP and a satellite dataset, So2Sat. Experimental results show that ChanSFormer outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 3.93%-4.27% on JUMP-CP in classification accuracy. It also demonstrates exceptional cross-dataset transferability under a self-supervised setting, outperforming previous methods by up to 2.72% in accuracy in the same classification tasks. Furthermore, the disentangled attention reduces the quadratic complexity of channel-by-spatial sequence length of the global attention baseline, thus improving throughput by 55%-313%. Code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-stonybrook/ChanSFormer.
authors: Jingwei Zhang, Srinivasan Sivanandan, Dimitris Samaras
bullets: Addresses the limitation of channel-adaptive transformers that depend on predefined channel embeddings and handle new channels poorly.
Uses disentangled spatial-channel attention with individual channel CLS tokens to retain channel identities and enable cross-channel information flow.
Supports more informative self-supervised representations and representation-based channel sampling.
Evaluated on CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat; on JUMP-CP, it improves classification accuracy by 3.93–4.27% over state-of-the-art methods and improves cross-dataset transfer by up to 2.72%.
Reduces attention complexity and improves throughput by 55–313% compared with global attention baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Disentangled spatial-channel attention replaces expensive global self-attention over channel-by-spatial tokens, improving throughput and reducing attention complexity.
papers.title: ChanSFormer: A Channel Agnostic Vision Transformer for Multi-Channel Cell Painting Images
papers.tldr: ChanSFormer is a channel-agnostic vision transformer that preserves channel identity and cross-channel interactions while improving accuracy, transferability, and computational efficiency.

papers.abstract: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.
authors: Varun A. Paturkar, Shankar Gangisetty, C. V. Jawahar
bullets: Contains 949 maneuver clips and trajectory annotations for more than 31,000 agents, including over 16,000 motorized two-wheelers.
Supports Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP), with challenge-aware annotations for ego-motion, weak structure, and occlusion.
Video backbones achieve most of their full-observation accuracy early, while zero-shot VLMs generally remain near simple baselines.
LoRA adaptation substantially improves maneuver anticipation but does not close the gap with conventional models for trajectory prediction.
Forecasting is hardest during left turns and under dynamic ego-motion across all evaluated models.

papers.title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic

papers.abstract: Hundreds of languages have written text but almost no translations, and whether a model learning one from untranslated text builds on a related language or familiar letters is unclear: they usually coincide. Here we show that familiar letters, not a related language, let an unseen language into a shared space of meaning. GlyphMind, a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels and lets any sentence be shown in any script, was pretrained to align translations across 27 writing systems. Adapted on untranslated Lao, a language and script it had never seen, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline. Rewritten in unfamiliar letters, Lao did not enter although its close relative Thai was in pretraining; Santali, which had none, entered in Devanagari, familiar from Hindi, but not in its own script. Transliteration into familiar scripts may thus open multilingual models to languages without translations.
authors: Yuliang Liu, Xinyu Wang, Xiang Bai
bullets: GlyphMind is a tokenizer-free vision transformer that reads text as pixels and aligns translations across 27 writing systems.
When adapted using untranslated Lao, it retrieved English translations seven times as often as the strongest simple baseline.
Lao entered the shared meaning space in familiar letters but not unfamiliar ones, even when related Thai was pretrained.
Santali entered when written in familiar Devanagari but not in its own script.
Transliteration into known scripts may expand multilingual models to languages with little or no translation data.

In training, translations are pulled together and masked spans are predicted. b, The shared space, drawn schematically. Each dot is a sentence, and translations lie close together. The cube shows a small part of the space. The lens enlarges the cluster for the first sentence of Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. c, Lao letters resemble the Thai letters seen in training. papers.tldr: Familiar writing systems, rather than linguistic relatedness, help multilingual models understand previously unseen languages.

papers.abstract: Federated Prompt Learning (FPL) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of pre-trained Vision-Language Models across decentralized clients without exchanging raw data. To cope with cross-client heterogeneity, existing FPL methods typically pair a globally shared prompt with a client-specific local prompt. However, this design personalizes only at the client level: the same local prompt is applied to all samples of a client, and the global and local prompts are combined in an input-agnostic, fixed manner. Consequently, it overlooks the substantial visual variations among samples within the same client and cannot adjust the balance between shared and personalized knowledge to each input. To address these limitations, we propose Federated Prompt Learning with Instance-Aware Cross-Modal Representations (FedIA), an FPL framework that learns instance-aware cross-modal representations. Specifically, FedIA first uses global text prompts as client-invariant semantic anchors to select image patches most relevant to each candidate class, suppressing distracting regions. The selected visual evidence then conditions the generation of instance-aware local text representations. Finally, an adaptive global-local fusion module calibrates the contributions of local and global text representations for each image-class pair. In this way, FedIA shifts personalization in FPL from the client level to the instance level while preserving the semantic knowledge shared across clients. Extensive experiments under domain shift, pathological label skew, and Dirichlet-based label skew show that FedIA outperforms FPL baselines, with maximum accuracy gains of 1.44\%-4.37\% over the latest baseline across the three settings. Ablation studies and analyses further verify the complementary contributions of instance-aware representation generation and adaptive global-local fusion.
authors: Xuanjing Zhang, Qi Guo, Yanan Qiao, Yong Han, Junge Bo
bullets: Addresses within-client visual variation and the limitations of fixed global–local prompt combinations.
Uses global text prompts as semantic anchors to select class-relevant image patches while suppressing distractions.
Generates instance-aware local text representations conditioned on the selected visual evidence.
Adaptively balances global and local representations for each image–class pair.
Outperforms the latest FPL baseline by 1.44–4.37% across domain shift and two label-skew settings; ablations support both proposed components.

papers.abstract: Video editors often work with large collections of fragmented footage and must select and organize relevant clips into a coherent story. However, many existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and aim to preserve its original narrative and temporal structure. In this paper, we introduce Clips2Story, a training-free, LLM-based pipeline that enables users to create keyword-specified short videos from a pool of video clips. Given a pool of clips and a user-specified keyword, we first extract text-based multimodal descriptors for each clip and retrieve the clips most relevant to the keyword. We then provide the textual descriptors of these candidate clips to an LLM, which selects and arranges them into an editable storyboard with connective narrations. Finally, we assemble the selected clips and retrieve accompanying visuals for the narrations to compose the output video. To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.
authors: Junnuo Wang, Weihan Xu, Hao-Wen Dong

On a synthetic dataset spanning 100 videos and five genres, human evaluation found improved narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and realism over a strong baseline.

papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.
authors: Xiangdong Zhang, Xiaohan Qin, Sunan Zou, Tuo Dai, Bizhao Shi, Zhuo Xia, Yebin Yang, Yizhou Chen, Yuliang Liu, Yu Cheng, Junchi Yan

papers.abstract: Manipulating diverse objects with multi-fingered dexterous hands is challenging due to the high dimensionality and complex dynamics. Human-Object Interaction (HOI) datasets provide rich knowledge about task information and embodied interactions. Instead of solely imitating the human demonstrations, our method learns to holistically predict future hand-object states by leveraging these datasets. The predicted future states of the object can serve as a general-purpose reward term for reinforcement learning, reducing reliance on task-specific reward engineering and enhancing generalization across tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on three manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world. Our approach outperforms existing SOTA methods in both success rate and generalizability on novel objects. Furthermore, we validate the cross-embodiment compatibility of our methods by successfully deploying the skills on different robot hands.
bullets: Addresses the high-dimensional, complex dynamics of multi-fingered manipulation of diverse objects.
Predicts future hand–object states holistically rather than directly imitating human demonstrations.

Evaluated across three simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, including novel objects.

papers.abstract: For decades, diagnostic pathology has relied on thin two-dimensional (2D) tissue sections, despite biological tissues exhibiting inherently three-dimensional (3D) morphological organization. Because a single section captures only one focal plane, important morphological cues along the z-axis are inevitably discarded, limiting tissue representation for both human interpretation and computational analysis. In this work, we propose a generative framework that learns z-axis morphological priors from pathology z-stack data, offering a cost-effective alternative to dedicated volumetric imaging, and transfers this knowledge to conventional single-plane histopathology. Specifically, an image-to-video (I2V) latent diffusion model (LDM) is trained to synthesize a pseudo z-stack from a single 2D image, capturing plausible morphological variations across adjacent focal planes rather than reconstructing physical tissue volumes. To enable deployment on large-scale clinical datasets without native z-stack acquisition, we further introduce a prior-preserving mixture fine-tuning strategy that adapts the model to new domains while retaining the learned z-axis morphological prior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the synthesized pseudo z-stacks exhibit realistic cross-plane morphological continuity and consistently improve downstream prostate cancer classification compared with conventional 2D representations. Our results suggest that learning transferable z-axis priors from limited z-stack data provides a practical way to enrich routine pathology images with complementary morphological information. authors: Jiamu Wang, Keunho Byeon, Ji-Uk Kim, Jin Tae Kwak, Heounjeong Go

papers.abstract: Graphs play an increasingly important role in large language model (LLM) systems, supporting structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, and memory. As these systems evolve toward the agentic era, graphs also organize execution dependencies and multi-agent communication, linking intermediate observations and retained information to subsequent decisions. However, understanding their contribution requires distinguishing the function of each graph operation, the component responsible for its computation, and the subsequent use of its output. This survey introduces an operation-level role--locus taxonomy for reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. We compare how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery. These comparisons distinguish improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance while retaining the conditions under which results were reported. We then organize benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework. Finally, we identify open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery. The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages.
authors: Haihui Liu, Yang Chen, Zice Qiu, Yun Zhang, Jialun Zhong, Wenhua Wang, Yanzeng Li, Tian Wang
bullets: Graphs increasingly connect observations, retained information, execution dependencies, and agent communications in LLM systems.
The operation-level role–locus taxonomy distinguishes what each graph operation does, which component computes it, and how its output is used.
The survey compares graph observations and external computations, memory updates, and dependency-based execution and information delivery.
Its evaluation framework covers benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs while separating local metric gains from downstream task performance.
Open challenges include adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery.

papers.abstract: Integrating six-axis tactile feedback into robotic interfaces requires compact sensors with accurate load measurement and rapid online reconstruction. This paper presents LumiTac, a low-profile, camera-free optoelectronic tactile sensor combining spatially distributed illumination with spectral encoding. Five photoemitters and five RGBW photoreceivers are mounted on opposing circuit boards coupled through translucent silicone. Load-induced interlayer motion modulates the internal light field under compression, shear, bending, and torsion. The sensing head measures 12 mm in diameter and 4.75 mm in thickness, weighs less than 2 g, and has a component cost of approximately USD 7. A compact multilayer perceptron reconstructs three force and three moment components from 20 optical channels. Independent testing yielded coefficients of determination (R-squared) of 0.9657-0.9941, with mean absolute errors of 0.054-0.190 N for forces and 0.304-1.419 mN m for moments. Online prediction achieved an average update rate of 303.57 Hz and a median software processing latency of 0.722 ms. Experiments involving combined loading, light weights, and rapid tapping evaluated load tracking, sensitivity to small forces, and transient response, respectively. Robotic demonstrations further validated its applicability to tactile-guided manipulation and physical human-robot interaction. This study paves the way for compact, high-rate optical tactile sensing in robotic manipulation and human-robot interaction.
authors: Hao Wu, Haotian Guo, Yu Feng, Yutong Wang, Jianshu Zhou

papers.abstract: Off-policy deep reinforcement learning trains on random samples from a replay buffer of past experience. In physical robot settings, that buffer is dominated by routine: thousands of near-identical transitions from normal operation, while the rare events that define the edges of the task are rarely sampled. We propose scoring every stored transition by its statistical leverage, which measures how unusual it is relative to the buffer's own data, computed from the stored numbers alone, with no labels, rewards, or value network. We draw each mini-batch from a mixture of this score and uniform sampling. First, the natural way to build the score along the directions where the data varies most turns out to be blind when actions are stored as one-hot indicators, because indicator columns always win the variance ranking; we instead select the feature columns with the heaviest tails (largest kurtosis) where small far-away populations are revealed. Second, the importance weights that prioritized replay uses to keep gradients unbiased cancel the method exactly: with full correction, training matches uniform sampling, so we drop the correction and deliberately optimize the rebalanced objective. Third, when the rare situations of a log are relational, visible only in how a stretch of behavior relates to its goal, not in any single stored coordinate-per-transition scores are blind; applying the same tail rule to short trajectory windows described relative to their goal restores the signal, and on a three-joint arm that must push an object around an obstacle it raises the rare-task success from 0.49 to 0.69 against a labeled-oracle ceiling of 0.74.
bullets: Addresses replay-buffer imbalance, where routine transitions overwhelm rare edge cases in off-policy robot learning.
Scores transitions without labels, rewards, or a value network, mixing leverage-based sampling with uniform sampling.
Uses kurtosis to select heavy-tailed features because variance-based selection is misled by one-hot action indicators.
Omits importance-weight correction because full correction cancels the prioritization effect and recovers uniform training.
For relationally defined rare events, applies the same approach to goal-relative short trajectory windows; success reaches 0.69 versus a 0.74 labeled-oracle ceiling.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($\Delta H$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.
bullets: Targets MoE expert parameters, which dominate the memory footprint of multimodal large language models.
Separates expert importance for vision and language in a single forward pass using redistribution-aware output change and low-attention vision tokens.
Uses text-side importance for preservation, vision-side importance for pruning, and globally ranks experts across layers.
Across three MoE-MLLMs, outperforms modality-agnostic pruning on most multimodal benchmarks and remains competitive on text-only tasks.
Reduces the BF16 expert footprint by about 27 GB, enabling an approximately 58 GB model to fit on one 40 GB GPU.

papers.selection_reason: Modality-aware expert pruning for MoE-based multimodal LLMs, reducing memory footprint and fitting both efficient AI and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: MAEP is a training-free, modality-aware expert-pruning method that substantially reduces MoE-MLLM memory while preserving multimodal and text performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by denoising multiple draft tokens in parallel. Their training uses anchor sampling to construct compact draft queries and performs cross-attention with a block-sparse mask over a much longer context. We empirically show that acceptance length remains stable as context scales with a fixed query budget, while increasing the query budget yields diminishing quality gains, jointly establishing a practical regime with queries far shorter than the context. No existing context parallelism (CP) method jointly exploits this query--context asymmetry and meets the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement created by anchor sampling. We present Split-KV, an exact CP method that keeps key/value shards local and limits per-layer attention communication to query-sized tensors, making this communication independent of context length. Its global query view further enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost. At a CP size of 64, Split-KV retains 85--91\% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to $3.67\times$ speedup over the fastest available CP baseline. LPT achieves $<$1\% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/zxgx/verl.
authors: Geng Zhang, Fangzhao Zhang, Cong Xie, Tiantian Fan, Yang You
bullets: Diffusion drafters use compact draft queries to attend over much longer, block-sparse contexts.
Split-KV keeps key/value shards local and communicates only query-sized tensors, making attention communication independent of context length.
A global query view enables longest-processing-time-first scheduling to balance sample-dependent attention costs.
At context-parallel size 64, Split-KV achieves 85–91% weak-scaling efficiency and up to 3.67× speedup over the fastest baseline.
LPT reduces load imbalance to below 1% and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best compared balancer.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models allocate test-time compute across distinct behaviors such as planning, deriving, and verifying. However, models frequently "overthink," continuing to verify and re-derive long after finding a correct answer. This wastes expensive compute and can even degrade performance. Existing interventions, such as token budgets or steering, primarily regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors. In this work, we demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers provide a natural, training-free interface for behavioral control. We first split reasoning traces into sentence-level segments and label each with one of six reasoning behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, and conclusion), so that every token carries the behavior of its segment. Linear probes on router logits predict this label nearly as well as probes on the residual stream, the model's full hidden state and the standard target for probing, while using about half as many features. These signals generalize: experts associated with a reasoning behavior on one dataset predict the same behavior on the others, across six datasets spanning five domains (math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense). Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.
authors: Shengjie Wang, Mohsen Fayyaz, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Problem: Reasoning models may continue planning, deriving, or verifying after reaching a correct answer, wasting compute and sometimes degrading performance.
Method: Label sentence-level reasoning segments with six behaviors, probe MoE router logits for these behaviors, and selectively edit expert scores during inference.
Routers predict reasoning behavior nearly as well as full residual representations while using about half as many features.
Behavior-associated experts generalize across six datasets and five domains, suggesting routing captures reusable reasoning states.
Across four models and four benchmarks, router editing cuts generated tokens by a median of 30.4%—up to 63.3%—with accuracy decreases no larger than 0.5 percentage points and occasional improvements.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates few-step video diffusion transformers by computing a few key blocks exactly and compensating for the rest. However, existing sparse attention still faces key challenges, including identification overhead from finding critical blocks at every denoising step, suboptimal budget allocation that sets sparsity budgets uniformly or by local metrics, and cross-step error accumulation as reused masks or clusters go stale. Observing that the errors left on skipped blocks cancel each other once every key is compensated, we propose DecoupAttn, a new paradigm of decoupled sparse attention: semantic clusters compensate every key, and exact attention corrects their error on a few blocks fixed once offline by position. To support this paradigm, we introduce Distortion Budget, a rate-distortion objective for budget allocation that places exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads where it removes the most distortion that compensation leaves in the final latent. Built on this budget, we further propose Reassign Cache, in which each step reassigns the drifting keys to cached centroids and refreshes compensation while the budgeted blocks stay fixed. Moreover, DecoupAttn is training-free: a few calibration clips compile one plan offline, and inference runs standard block-sparse kernels with one fused compensation kernel. Our code will be released after submission.
authors: Yanjin Li, Bingbing Qiu, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanfeng Li, Jian Wang, Xiaoying Tang, Mingda Zhang
bullets: Targets identification overhead, poor uniform/local budget allocation, and stale masks or clusters in sparse video diffusion attention.
Uses semantic clusters to compensate skipped keys and exact attention on a small set of offline-fixed blocks to correct residual error.
Introduces Distortion Budget to allocate exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads based on its effect on final-latent distortion.
Uses Reassign Cache to update drifting key-to-centroid assignments and refresh compensation at each denoising step.
Compiles the plan from a few calibration clips and performs inference with block-sparse kernels plus one fused compensation kernel; no training is required.

papers.abstract: As sequence lengths continue to grow, distributed attention based on sequence parallel (e.g., Ring-Attention) has become a mainstream solution for large language models (LLMs). Nevertheless, inherent communication dependencies limit computation-communication overlap, reducing GPU utilization. Moreover, in cross-hardware (NUMA or node) architectures, due to imbalanced communication bandwidth, frequent communication synchronization will limit overall performance. Based on these insights, we propose CHARM+, Cross-Hardware Attention with Re-Merge Multistream Mechanism. We reorganize sequential communications into several levels and achieve intra-level parallelism and computation overlap. Furthermore, we decouple cross-hardware communication from intra-hardware communication, eliminating synchronization overhead caused by bandwidth imbalance. Forward and backward algorithms were evaluated on multiple hardware architectures and consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods. Compared to Ring-Attention, our forward and backward algorithms achieve average speedups of 1.3x and 1.7x on a dual-NUMA PCIe architecture, and 2.8x and 2.9x on a dual-node NVLink architecture, respectively.
authors: Xinhang Zhang, Boning Zhang, Chengchun Liu, Chunpu Li, Lei Sun, Weifeng Zhang, Limin Xiao
bullets: Targets poor GPU utilization from communication dependencies in sequence-parallel attention, especially under cross-hardware bandwidth imbalance.
Uses hierarchical sequential communication to enable intra-level parallelism and overlap communication with computation.
Decouples cross-hardware and intra-hardware communication to remove synchronization overhead caused by unequal bandwidth.
Evaluated forward and backward attention across multiple hardware architectures, outperforming prior methods.
Against Ring-Attention, reports 1.3×/1.7× average forward/backward speedups on dual-NUMA PCIe and 2.8×/2.9× on dual-node NVLink.

papers.abstract: KV cache eviction is not merely a token-ranking problem: the workspace retained for generating eviction queries also determines the quality of those queries. Consequently, an early workspace error can distort later query observations and reinforce an incorrect final eviction decision, particularly when evidence is dispersed across a long context. We present EchoKV, which discovers and addresses this failure mode with iterative correction. It initializes a feedback-compatible bootstrap workspace using proposals at future decode positions, then uses early decode-generated queries to recover the workspace before the remaining lookahead steps. It uses the same number of workspace forward passes as LAQ while adding a tensor re-scoring operation for workspace repair. On LongBench (16 tasks, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), EchoKV shows notable improvements over LAQ on several tasks requiring dispersed evidence, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long single-document comprehension. Across budgets and backbones, EchoKV selectively improves evidence-intensive tasks while maintaining comparable performance on the remaining LongBench subsets. These results identify query--workspace coupling as a practical failure mode of query-driven KV eviction.
bullets: Problem: Early workspace errors can corrupt later queries and reinforce incorrect eviction decisions.
Method: Bootstrap a feedback-compatible workspace, use early decode queries to recover it, then continue lookahead-based eviction.
Efficiency: Matches LAQ’s number of workspace forward passes and adds tensor re-scoring for workspace repair.
Results: Improves several LongBench evidence-intensive tasks, including multi-hop cross-document QA and long-document comprehension, across budgets and two model backbones.
Scope: Gains are selective, while performance remains comparable on other LongBench subsets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EchoKV overview. papers.title: EchoKV: Self-Corrective KV Cache Eviction via Iterative Query Feedback

papers.abstract: An ordered sequence of end-effector poses can give a redundant robot arm multiple valid joint configurations at each waypoint. Inverse kinematics (IK) computes these configurations. Choosing a configuration only for the next waypoint can leave the arm poorly placed for later waypoints. This may increase planned motion time or cause a later planning failure. This paper presents Future-Window Inverse Kinematics (FWIK), an online method that selects IK solutions by considering a small window of future waypoints. FWIK generates several IK candidates, connects them in a layered joint-space graph, and ranks candidate paths with a simple motion-time estimate. A learned model removes paths whose transitions are likely to cause self-collision. A standard MoveIt 2 planner then checks the next-waypoint IK goals from the remaining paths in ranked order, and the first goal that yields a valid trajectory is selected for execution. We evaluate FWIK in simulation on two 7-DoF manipulators, the Franka Emika Panda and the KUKA LBR iiwa. Each method-planner setting contains five repetitions of 100 sequences with 50 waypoints. Across Pilz, RRT-Connect, CHOMP, and STOMP, FWIK completes 96.8-100% of sequences and gives the shortest planned trajectory duration in all eight robot-planner settings. Its mean duration is 12.8-13.1% lower than STAMPEDE, 22.5-25.6% lower than IKLink, and 27.5-37.2% lower than retry-based TRAC-IK. The results show that a small future window can improve sequence completion and reduce planned motion time while leaving final trajectory validation to the motion planner.
authors: Jinglan Cao, Guohui Zhong, Chengwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses failures and inefficient motions caused by choosing IK solutions greedily for only the next waypoint.
Builds a layered joint-space graph of candidate IK solutions and ranks paths using estimated motion time.
Uses a learned model to filter likely self-collision transitions, then validates candidate next-waypoint goals with MoveIt 2.
In simulation on Panda and KUKA LBR iiwa arms, FWIK completed 96.8–100% of sequences and achieved the shortest planned duration across eight robot-planner settings.
Reported mean durations were 12.8–13.1% lower than STAMPEDE, 22.5–25.6% lower than IKLink, and 27.5–37.2% lower than retry-based TRAC-IK.

papers.abstract: Recycling a target model's own predictions offers a training-free source of proposals for speculative decoding. In vision-language models, however, existing recycling indexes predictions by the last token alone, conflating predictions computed under different images and prefixes; we find that such reuse fails most often at image-sensitive decoding states. Longer keys reduce this aliasing but match fewer states. We introduce \method, which stores target predictions under one-, two-, and three-token keys: contextual memories live only for the current request and are thus implicitly conditioned on its image, while token-level memory persists across requests to retain coverage. At each lookup, entropy-confidence weighting fuses the retrieved predictions according to their key specificity and concentration. Best-first search composes the fused transitions into a candidate tree, supplemented by suffix-matched continuations, and one target pass verifies the tree under greedy decoding. Without training or an auxiliary draft model, \method\ achieves mean speedups over autoregressive decoding of $1.66\speed$ and $1.56\speed$ across seven single-turn benchmarks on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-7B, exceeding the strongest training-free baseline, Token Recycling ($1.51\speed$ and $1.37\speed$). Our implementation is available in https://github.com/Senmo996/RECAP-official-code.
authors: Hengjie Zhu, Dayan Wu, Xinze Liu, Peng Fu, Zheng Lin, Weiping Wang
bullets: Addresses prediction reuse errors caused by indexing only the last token, especially at image-sensitive states.
Combines request-local one-, two-, and three-token memories with persistent token-level memory to balance specificity and coverage.
Uses entropy-confidence weighting, best-first candidate-tree construction, suffix continuations, and one target pass for greedy verification.
Reports mean speedups of 1.66× on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 1.56× on LLaVA-1.6-7B across seven single-turn benchmarks.
Outperforms the cited Token Recycling baseline, which achieves 1.51× and 1.37× respectively; results are scoped to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Identity-preserving video generation aims to synthesize high-quality and visually realistic videos from textual and visual conditions while faithfully maintaining the subject's identity across diverse motions. Prior methods have extensively introduced reference-guided control signals and identity-aware conditioning to improve facial alignment from reference images. However, improving static identity alignment alone creates a fundamental tension between identity fidelity and temporal controllability, which frequently causes identity drift or motion suppression under large pose variations and multi-segment sequential actions. To address this, we propose Chronos, a framework that unifies single-segment facial identity preservation and multi-segment sequential action generation under a common temporal formulation. Specifically, Chronos integrates Semantic Prompt Anchoring to adaptively refine the user prompt, Visual Frame Anchoring to transform conditions into visually grounded keyframe anchors for visual guidance, and Metric-Guided Candidate Routing to select the highest-quality videos from heterogeneous generators via multi-dimensional evaluation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our approach, which achieved first place in both Track 1 and Track 2 of the ACM MM 2026 Identity-Preserving Video Generation Challenge, demonstrating its effectiveness across both facial identity preservation and sequential action generation settings.
authors: Mengqi Huang, Wenchuan Wang, Zhendong Mao, Yijing Tu, Zhike Liu, Luoni Wang, Ning Tong, Xiaoxiao Sheng, Tianyu Huang, Xuecheng Qi, Yongdong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the conflict between strong identity fidelity and controllable motion, which can cause identity drift or motion suppression.
Unifies single-segment facial identity preservation with multi-segment sequential action generation in a common temporal framework.
Uses Semantic Prompt Anchoring to refine prompts and Visual Frame Anchoring to create visually grounded keyframe guidance.
Applies Metric-Guided Candidate Routing to select high-quality videos from heterogeneous generators.
Won first place in both tracks of the ACM MM 2026 Identity-Preserving Video Generation Challenge.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Our framework of Chronos. Given reference images, a raw prompt, and optional temporal captions, the pipeline first performs Semantic Prompt Anchoring, then generates frame anchors through Visual Frame Anchoring, where Track 1 uses a single anchor 𝐴1, and Track 2 may use additional segment-level anchors {𝐴𝑡 }𝑇𝑡=2. The enhanced prompt and anchors are passed to track-specific video generators, followed by metric-guided evaluation and automatic routing to obtain the final video.

Figure 3: Visualization results of different methods on Track 1 (left) and Track 2 (right). For Track 1, while Stand-In and IPT2V generate actions corresponding to the prompt, they suffer from low identity consistency; conversely, RefAlign and Phantom maintain better identity consistency but fail to perform the prompt-specified action (e.g., placing a golf ball). In contrast, Chronos achieves high identity fidelity while accurately executing the correspondingmotion. For Track 2,Chronos demonstrates robust responsiveness to sequential actions and achieves superior temporal and multi-reference identity consistency.

Table 2: Quantitative comparison of Different Methods on Track 1 and Track 2. Chronos achieves the highest Total Score in both Track 1 and Track 2, demonstrating its superior overall performance. The best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 3: Quantitative ablation studies on each component on Track 1 and Track 2. Chronos achieves the highest Total Score in both tracks, validating the individual and synergistic contributions of each module toward improving overall video quality.

papers.selection_reason: Identity-preserving sequential video generation with temporal anchoring, relevant to video generation broadly.
papers.title: Chronos: Sequential Identity-Preserving Video Generation by Temporal Anchoring
papers.tldr: Chronos preserves subject identity during realistic video generation while enabling large-pose, multi-segment sequential actions through temporal anchoring and quality-based candidate selection.

papers.abstract: Humans can easily recognize the same objects across different viewpoints of a 3D scene, whereas teaching models such multi-view-consistent perception typically requires videos or calibrated multi-view captures, which are considerably more expensive and less diverse than large-scale monocular data.~In this paper, we introduce Feature Puzzles, a novel framework for learning multi-view-consistent segmentation using only single-image semantic segmentation supervision. Specifically, we propose a simple yet effective pipeline that constructs multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations. We further introduce a lightweight, plug-and-play network that leverages the multi-view-consistent image features learned by existing pretrained 3D foundation models and the generated pseudo-labels to perform multi-view-consistent segmentation. Importantly, our flexible framework supports various types of prompts provided from one or multiple views and can be readily extended to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Under this single-image supervision, our feed-forward model achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++ against baselines using per-scene optimization or in-domain multi-view training, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Visual comparisons are available on our project page: https://featurepuzzles.github.io/
authors: Jiahao Ma, Qiang Zhang, Miaomiao Liu, David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Chuong Nguyen
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited diversity of video or calibrated multi-view supervision.
Builds multi-view-consistent segmentation pseudo-labels through image cropping and geometric transformations.
Adds a lightweight, plug-and-play feed-forward network using pretrained 3D foundation-model features.
Supports prompts from one or multiple views and can extend to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.
Achieves the best mIoU on NVOS, remains competitive on SPIn-NeRF and ScanNet++, and transfers zero-shot to open-vocabulary 3D segmentation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Feature Puzzles network architecture. A shared Image Encoder + Aggregator produce tokens feeding three decoders: Geometry (poses, 3D points), prompt-conditioned Mask (mask/point/box → masks), and Feature (⊕ text-prompt → open-vocab masks). Mask and feature decoders share cross-view attention and a weighted pixel decoder.

Figure 2: Feature Puzzles pipeline. From a single RGB(-D) parent image (A), we sample overlapping crops as a puzzle (B), optionally calibrate their cameras and apply 3D augmentation (C), and pull back SAM masks (D) and DINO features (E) into every crop (bottom).

Figure 4: Ablation study. (a, b) Precision/recall, memory, and runtime versus view count. papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near--far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7\% (flat LeWM) to 63.0\% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.
bullets: Flat JEPA Euclidean goal costs may fail to distinguish states by temporal proximity, especially at long offsets.
T2G trains a lightweight metric on offline trajectory latent triples using a margin-ranking loss, without rewards or policy labels.
The metric replaces Euclidean planning costs while keeping the JEPA encoder and predictor frozen.
Diagnostics show stronger temporal contrast and improved near–far ranking on AntMaze and FourRoom.
Across four benchmarks, average success rises from 32.7% to 63.0%, matching or surpassing hierarchical H-JEPA baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of T2G metric training. A latent triple (zt, zt+k, zt+k+∆) is sampled from an offline trajectory, where the near and far states are separated from the anchor by k and k+∆ steps, respectively. The three encoder blocks denote the same frozen JEPA encoder applied to the corresponding observations. T2G evaluates the learned temporal distances from the anchor to the near and far latents and optimizes the metric with a margin ranking objective, so that the near state is closer to the anchor than the far state by at least a margin m. Only the metric network and its scale are updated, and the world model remains frozen.

Horizontal axes report temporal separation in environment steps. At long offsets, T2G maintains a larger positive contrast and higher ranking accuracy in both environments.

Figure 4: Overview of T2G planning. The current observation o1 and goal observation og are encoded into latents z1 and zg by the frozen JEPA encoder. A solver optimizes an action sequence a1:H , and the frozen predictor rolls out the resulting latent trajectory z1→z2→· · ·→zH . Each predicted latent is scored by its learned temporal distance to the goal, dθ(zt, zg), and the solver updates the actions to minimize the aggregated cost. The updated actions are executed and planning is repeated from new observations in a receding-horizon loop, while the encoder, predictor, and solver remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Assessing the deployment performance of learned robot policies during training is challenging, as directly measuring task success requires costly real-world trials for each candidate checkpoint. Averaged validation loss offers a rollout-free alternative, but its checkpoint rankings can be inconsistent with deployment performance. We analyze two limitations of this criterion: it penalizes action deviations without considering whether the policy can recover from them, and gives later reference predictions equal weight even when earlier deviations may lead execution away from the reference. We propose RACE, a novel rollout-free metric for ranking checkpoints using a fixed set of held-out successful trajectories. RACE calibrates action deviations against state-conditional thresholds derived from action differences at similar states in these trajectories. We aggregate these scores through a running product, so that a substantial deviation reduces the contribution of subsequent reference predictions. Averaging the resulting cumulative scores over time and across trajectories yields the checkpoint score. In simulation, RACE outperforms baselines across validation sources, while several baselines degrade sharply when the validation set changes. On real robots, its rankings align with deployment success across the evaluated policy backbones and tasks of varying difficulty. Perturbation analyses further show that RACE distinguishes deviations with markedly different effects on task success, even when baselines respond similarly.
authors: Changyeon Kim, Yekyung Nah, Kimin Lee
bullets: Problem: Validation loss can rank policy checkpoints poorly because it ignores recovery from deviations and overweights later predictions after earlier errors.
Method: Calibrate action deviations using state-conditional thresholds from held-out successful trajectories, then combine scores with a running product.
Contribution: Produce checkpoint scores by averaging cumulative scores over time and trajectories without requiring real-world rollouts.
Results: RACE outperforms baselines in simulation, remains consistent across validation sources, and aligns with real-robot deployment success across tasks and policy backbones.
Scope: Evaluated in simulation and on real robots; the abstract does not specify broader generalization beyond these settings.

papers.abstract: Digital human e-commerce video generation requires preserving product appearance, human identity, and overall video style during dynamic demonstrations. Although recent models support multiple reference images, their general conditioning schemes do not explicitly distinguish the asymmetric roles of "what is presented" and "who presents it." Consequently, generated videos may favor a single reference, resulting in product distortion, identity drift, or single-reference collapse. To address this issue, we propose DualCast, a role-addressed dual-image conditioning framework for video generation. By explicitly modeling the distinct roles of product and human conditions, DualCast reduces role ambiguity and feature competition between references. First, a dual-spatiotemporal slot injection mechanism VAE-encodes the product and human images separately and places their latent features at the front and rear boundaries of the DiT sequence, enabling sequence-level condition separation and directed injection. Second, a mask-guided region-weighted loss strengthens supervision over product, face, and product-face overlap regions, improving generation fidelity in critical areas. Third, image condition dropout enables a single model to support dual-image, product-only, and human-only generation. In addition, we construct a curated dataset of 10K e-commerce videos for model training. Experimental results demonstrate the strong performance of DualCast.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yibo Zhao, Senlin Cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses product distortion, identity drift, and single-reference collapse caused by ambiguous multi-image conditioning.
Uses separate VAE-encoded product and human features injected into opposite ends of a diffusion-transformer sequence.
Applies mask-guided region-weighted loss to emphasize product, face, and product–face overlap regions.
Uses image-condition dropout to support dual-image, product-only, and human-only generation.
Trained on a curated dataset of 10K e-commerce videos; the abstract reports strong experimental performance without specific metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DualCast. The product and presenter images are independently VAE-encoded and placed at the front and rear boundaries of the extended latent sequence, respectively. Only intermediate video latents are denoised, supervised, and decoded. Both reference CLIP embeddings combine with the text prompt as cross-attention context. Product and face masks define region-weighted supervision, while condition dropout enables dual-image, product-only, and human-only inference.

Figure 4. Qualitative Comparison Results. Compared with existing methods, our approach demonstrates advantages in three aspects: (1) Facial Feature Consistency — Our method preserves the source person’s facial identity during video generation, avoiding identity drift or distortion; (2) Product Consistency — Product details from the reference image, including appearance, texture, and logos, are accurately reproduced, maintaining high visual fidelity; (3) Style Decoupling Capability — The overall style of the generated video is not irreversibly influenced by the reference image, achieving flexible decoupling between content transfer and style control, making the generation results more suitable for e-commerce live streaming scenarios.

Figure 1. A single fine-tuned DualCast model unifies three inference modes. A (Dual-image): Using dual-spatiotemporal slot injection, the model assigns roles to and preserves both product appearance and presenter identity. B (Product-only): When the human condition is omitted, the model generates high-quality presenter-led promotional videos based on the product. C (Human-only): When the product condition is omitted, the model generates high-quality presenter-led promotional videos based on the person.
