papers.abstract: Marine surface vehicles (MSVs) have attracted considerable attention for their commercial, scientific, and military applications. Owing to their favorable performance-to-cost ratio, shipboard cameras are widely used to detect and recognize potentially hazardous situations across diverse operational scenarios. However, visual perception is inevitably degraded by restricted conditions, including irregular motion of the imaging platform, adverse weather, and long imaging distances. To improve situational awareness and navigation capabilities, complementary sensors, such as the automatic identification system (AIS), radar, and light detection and ranging (LiDAR), etc., have become essential shipboard equipment. Multi-sensor fusion can provide richer perceptual information and help ensure navigational safety of MSVs in restricted visibility. This article reviews recent progress from intelligent vision to vision-centered multi-sensor fusion for newcomers and researchers in intelligent ship navigation and intelligent waterborne transportation system (IWTS). After introducing the generation of quality-degraded images in restricted visibility, we will review intelligent vision methods for four key issues, i.e., shipboard video stabilization, visual perception enhancement, object detection and tracking, and navigable area segmentation. We then examine vision-centered multi-sensor fusion methods, including infrared-visible image fusion, radar-vision fusion, LiDAR-vision fusion, AIS-vision fusion, and other multi-sensor fusion scenarios. Open-source datasets and safety-critical applications are also summarized and discussed. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future research directions. The collected maritime datasets are available at https://github.com/MAPGroup/Datasets and will be regularly updated.
authors: Ryan Wen Liu, Fengchuan Song, Tianxiang Wang, Guobei Peng, Youngrong Kim, Xian Zhong, Hooi-Siang Kang, Maohan Liang, Junzhi Yu, Shanliang Yao
bullets: Restricted visibility caused by platform motion, adverse weather, and long distances degrades camera-based maritime perception.
Reviews four vision tasks: video stabilization, visual enhancement, object detection and tracking, and navigable-area segmentation.
Covers fusion of vision with infrared, radar, LiDAR, AIS, and other complementary sensors.
Summarizes open-source maritime datasets, safety-critical applications, open challenges, and future research directions.
Dataset resources are provided through the MAPGroup repository and are intended to be regularly updated.

papers.abstract: Recent pansharpening models achieve strong fusion performance on trained sensors, yet often generalize poorly to unseen sensors. Existing cross-sensor adaptation is limited by target-sensor retraining, which requires target-sensor training pairs and a dedicated training stage, and by per-image zero-shot adaptation, which is computationally expensive due to whole-network optimization for each test image. To address these problems, we propose ReTailor, a real-time sequential cross-sensor adaptation framework. Only a lightweight residual Feature Tailor is rapidly optimized under self-supervised, physics-aware constraints to correct cross-sensor shifts without modifying the well-learned fusion prior. For efficient and effective deployment, ReTailor combines content-aware patch selection, which identifies a few informative patches per image for optimization at negligible cost to improve both quality and efficiency, with rolling residual bootstrap, which inherits sensor-related knowledge across the image stream to further improve quality. Extensive experiments on cross-sensor adaptation settings show that ReTailor mitigates cross-sensor degradation both effectively and efficiently. Moreover, we compare ReTailor with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a widely used method for fine-tuning, to demonstrate the advantages of our approach. We further evaluate the core principle of ReTailor on two additional remote sensing tasks: super-resolution pansharpening and image segmentation, where it consistently improves performance. In general, ReTailor provides a highly effective and efficient strategy for deploying pansharpening models under real-world cross-sensor degradation, while also offering useful insights into managing cross-sensor degradation in other remote sensing tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/JingZe-Liang/ReTailor .
authors: Jing-Ze Liang, Wei-Jie Xiao, Zi-Han Cao, Yang-Dong Li, Tian-Yi Hu, Liang-Jian Deng
bullets: Addresses poor cross-sensor generalization without target-sensor training pairs or costly whole-network per-image optimization.
Uses a lightweight Feature Tailor optimized with physics-aware, self-supervised constraints while preserving the pretrained fusion prior.
Selects a few content-aware patches for efficient adaptation and uses rolling residual bootstrap to transfer sensor knowledge across image streams.
Experiments show effective and efficient mitigation of cross-sensor degradation, with advantages over LoRA in the reported comparisons.
The approach also improves performance on super-resolution pansharpening and image segmentation, though its stated scope is remote sensing adaptation.

papers.abstract: Expert deactivation at inference time changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how these changes are implemented. We compare removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, with a base OLMoE checkpoint as an additional comparison. We develop a weight-sum model that relates the loss of expert contributions and changes in branch scale to the weight rule used during training. With half of the experts deactivated according to activation-based rankings, remaining-expert renormalization yields the highest perplexity in models trained with raw router probabilities, whereas unnormalized re-routing yields the highest perplexity in models trained with normalized weights. Perplexity ranges from 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is retained, and from 14 to 28,740 times the baseline under a rule mismatch. Task outcomes vary across evaluation types: on OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. Extending the model to changes in the number of active experts yields a further prediction, supported by the OLMoE experiments: the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization increases as fewer experts are activated.
authors: Hao Cheng (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Zhiyu Yang (Chang'an University), Bo Ma (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Hanzhang Jia (University of Sussex)
bullets: The study compares removal, freezing, renormalized re-routing, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled experts across multiple checkpoints.
A weight-sum model explains how lost expert contributions and branch-scale changes depend on the training-time weight rule.

With half the experts disabled, renormalization performs worst for models trained with raw router probabilities, while unnormalized re-routing performs worst for models trained with normalized weights.
Perplexity penalties are much larger under rule mismatch, ranging from 14–28,740× the intact baseline versus 1.4–73× when the rule is retained.
On OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy drops to zero for all tested implementations; additional renormalization is increasingly harmful with fewer active experts.

papers.abstract: Recent LLM-centric advances can generate attractive furnished rooms by selecting and arranging assets. Yet evaluation remains limited to specific perspectives or predefined questions, failing to reflect overall scene quality. To address this pressing need, we introduce GREP. Its core is a focus shift from defining specific questions to establishing a three-tier evaluation philosophy: basic physical validity checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints; visual coherence concerns compatibility in object scale, style, and composition; and, at the highest level, human-use logic requires object arrangements to align with everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent autonomously and adaptively identifies issues from scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. This supports scene-specific issue discovery and reliable judgments. Experiments show that (1) GREP achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences, substantially outperforming baseline evaluators. (2) GREP reports improve scene quality through refinement, whereas score-only and no-feedback baselines show slight declines. (3) GREP suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can move from relying on pipelines and harnesses to challenging their guidance and constraints, but still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. Stronger models are therefore expected not only to plan well, but also to adapt to external guidance and constraints more flexibly. Project page: https://han-808.github.io/GREP/
authors: Mohan Cao, Yongsen Mao, Chucheng Xiang, Zhongyuan Liu, Zhihang Zhong, Haiping Wang, Yuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of viewpoint- or question-specific room evaluation by assessing overall scene quality.
Uses a three-tier philosophy: physical constraints, object scale/style/composition compatibility, and everyday usability.
An evaluation agent discovers scene-specific issues, gathers evidence, and produces scores plus refinement reports.
Achieves 87% agreement with human majority preferences and outperforms baseline evaluators.
Feedback from GREP improves scene quality, while score-only and no-feedback approaches slightly reduce it; evaluation remains focused on generated room scenes.

papers.abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.
authors: Rohit Mohan, Maximilian Luz, Swarnava Chowdhury, Yao Lu, Florian Drews, Thomas N\"urnberg, Yakov Miron, Federico Tombari, Stefano Gasperini, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses the gap between image-level open-set benchmarks and closed-set panoramic tracking benchmarks.

Provides unknown-object tracks, camera masks, and auxiliary LiDAR observations for evaluation.
Defines tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking.
Benchmark results show current methods struggle with unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views.

papers.abstract: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, 53% of contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28.5% of test episodes. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, ZipDrift is collision-free in all 600 test episodes and matches the best evaluated candidate, whereas an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor crashes in 4.0% (16.0% with inconsistent expert labels) and critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget in 2.0%.
bullets: Short-horizon MPC is fast but myopic, and optimal cost corrections can be multimodal when multiple maneuvers are viable.
A deterministic regressor may average these modes or depend on inconsistent expert tie-breaking.
ZipDrift uses a one-step drifting generator trained from candidate cost evaluations, without differentiating through the optimizer.
A learned critic ranks a few generated corrections, while MPC enforces dynamics and constraints.
In the benchmark, ZipDrift had 0% collisions versus 4.0% for an idealized regressor and 2.0% for critic-ranked random candidates.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.
bullets: Applies FlyHash—sparse random projection with winner-take-all hashing—to LLM agent memory retrieval.
Confirms a robust quality advantage over SimHash across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, using matched-bit comparisons.
Identifies and corrects a previously undocumented comparison pitfall in evaluating FlyHash against SimHash.
Finds no general memory or latency advantage: FlyHash codes are larger and slower to compare at equal bits, while HNSW dominates at ordinary scale.
Introduces a sparse-set comparison that narrows, but does not eliminate, the latency gap; the quality benefit also holds with non-circular relevance labels.

papers.abstract: Adaptive sampling can substantially improve the value of sparse ocean observations by directing mobile robots toward measurements that are most informative for an evolving environment. Recent learned generative ocean models can produce high-resolution forecasts and ensembles at substantially lower computational cost than traditional numerical models, creating an opportunity to use rich predictive forecasts directly in closed-loop robotic sampling. However, these models do not natively provide the explicit uncertainty representations assumed by classical informative-planning methods, and their forecasts often evolve in learned latent spaces rather than directly in physical ocean variables. We develop a multi-robot closed-loop adaptive sampling framework that uses a single learned generative model for forecasting, uncertainty estimation, planning, and measurement assimilation. The model forecasts an ensemble in latent space, decodes it to physical ocean states, and uses ensemble statistics to construct A- or D-optimal sampling objectives. We select sampling locations subject to robot reachability under predicted currents. The collected measurements are assimilated back into the latent state using observation-conditioned diffusion sampling. Across 120 test scenarios A- and D-optimal sampling generally outperforms static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines while adding little planning overhead. Our experiments uncover several scenarios in which model uncertainty diverges from forecast error, motivating future work in uncertainty quantification.
bullets: Addresses sparse ocean observations and the lack of explicit uncertainty estimates in generative forecasting models.
Generates latent-space ensembles, decodes them to physical states, and derives A- and D-optimal sampling objectives from ensemble statistics.
Plans reachable robot locations under predicted currents and assimilates measurements through observation-conditioned diffusion sampling.
A- and D-optimal strategies generally outperform static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines with little additional planning overhead.
Some scenarios show divergence between model uncertainty and forecast error, highlighting a limitation in uncertainty quantification.

papers.abstract: We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.
authors: Yang Liu, Tong Wang, Yiming Bao, Heng Yang
bullets: Targets retargeting of human demonstrations under contact-rich robot dynamics.
GRASP-TO fits local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and uses recovered gradients to guide MCMC proposals, with Metropolis-Hastings correction.
GRASP-MPC extends the approach to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning.
Achieves 92.8% success on 1,352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations using a shared tracking objective without task-specific contact rewards.
Improves PPO tracking and transfers to dexterous and whole-body humanoid manipulation on real hardware.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus-Turbo https://github.com/AMD-AGI/Primus
authors: Gengyu Rao, Ghadeer Ahmed H Alabandi, Su Ann Chong, Thomas Huber, Kailash Gogineni, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Saleel Kudchadker, Suchita Pati, Zirui Zhang, Zhen Huang, Yanyuan Qin, Xiaoming Peng, Lihuan Zhang, Botao Hu, Wei Huang, Yang Bo, Wen Xie, Xiangyu Zhao, Ruibin Zhang, Xiaobo Chen, Vidushi Goyal, Anshu Raina, Claire Songhyun Lee, Jiakun Yan, Yao Fu, Nusrat Islam, Ravi Dwivedula, Jie Zhang, Maria Garzaran, Zhenyu Gu, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Targets idle compute caused by data arriving late from off-chip memory or other GPUs.
Uses Tensor Data Mover (TDM), transpose-load, System DMA (SDMA), and Remote DMA (RDMA) to pipeline data movement.
Reports average kernel speedups of 1.88× with TDM and 1.19× with transpose-load.
Reports average speedups of 1.16× with SDMA and 1.33× with RDMA when computation overlaps communication.
Integrated into the open-source Primus-Turbo and Primus frameworks for AMD GPUs.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) are bottlenecked by the length of their input token sequence. Standard patchification fixes this length with a single patch size applied across the image, regardless of regional content. Prior work on adaptive patch sizing reduces token count by assigning coarser patches to visually simple regions, but relies on noisy pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy to make patchification decisions. We argue that this compute allocation should be grounded in the model's interpretation of task relevant information, not in raw pixel statistics. We introduce Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization which learns to allocate token resolution based on what the model finds meaningful, producing shorter token sequences that are better matched to task-relevant content. SPLIT matches the accuracy of full-resolution ViT classification baselines while using 30% fewer tokens. The same gains hold on dense prediction: SPLIT achieves competitive accuracy on COCO and ADE20K, demonstrating that semantically aligned patchification generalises well beyond classification.
authors: Aditya Gupta, Jean Sebastien Dandurand, Kai Qiu, Rohan Choudhury, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Standard fixed-size patchification ignores regional complexity and creates unnecessarily long sequences.
SPLIT replaces pixel-level heuristics with a learned hierarchical patch-splitting policy guided by the model’s interpretation.
It matches full-resolution ViT classification accuracy while using 30% fewer tokens.
The approach also delivers competitive dense-prediction accuracy on COCO and ADE20K.
The abstract focuses on image classification and dense prediction; broader scope is not established.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SPLIT. An input image is first divided into coarse patches. For each parent-child group, a lightweight cross-attention module pools the four child embeddings with the parent embedding as the query. The pooled summary is concatenated with the parent embedding and passed to a two-layer MLP to predict the split probability pi.

papers.abstract: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.
authors: Changyeon Lee, Kelin Yu, Zheng Wei, Shuna Ni, Ruohan Gao
bullets: Addresses the limited study of olfactory sensing in embodied AI beyond semantic odor perception.
Extends Habitat-Sim with FDS-based 3D odor transport and dispersion in photorealistic indoor scenes.
Covers gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization as source-seeking tasks.
Provides a multimodal reinforcement-learning policy that integrates visual and olfactory observations over time.
The policy outperforms diverse baselines, offering a reference point for future research.

papers.abstract: Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests. Crucially, remembering the right intention does not guarantee acting at the right time: a related observation may call for waiting, while a later cue may make the same intention actionable. Inspired by cognitive theories of human prospective memory, we introduce Pro-Memory, a memory framework that separates maintaining future intentions from deciding when and how to realize them. Pro-Memory preserves pending objectives linked to their supporting evidence, assesses new observations against their original goals and activation conditions, and coordinates appropriate contributions with the agent's ongoing actions. It further updates intention states based on actions actually issued or evidence of resolution, while an experience memory distills feedback from completed episodes into guidance for future decisions. Experiments on two benchmarks spanning delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance demonstrate consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches across multiple LLM backbones, while limiting unnecessary interventions.
authors: Yuanchen Bei, Zhining Liu, Tianxin Wei, Weizhi Zhang, Zhichen Zeng, Philip S. Yu, Hendrik Hamann, Jingrui He, Hanghang Tong
bullets: Addresses the gap between remembering future goals and deciding when they should become actionable.
Separates intention maintenance from realization, linking pending objectives to supporting evidence and activation conditions.
Updates intention states based on issued actions or resolution evidence, while learning from completed episodes.
Improves proactive performance across delayed-intention and open-ended assistance benchmarks with multiple LLM backbones.
Limits unnecessary interventions by distinguishing cues that require waiting from those that warrant action.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated significant advances in reasoning with visual data, which is particularly important given that much of human knowledge is encoded visually in scientific articles and other sources. However, a gap remains in understanding how artificial agents, powered by VLMs, perceive and navigate decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of visual data. This study explores this gap by evaluating and analyzing autonomous decision-making processes. Building upon prior work in visualization literacy and decision theory, we conducted two complementary studies: one examining how agents perceive and quantify uncertainty encoded in visualizations, and another investigating how artificial agents make decisions based on visual data in the form of images. We analyzed perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization types. Our results show that GPT-4o demonstrates the highest accuracy in perceiving uncertainty in pie and bar charts among the tested models. For decision-making, autonomous agents showed the best alignment with rational decision theory when uncertainty was represented through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.
bullets: Investigates artificial agents’ decision-making under uncertainty using visual information.
Conducts two studies: uncertainty perception in visualizations and decisions based on images.
Analyzes perception accuracy and decision performance across models and visualization formats.
GPT-4o achieved the highest uncertainty-perception accuracy for tested pie and bar charts.
Agents aligned most closely with rational decision theory when uncertainty was shown through circle charts, icon arrays, or text.

papers.abstract: This paper presents Proactive Human-in-the-Loop (PHIL), a framework for proactive policy correction and preference-based post-training. PHIL enables operators to preview policy-predicted future motion and intervene before anticipated undesirable actions. During takeover, PHIL continues querying the policy and displaying its predicted trajectories in the physical workspace through an extended reality (XR) interface. PHIL pairs rejected policy predictions with corrective action chunks subsequently executed from the same physical state over the same horizon, and preference-based post-training encourages the policy to favor these corrections. This paper evaluates PHIL on four real-world manipulation tasks using a diffusion policy and a pretrained vision-language-action policy. With five correction episodes per condition, PHIL increases mean success rates across the evaluated tasks and demonstration budgets from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA, compared with HG-DAgger. Separately, policies trained with proactive corrections show fewer unnecessary recovery behaviors in successful episodes. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/PHIL-page/.
authors: Xinkai Jiang, Jing Jiang, Hongyi Zhou, Pankhuri Vanjani, Ahmad Baki, Jakub Suliga, Ge Li, Zhuoyue Li, Gerhard Neumann, Rudolf Lioutikov
bullets: Addresses the limitation of correcting robots only after undesirable actions begin.

Pairs rejected predictions with corrective action chunks from the same state and horizon for preference-based post-training.
Evaluated on four real-world manipulation tasks with diffusion and vision-language-action policies.
Compared with HG-DAgger, mean success increased from 44.0% to 70.3% for the diffusion policy and from 57.8% to 76.9% for X-VLA.

papers.title: Correct Robots Before They Make Mistakes: Proactive Human-in-the-Loop Intervention via Preference Learning

papers.abstract: The memory of production agents is increasingly becoming a bottleneck and is built almost exclusively from text: key points are extracted from out-of-limit context and retrieved into context at query time. Therefore, every new query incurs an additional cost that grows with the accumulated history. Weight memory is a complementary alternative that internalizes knowledge into model parameters and answers with no context at all, and has recently proven effective in self-evolving agents for internalizing skills and behaviors. However, its application in episodic and semantic memory, such as user-specific facts, remains comparatively unexplored, and a gap remains between earlier attempts at weight memory and text-based systems regarding recall performance. We study how to make weight memory competitive as a long-term factual store by applying on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). It trains a context-free student from a teacher, which is the same model conditioned on the user's memory, together with a verify-then-regenerate router that lets weight and text memory each cover the queries they handle best. On the HaluMem benchmark, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query. We further conduct an extensive study that characterizes the behavior of weight memory and analyzes how different training recipes affect its performance. As agent harnesses move toward persistent, multi-session deployments, these results position weight memory as a practical, low-cost component of agent memory and provide insights into feasible training and evaluation protocols for combining it with retrieval.
authors: Zeyu Fang, Jun Yin, Yongsheng Mei, Xu Han, Chaitali Joshi, Zhongkai Sun, Jie Hao, Bin Guo, Chengyuan Ma, Benjamin Z. Yao, Chenlei Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost and scaling limits of text-only memory, where each query requires retrieving accumulated history.
Trains a context-free student from a memory-conditioned teacher using on-policy self-distillation (OPSD).
Uses a verify-then-regenerate router to assign queries to weight memory or text memory based on which handles them best.
On HaluMem, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines while reading fewer tokens per query.

papers.abstract: Many temporal approaches for video recognition rely on explicit cross-channel aggregation projections, which have quadratic complexity in the number of channels, introducing significant computational overhead. In addition, the spatio-temporal representation used for video recognition is biased either toward local order interactions (for CNNs) or toward global order interactions (for transformers). Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, our method introduces two complementary contributions to tackle these problems. First, for the temporal modelling, we introduce parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation, which is linear in the number of channels, inducing a considerable computational reduction. Second, we propose a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions, which allows a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing the computational cost. By combining these two contributions, our proposed VideoMogaNet achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches across multiple video benchmarks (UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, Diving48), while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.
authors: Kevin D. Nguetche, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli
bullets: Targets the quadratic channel cost of explicit cross-channel aggregation in temporal video models.
Uses parallel multi-order depthwise-only convolutions with implicit gating-based aggregation for linear channel complexity.
Introduces dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions to improve representation without added computational cost.
Matches or exceeds state-of-the-art action-recognition performance across UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, and Diving48.
Scope: focuses on reducing temporal modeling overhead while balancing local and global order interactions.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up large language model (LLM) serving, but its gain depends on the workload's \emph{shape}, such as batch size and context length, and on its \emph{content}. A model-based drafter proposes a short block on any content, while a model-free drafter such as n-gram lookup proposes long copies at almost no cost when the output repeats its input, as in code editing. Adaptive verification spends a batch-wide verification budget on the draft tokens most likely to be accepted, but it supports only one model-based drafter. Model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in budget allocation, and deployments must either fix one drafter or split their GPUs between drafters. We present \sys, a framework that runs a model-based and a model-free drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, within adaptive verification and entirely on the GPU, which keeps asynchronous scheduling intact. The key idea is a price per verified draft token: the goodput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch. Once the model-free drafter's tokens carry calibrated acceptance estimates, fit once on general text, this price puts both drafters' chains on one scale. Instantiated with \dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, \sys achieves 1.10--1.62\x the output throughput of \dspark on code editing at batch size~4 and 1.04--1.27\x at batch size~128, while staying at 0.97--1.01\x of it on chat at temperature~0. A single deployment can therefore serve both workloads.
bullets: Addresses workload- and content-dependent speculative decoding gains, especially repeated-input workloads such as code editing.
Runs both drafters on every step and selects the better proposal chain within a shared adaptive verification budget.
Uses calibrated acceptance estimates and a per-token opportunity-cost price to compare model-free and model-based drafts.
Implemented in vLLM, it reaches 1.10–1.62× throughput on code editing at batch size 4 and 1.04–1.27× at batch size 128 versus the model-based drafter.
Maintains 0.97–1.01× throughput on temperature-0 chat, enabling a single deployment for both workloads.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised world models are often said to organize their latents around physical quantities. We test this on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow in three pre-registered studies, each tested once on held-out data. In Study 1, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained to predict the flow fails the pre-registered criteria for organizing its latent around fluid quantities better than an untrained network of the same architecture (not supported); a JEPA trained on non-physical linear dynamics and a static invariance model that never sees time do as well or better. In Study 2, plain autoencoders that render the field make enstrophy prominent in their slowest unsupervised latent directions (best r 0.80-0.86 vs 0.38 untrained; fresh seeds, sealed data). Adding VICReg lowers this prominence in every comparison, though not by the pre-registered margin for vorticity, while raising the autoencoders' linear decodability (partially supported). In Study 3, we build steerable directions ("dials") by routing: the decoder gets overall scale only through a small conditioning code, while its other pathway carries a degraded copy of spectral shape. Label-free rules find a loudness dial in all 8 trained models and a shape dial in 3 of 5 fresh seeds on sealed data, against a pre-registered bar of 4; neither control shows a shape dial (partially supported). Across the studies, what a latent contains and what can be controlled through it come apart. In exploration, a supervised direction reading spectral shape almost perfectly moved nothing when steered. During the build, the loudness dial had to be found by its effect on the output (closest to a pure rescaling), not by data variance; for shape, a variance rule and an effect-constrained rule each worked in 3 of 5 seeds. The program used about 70 logged hours on one consumer GPU; all pre-registrations, deviations, code and outputs are public.
bullets: Three pre-registered studies test physical organization and steerability in 2D decaying Navier–Stokes representations.
A predictive JEPA did not organize latents around fluid quantities better than an untrained counterpart; non-physical and static controls matched or exceeded it.
Plain autoencoders made enstrophy prominent in slow latent directions, while VICReg reduced this prominence but improved linear decodability.
Decoder-routing produced a reliable loudness dial and an inconsistent shape dial; neither control produced a shape dial.
A direction that read spectral shape almost perfectly failed to change shape when steered, showing a gap between representation and control.

papers.title: Readable Is Not Steerable: Pre-Registered Tests of Physical Structure in Learned Fluid Representations
papers.tldr: In learned fluid representations, latent readability does not reliably imply that the corresponding physical properties can be controlled.

papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant. Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions. This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives. Additional materials can be found on: https://end2end-latent-action.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of action-labeled robot data by leveraging action-free video demonstrations.
Jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder for downstream control.
Uses lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders without changing existing policy architectures or training objectives.
Outperforms prior latent-action baselines on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Scope: applies to imitation learning with video demonstrations and limited robot action labels.

In the Policy-update pass, the LAM is frozen and the alignment and policy losses are used to update the policy network.

papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: https://pairlab.github.io/MESA.
authors: Albert Wilcox, Frank Chang, Nhi Nguyen, Aishani Chakraborty, Jeremy A. Collins, Vaibhav Saxena, Benjamin Joffe, Siddharth Karamcheti, Animesh Garg
bullets: Evaluates in-distribution performance plus four distinct generalization axes: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition.
Uses MESA-Gen, an improved MimicGen-based pipeline, to generate tasks and demonstrations at scale.
Releases single-arm MESA and BiMESA, a large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization.
Across seven baseline methods, the strongest model reaches 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, leaving substantial room for improvement.
MESA rankings broadly agree with RoboArena scores, suggesting relevance beyond simulation.

(2) Instantiate a task from the skeleton and generate BDDL files for the training and evaluation sets. (3) Optionally, collect a small number of source demonstrations. (4) Generate a large dataset for imitation learning. Using subtask stitching enables data generation for tasks without human data.

Figure 10: We compare confusion matrices for diffusion policy and π0.5. Entry i, j in these plots shows the frequency with which a given policy completed a distractor task by grasping j when it was supposed to grasp i (rows are target objects; columns are the objects picked up). For example, both confusion matrices show a lot of confusion for tomato, apple because the policy frequently grasped an apple when it was supposed to grasp a tomato. We condensed them to a reasonable size by selecting the top 15 most confusing entries in each matrix and removing rows and columns corresponding to objects not involved in those entries. For example, no object was commonly confused for mushrooms, so their rows and columns were removed.

(a) We see that with 1000 demonstrations it achieves reasonable performance, but with 100 demonstrations, the number present for each task in MESA-70, its performance drops sharply. We ablate the omission of roll, pitch and yaw (− RPY) and the starting point optimization procedure (− Opt). In (a) we study data generation rate, or the success rate of MimicGen at data generation time, and see that our changes lead to a consistent improvement. In (b) we study downstream policy performance and see that especially the starting point optimization leads to a substantial policy improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluation framework for language-conditioned robot manipulation generalization, fits embodied AI subtopics.
papers.title: MESA: An Evaluation Framework for Compositional, Semantic, and Spatial Generalization in Robotics
papers.tldr: MESA is a reproducible robotics benchmark that isolates spatial, object, category, and compositional generalization, revealing substantial weaknesses in current language-conditioned policies.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models score left/right relations near chance, but the symptom has two causes that call for opposite repairs: the relation may survive in the pooled embedding yet be unreachable by native image-text similarity, or pooling may discard it while the dense features retain it. On clean two object photographs, across ten encoders, the lateral polarity is linearly decodable from the flip odd component of the pooled vector at 0.77-0.99, yet a search over a million captions leaves nine of the ten at chance under native scoring: an access failure. On controlled C4 orbits, where the relation is the only thing that varies, pooling keeps the arrangement axis at 0.998-1.000 and loses its polarity, which the patch grid retains: a pooling failure. Both sit downstream of the dense features, so one readout covers both. Our zero parameter, query conditioned spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it as a vector beside the native embedding. On a 118,287 image index it raises left/right pairwise accuracy against reversed geometry negatives from 0.51-0.53 to 0.81-0.96 and conditional R@1 among 21 category matched candidates from 0.05 to 0.37-0.75, at under a millisecond per batched query, while reproducing the native ranking exactly for queries that name no relation.
bullets: Across ten encoders, left/right polarity is often linearly decodable from pooled embeddings (0.77–0.99) but remains inaccessible to native image–text scoring.
Controlled experiments show pooling can preserve arrangement while discarding polarity, which remains available in patch-grid features.
A query-conditioned spatial moment recomputes geometry from patch features and stores it alongside the native embedding.
On a 118,287-image index, pairwise accuracy improves from 0.51–0.53 to 0.81–0.96, and conditional R@1 from 0.05 to 0.37–0.75.
The method adds under 1 ms per batched query and exactly preserves native rankings for queries without spatial relations.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and repairs spatial relation failure in VLMs, directly relevant to spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Discarded or Unreachable? Diagnosing and Repairing Spatial Relation Failure in Vision--Language Similarity
papers.tldr: A zero-parameter spatial readout diagnoses whether vision–language models fail on left/right relations because similarity cannot access the information or pooling discarded it, and repairs both cases.

papers.abstract: In biodiversity monitoring, a single image raises several questions: which taxon, how many, which trait, and whether the individual has been seen before. Vision-language models (VLMs) could answer all of these from the image, but their ability is largely untested in biology, as existing benchmarks focus mostly on species identification within a few taxonomic groups. We present Bio-VQA, the largest biological visual question answering (VQA) benchmark and the only one to span four aspects of biological visual understanding: hierarchical taxonomic reasoning, fine-grained attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and individual re-identification. Bio-VQA contains 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, and extends right-or-wrong scoring to graded scoring, so a near-miss counts for more than a distant one. Evaluating 18 open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters, we find that general visual capabilities do not transfer to biological organisms: the best model counts animals exactly on 41.7% of images with 2 to 10 individuals, less than half its accuracy on everyday objects at the same counts. Taxonomic accuracy falls to one sixth, from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name, and scaling helps mostly at coarse ranks. The gap to a domain specialist widens accordingly, from 0.731 against BioCLIP-2's 0.874 at class (1.2x) to 0.269 against 0.544 at scientific name (2x). On trait size measurement, 15 of the 18 models do no better than an image-blind baseline that predicts one fixed number for every specimen, and on re-identification, 17 of the 18 models fall below chance under adversarial conditions. These failures persist across a tenfold range of model size. We hope Bio-VQA becomes a standard test of how well VLM capabilities transfer to the biological domain.
authors: S M Rayeed, Qian Ma, Charles V. Stewart, Yao Ma
bullets: Introduces a benchmark spanning four biological reasoning tasks: hierarchical taxonomy, attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and re-identification.
Covers 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, with graded scoring for near-miss answers.
Evaluates 18 open-weight VLMs and finds weak performance, especially for exact counting, fine-grained taxonomy, trait measurement, and re-identification.
Scaling improves mainly coarse taxonomic reasoning; many failures persist across a tenfold range of model sizes.
Shows substantial gaps versus domain-specialist models, with performance deteriorating as biological reasoning becomes more fine-grained.

papers.abstract: Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking. We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference. Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.
authors: Qi Xu, Zhigang Hua, Zijie Lei, Yan Xie, Jizhe Zhang, Lynn Lu, Delun Du, Sha Hua, Ren Mao, Ke Pan, Haomin Yu, Sandeep Pandey, Luke Simon
bullets: Whole-page ranking must jointly arrange ads and organic content while satisfying business and layout constraints.
Existing NAR methods are efficient but miss order-dependent item interactions; AR methods capture them but require costly sequential inference.
MIS combines global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring in a shared representation architecture.
It reuses per-request representations and applies lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search.
On two benchmarks, MIS achieved 4.07× and 3.54× faster CPU decoding; a large-scale randomized evaluation also reported gains in realization and watch time with lower CPU usage.

papers.abstract: We propose MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that equips diffusion-based trajectory planners with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety specifications. Building on the single-agent construction that embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, we: (i) formalize joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets; (ii) derive centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures with provable invariance under mild assumptions; (iii) address local-trap and deadlock phenomena via time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs; and (iv) develop a lightweight benchmarking suite including a multi-agent Maze2D domain. Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines, while retaining planning quality. We provide algorithms, proofs, and reference implementations.
authors: Kiran Ravish, Ankita Kushwaha, Preeti, Pawan Kumar
bullets: Models joint safety using per-agent and pairwise control barrier-function constraints.
Provides centralized and communication-aware decentralized constrained denoising procedures with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees under mild assumptions.
Uses time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs to mitigate local traps and deadlocks.
Introduces a lightweight benchmark suite, including a multi-agent Maze2D domain.
Experiments report fewer safety violations than unconstrained diffusion baselines while retaining planning quality.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion tracking has scaled to general policies that reproduce diverse human motion, but the resulting behavior is in free-space: the tracker knows where the body should be, not how it should interact with the environment. Other work makes the object part of the objective, yet abstracts that interaction to contact or geometry, which leaves the demanding cases under-explored. We argue that force is a natural command channel between motion imitation and object interaction, one that specifies not just where to make contact but how hard. We present Ctrl-F, a hierarchical motion-force framework that augments motion tracking with an explicit force command, a 3-D force at each designated contact body such as a hand or a foot. The hierarchical framework comprises: (1) A unified motion-force controller tracks the reference motion while applying the commanded force to the world. (2) A high-level force planner that issues a force command online based on object state and proprioception observations. In simulation and on hardware, Ctrl-F completes loco-manipulation that demands large, sustained interaction force and adjusts its command online as the load changes, both out of reach of a force-blind tracker. On hardware, Ctrl-F demonstrates hand-based dragging, pushing, and lifting, as well as foot-based kicking, successfully manipulating boxes weighing up to 20kg in pushing and kicking tasks where the force-blind baseline fails, while adapting online to additional loads introduced mid-task.
authors: Mengjie Zhao, Yuxin Chen, Yiyang Shao, Chuye Hong, Jiakang Chen, Koushil Sreenath, Masayoshi Tomizuka
bullets: Addresses the gap between free-space motion imitation and environment interaction requiring sustained physical force.
Uses a hierarchical framework with a unified motion-force controller and an online force planner informed by object state and proprioception.
Supports force commands at designated contact bodies, including hands and feet.
Simulation and hardware experiments show online adaptation to changing loads during dragging, pushing, lifting, and kicking.
On hardware, it manipulates boxes up to 20 kg in pushing and kicking tasks where a force-blind tracker fails.

figures.caption: Figure 9 | Weight added mid-task on hardware. Top: adapting to weight added mid-drag. In every setting the cart is loaded while the robot is already dragging the cart, whose wheels stay locked throughout (arrow marks the loading). Frames are composited at equal time intervals; the spacing between poses is therefore speed. SONIC is given the easier test, an empty cart that takes 8 kg, because it cannot start a loaded cart moving at all; even so, it stops once the weight goes in. The two variants of our method start at 8 kg and take a further 6 kg. Under a command frozen at what the high-level force planner itself issued for the initial load, the robot keeps walking but slows, its poses bunching together after the change, while the full hierarchy holds its pace. Those two share a tracker, an interface and a starting force command, and differ only in whether that command is allowed to change. papers.abstract: While discrete tokenization in Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) establishes strong semantic reasoning, it introduces a strict quantization bottleneck that degrades fine-grained visual details, often resulting in structurally accurate but artifact-heavy images. We introduce FlowShift, a parameter-efficient post-training framework that bypasses this bottleneck by converting pre-trained discrete UMMs into continuous rectified-flow generators. Instead of discarding the backbone's semantic priors, FlowShift replaces discrete visual interfaces with continuous latent projections and applies LoRA to the attention layers. To efficiently boost visual quality without semantic drift, we propose Dual-Objective Velocity Vector Distillation (DOVD), which aligns the model with a high-fidelity continuous teacher and ground-truth continuous trajectories. This approach drastically improves perceptual quality while preserving prompt adherence and reasoning. When applied to leading discrete UMMs, FlowShift significantly improves COCO-30K FID and aesthetic scores, while retaining over 99.5% of multimodal understanding capabilities. Ablations confirm DOVD drives generation quality. Ultimately, FlowShift achieves high-fidelity continuous generation without sacrificing pre-trained semantic grounding.
authors: Gayatri Deshmukh, Onkar Susladkar, Adheesh Juvekar, Halil Kilicoglu, Ismini Lourentzou
bullets: Addresses quantization bottlenecks that cause fine-detail loss and visual artifacts in discrete UMM image generation.

Ablations identify DOVD as the main driver of generation-quality improvements.

papers.abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.
authors: Shijue Huang, Hangyu Guo, Hengheng Zhang, Guo An, Zhitao He, Qi Tian, Yiren Feng
bullets: Benchmarks experience lifecycles across 18 interactive environments and 20 models.
Separates structural experience about environment organization from rule experience about reusable constraints and principles.

Tracks both task performance and how saved experience is retained, revised, or lost.

papers.abstract: Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/jev-ad-website.
authors: Yansong Qu, Jiancong Chen, Samuel Labi
bullets: Addresses the risk that language-based driving agents reason too slowly and infer action consequences implicitly.
Combines Jev, a typed probabilistic decision model, with a language world model forecasting two seconds of surrounding-vehicle motion.
Uses code to convert forecasts into explicit consequences that Jev compares across candidate actions.
In simulated highway merging, foresight reduced collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% while maintaining 0.25-second decision latency.
Across free-form commands and replayed NGSIM episodes, the system achieved 93% intent fulfillment and reduced replay collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%.

papers.abstract: Surgical world models have the potential to provide intra-operative guidance, accelerate risk-free training and facilitate transfer of expert surgical maneuvers. However, the use of world models for transferring surgical expertise has been largely unexplored. Moreover, recent approaches in this domain have mainly relied on ground truth kinematics actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, limiting their applicability beyond the narrow range of tasks with ground-truth annotations. In contrast, existing works in the natural domain have shown promising results in learning latent actions solely from unlabeled videos and transferring the learned actions across contexts. We observe that this paradigm is short-sighted for the surgical domain, failing to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. Thus, we propose a novel multi-step action learning framework to learn context-invariant latent actions that are easily transferable across various surgical contexts. We perform extensive experiments on the publicly available datasets, SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023, verifying our approach with both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts. We have published our code and the implementation details at https://github.com/bhattarailab/Surgical-Vision-World-Model.
authors: Saurabh Koju, Love Panta, Deepak Thapa, Rudra P. K. Poudel, Prajwal Ghimire, Angus Watson, Yash Raj Shrestha, Prashnna Kumar Gyawali, Binod Bhattarai
bullets: Addresses limited surgical world-model transfer methods that depend on ground-truth kinematics or task-specific expert annotations.

Evaluated quantitatively and through surgical-expert qualitative assessment on SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023.
Code and implementation details are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Existing benchmarks for joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation evaluate perceptual quality and audiovisual alignment, but balanced sound-source sam?pling and separate reporting by shot structure remain limited. This makes it dif?ficult to determine whether a specific sound is missing, attributed to the wrong source, or lost across shot transitions. To address this, we introduce CAST?BENCH, a benchmark designed to trace every generated sound back to its in?tended source in multi-shot audio-video generation. The core idea is to formu?late T2AV correctness as an audiovisual contract in which each requested sound must be emitted by the right source, synchronized with the corresponding visual action, and carry the right semantic content. Concretely, the benchmark orga?nizes 900 prompts into 9 sound-source categories, with 100 prompts per cate?gory, spanning speech, animals, instruments, ambient sounds, and other emitter types. The prompts include 439 single-shot and 461 multi-shot narratives, each derived from a structured specification that links every audio event to its emit?ter, subject, and temporal slot. The benchmark provides an 18-metric evaluation suite covering three dimensions: Visual Performance, Content Consistency, and Audio & Semantic Alignment. We further benchmark 12 representative gen?erators and find that visual quality is nearly saturated across leading systems, yet audio semantic scores still differ markedly. Across the nine shared mod?els, multi-shot prompts receive lower aggregate scores under the subset-specific scoring rules and yield different model rankings. Multi-person speech, con?sistent speaker identity across shots, and cross-shot event retention remain the main unresolved challenges. All prompts and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/yucong-liu/CAST-Bench-public.
authors: Yucong Liu, Qi Tian, Shuyuan Tu, Kaihang Pan, Weijie Kong, Chao Pan
bullets: Introduces an audiovisual-contract framework for tracing each generated sound to its intended emitter, semantic content, and temporal slot.

Multi-person speech, speaker identity consistency, and cross-shot event retention remain key challenges.

papers.abstract: The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.
bullets: The driver limits FP16 matrix-multiplication throughput despite the GPU’s Tensor Core hardware capabilities.
A kernel-module unlock raises published cuBLAS FP16 throughput from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS.
On a fixed from-scratch pre-training setup, gains are negligible for pico-micro, 4.7% for tiny, and 11.8% for small.
The small model’s wall time falls from 1.77 to 1.61 hours; peak memory remains bit-identical.
Training quality metrics remain bit-identical or within 10^-3, indicating unchanged training dynamics.

papers.abstract: Diffusion image generators are successful due to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. Yet the two components are not fully matched. During sampling, the denoiser predicts for the next step based on flawed input that differ much from the real data. This train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality (i.e., blurry, lacking in details or awkward in shape). To mitigate the problem, we propose PEEK, a novel training-free deterministic sampler plugin. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates it with the one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more-image-like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating the exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule search made efficient by the prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. On 8 pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings across various output resolutions, PEEK consistently improves over NFE-matched baselines, with FID improvements up to 49.3\% at minimal extra computation cost (e.g., the one-time-per-model calibration takes at most 2.2 minutes across our experiments.). Project website is at https://dachengruoque.github.io/PEEK-Video/.
authors: Yunwei Bai, Ying Kiat Tan, Tsuhan Chen
bullets: Addresses the train-test gap caused by denoisers receiving imperfect intermediate states during sampling.

papers.title: PEEK: One-Step-Look-Ahead Exposure Bias Correction for Diffusion Sampling

papers.abstract: Contrastive pretraining has advanced image-text understanding, yet image, video, and audio encoders are still trained independently, with cross-modal alignment realized mainly through post-hoc binding to a frozen anchor space. We present Omni-Encoder, a general multimodal encoder that processes image, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs within a single SigLIP-2 Vision Transformer with fully shared parameters. Unlike anchor-centric binding or per-modality adapters, all modalities are optimized jointly end-to-end, and the framework is organized from input to training. A modality-native input stage first maps each signal into the shared embedding space, including a 1D-convolutional audio tokenizer that converts mel-spectrograms into tokens aligned with visual patches. A multimodal rotary position embedding parameterized by absolute timestamps then places visual frames and audio segments in a unified spatiotemporal coordinate system. Finally, alternating-modality training interleaves image, video, audio, and temporally aligned audio-visual batches and accumulates their gradients into one update, which we find central to stable joint optimization. Omni-Encoder achieves competitive results on 16 benchmarks across all four modalities with one shared parameter set, and joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart. Code and models will be publicly released.
authors: Xiaofei Sun, Peng Wang, Huayao Liu, Xiaoxiao Xu, Jun Song, Deqing Li, Lin Qu
bullets: Addresses independently trained modality encoders and post-hoc alignment to a frozen anchor space.
Maps each modality into a shared embedding space using modality-native input layers, including an audio tokenizer aligned with visual patches.
Uses timestamp-based multimodal rotary embeddings to unify visual and audio signals in a shared spatiotemporal coordinate system.
Alternates image, video, audio, and aligned audio-visual batches, with joint gradient accumulation for stable optimization.
Joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart while using one shared parameter set.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Omni-Encoder. One SigLIP-2 ViT backbone is shared across image, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs. The framework is organized along the path from input to training: modality-native input tokenization (so heterogeneous signals enter the shared space without distortion), absolute-timestamp multimodal positional alignment (so visual frames and audio segments live on the same temporal axis), and alternating-modality training with cross-modality gradient accumulation (so every update is balanced across modalities).

Figure 3: Multimodal 3D RoPE with absolute timestamps. (a) Video frames and audio tokens share one physical time axis: each token’s temporal coordinate is its absolute timestamp in seconds, so different sampling rates become commensurable and co-occurring content is aligned. (b) Modality-specific position assignment: images use t=0 over the full (h,w) grid; video frames use per-frame timestamps (τk, hi, wj); audio replicates its timestamp into all three sub-spaces (τ, τ, τ). (c) The attention head dimension is split into decoupled T/H/W frequency sub-spaces (33/33/33%, θt=104, θh=θw=103); audio fills all three with τ so the full rotary bandwidth encodes time.

Figure 1: Per-axis normalized R@1 across 14 benchmarks spanning image classification, image-text retrieval, videotext retrieval, and audio-text retrieval. With a single set of shared parameters, our Omni-Encoder (red, solid) maintains balanced performance on every axis, whereas modalityspecific encoders (dashed) excel only in their target domain.

Table 4: Comprehensive comparison of vision-language models across modality capabilities. We categorize methods into four tiers based on their supported modalities: Image-Text only, Video-Text only, Image+Video-Text, and Omni-modal (Image+Video+Audio+Text). Our Omni-Encoder achieves strong performance across all modalities and tasks. All retrieval metrics are R@1 (%). Bold, green, and red indicate the best, second-best, and third-best result in each column, respectively.
Table 3: Overview of the four-modality training corpus.
