papers.title: When Does Sharing Work? Scaling a Shared SigLIP2 Across Image, Video, Audio, and Audio-Visual Representations
papers.tldr: Omni-Encoder uses one jointly trained, fully shared SigLIP2 encoder to represent images, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs, achieving competitive performance across 16 benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host. We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points. A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.
bullets: Maps frozen Evo 2 gene features to early-layer LLM representations of gene symbols, names, and descriptions.
Uses one closed-form ridge fit; the host LLM receives the mapped output at placeholder positions without gradient-based training.
On GeneHop, real DNA improved five-way accuracy over shuffled DNA by 16.7–26.1 points across four LLMs, with all effects surviving correction.
Null controls stayed near sham levels, development results matched test results closely, and a task-independent layer rule generalized across hosts.
The socket primarily conveys gene identity, but outperformed nearest-neighbour retrieval by 3.0–5.2 points and transferred across hosts with at most a 0.9-point test cost.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free closed-form connector from DNA foundation model features to frozen LLM hidden states, extending LLMs with a new modality.
papers.title: A Training-Free Socket for DNA in Frozen Language Models
papers.tldr: A single training-free ridge-regression “socket” connects frozen DNA-model features to frozen LLMs, enabling gene-level reasoning and outperforming shuffled-DNA controls across four hosts.

papers.abstract: Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.
bullets: Models tiered inference as a binary routing test between local execution and escalation.
Derives signal-quality bounds: below a floor, cascades are feasible regardless of signal quality; above a ceiling, they are infeasible even with a perfect signal.
Shows that the role of local compute cost reverses with the architecture cost ratio: billed local compute can make cost binding, while sunk local compute makes feasibility unconditional.
Translates the condition into three design requirements and notes that existing trained-in components satisfy them only separately.
Proposes a co-designed architecture and evaluation protocol as future work; the feasibility condition itself is architecture-independent.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The tier model and the seam. Forward tiers (local, edge, regional) resolve queries that a routing decision at the seam accepts; the datacenter backstop receives escalations. The architecture cost ratio κ (Section 2.4) is small where forward-tier compute is sunk and appreciable where it is billed.

Figure 2: The feasibility region of Proposition 1 in the cost-ratio / signal-quality plane. Below κ⋆ floor a cascade is feasible at any signal quality; above κ⋆ ceil it is infeasible at every signal quality; between them feasibility is contingent on the signal. Decentralization moves a deployment leftward, where feasibility is unconditional below κ⋆ floor and signal quality sets the operating point a feasible cascade achieves. Illustrative parameters q = 0.6, u = 0.05, δ = 0.02.

Table 3: Each requirement of Section 7.1 is satisfied in isolation by a trained-in primitive; no single trained model satisfies all three. The primitives originate in three separate literatures, adaptive-depth inference, split computing, and mixture-of-experts systems, developed for unrelated ends.

Table 2: Four families of tiered inference, organized by whether a confidence signal gates what crosses the seam. All operate on frozen checkpoints; the signal dependency, not the systems detail, separates the structural splits (top two) from the difficulty-routed forms (bottom two).
Table 1: Notation used throughout. Section 6 derives the feasibility condition in these terms.

papers.selection_reason: Closed-form feasibility condition for confidence-gated tiered LLM inference is directly relevant to efficient AI and low-cost LLM serving.
papers.title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
papers.tldr: A closed-form cost condition determines when confidence-gated tiered LLM inference can outperform always using a backstop model, depending on routing-signal quality and the local-to-escalation cost ratio.

papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.
bullets: Agentic pipelines have runtime-dependent, stochastic, heavy-tailed compute, bandwidth, and latency demands.
The orchestration goal is to reserve resources at dispatch while meeting demand and deadlines with prescribed probabilities.
CRO converts a sliding window of past traces into dispatch-time allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees.
Simulations on heterogeneous, multi-modal, heavy-tailed workloads show CRO meets target coverage across risk levels and roughly halves over-reservation versus a Chebyshev baseline.
The evaluation is simulation-based and focuses on the tested workload mixes and risk settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. System model overview. The agentic system A (LLM backbone, memory, tool set) executes a ReAct loop that produces a runtime pipeline G = (v1, . . . , vN ) whose depth N and tool sequence are unknown at dispatch. Each step incurs compute and network demands that aggregate into total consumption C, B, and latency L. Four structural sources (path, depth, per-step demand, duration) make these quantities stochastic, motivating the uncertainty-aware orchestration problem (3).

Fig. 2. Simulation results (n=100 unless noted, ϵ=0.10, 400 trials). (a) Compute coverage Pr(C ≤ ρc) vs. target 1−δ; (b) bandwidth coverage Pr(B ≤ ρb) vs. target; (c) normalized compute over-reservation vs. target coverage; (d) compute coverage vs. calibration window size at δ=0.10. CRO tracks the ideal diagonal in (a)–(b) and meets the 0.90 target in (d) for all n ≥ 10; EmpQ, Gaussian, and Parametric under-reserve; Chebyshev over-covers at nearly 2× the waste of CRO in (c).
TABLE I SIMULATION PARAMETERS (j∈{LT, MD, HV})

papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-aware conformal resource orchestration for agentic AI directly targets efficient use of compute and bandwidth, fitting the Efficient AI topic.
papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems
papers.tldr: CRO uses conformal prediction on recent execution traces to provision resources for unpredictable agentic AI pipelines with probabilistic coverage and lower waste.

papers.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory (SRRM), a lightweight and fully reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates Targeted Retrieval and Global Information Reconstruction. This study also proposes the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR), a benchmark-level metric that quantifies the relationship between retrieval and reconstruction performance. SRRM was evaluated using a synthetic dataset on three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters) across context loads ranging from 10 to 100 factual statements. Experimental results show that reconstruction performance deteriorated substantially faster than retrieval accuracy as contextual information increased, indicating that retrieval alone is insufficient to characterize long-context memory preservation. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieved the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%), and MPR (0.53), outperforming the larger Qwen2.5-3B model (72.2%, 18.5%, and 0.26, respectively). These findings demonstrate that increasing parameter count does not necessarily improve long-context memory preservation. Overall, SRRM provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for systematically evaluating long-context memory while revealing complementary memory behaviors that remain hidden under retrieval-only evaluation frameworks.
bullets: Introduces SRRM, a lightweight benchmark combining targeted retrieval with global information reconstruction.
Defines Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR) to relate retrieval and reconstruction performance.
Evaluates three Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 3B parameters on synthetic contexts containing 10–100 factual statements.
Qwen2.5-1.5B performed best, while the larger 3B model performed worse, showing that more parameters do not guarantee better memory preservation.
Scope: results are based on a synthetic dataset and the evaluated Qwen2.5 models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of the proposed SRRM benchmark. Synthetic information is generated and organized into conversational context before being evaluated through Sequential Retrieval and Summary Reconstruction tasks. Performance is measured using retrieval accuracy, Critical Information Recall (CIR), token consumption, inference time, and hardware memory usage.

Figure 2: Overall organization of the proposed SRRM benchmark. The benchmark begins with four independently generated synthetic information categories, which are subsequently organized into a balanced benchmark sequence using a deterministic Round-Robin strategy. Each information item is assigned a sequence identifier and category identifier before being grouped into predefined context sizes. The constructed benchmark is then evaluated through two complementary tasks, namely Sequential Retrieval and Summary Reconstruction, while multiple performance metrics are collected to provide a comprehensive analysis of the short-term memory capability of the evaluated language models.

Figure 4: This figure illustrates the evaluation workflow of the Sequential Retrieval Test. After the complete conversation history has been constructed, benchmark questions are automatically generated from the corresponding ground-truth annotations. Each model response is subsequently compared with the expected answer to determine whether the retrieved fact is correct or incorrect. The final retrieval performance is then calculated using the proportion of correctly answered questions.

Figure 7: As shown in Figure 7, retrieval performance varies across the evaluated models as the context size increases. The figure presents the overall accuracy trend for Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-3B under identical benchmark conditions. The numerical retrieval accuracy corresponding to each evaluation level is summarized in Table 13.

Figure 10 visualizes the mean retrieval accuracy for each evaluated language model across the four benchmark information categories. Color intensity represents retrieval performance averaged over all evaluated context sizes, while the numerical values indicate the corresponding percentage accuracy for each model–category combination.

Figure 13: Demonstrates that all evaluated models achieved substantially higher retrieval performance than reconstruction performance. Although the magnitude of this difference varies across the Qwen2.5 model family, the same overall pattern is consistently observed, indicating that successful retrieval of previously presented information does not necessarily translate into equivalent preservation of that information during summary generation. This observation suggests that retrieval and reconstruction represent related but distinct memory capabilities, supporting the motivation for evaluating both tasks independently within the proposed SRRM benchmark.
Figure 9: Overall comparison between mean retrieval accuracy and mean CIR score.

Figure 5: Figure 5 illustrates the evaluation workflow of the Summary Reconstruction Test. After the complete conversation history has been constructed, the language model is instructed to reconstruct every previously presented factual statement as a structured summary. The generated summary is subsequently compared against the benchmark ground-truth facts through automatic line-by-line matching, producing the Critical Information Recall (CIR) score that represents the proportion of correctly reconstructed information.
Figure 11: Category-specific reconstruction performance heatmap matrix

Table 12: The SRRM benchmark records multiple computational metrics alongside memory performance to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of language models. These metrics quantify computational efficiency by measuring context size, response length, inference latency, and hardware resource utilization throughout the benchmark. Together, they complement the retrieval- and reconstruction-based evaluations by revealing the computational trade-offs associated with increasing model parameters and context sizes.

Table 5: As shown in Table 5, the benchmark evaluates three parameter scales within the Qwen2.5 family while maintaining the same inference framework and context length. This controlled selection enables the study to isolate the effect of parameter scaling on information retention performance.
Table 1 : Comparison of Existing Long-Context Benchmarks

Table 11: The SRRM benchmark evaluates language models under five progressively increasing context sizes to analyze the effect of information load on short-term memory performance. Instead of modifying the dataset itself, the benchmark gradually increases the number of information items presented to the model while preserving the same information order and distribution. This controlled context scaling enables consistent comparisons across different parameter sizes under identical experimental conditions.

Table 15 : Reports the exact CIR scores obtained by each evaluated model at every benchmark level. The tabulated values complement the graphical representation shown in Figure 8 by providing precise reconstruction scores for each context size, facilitating direct comparison across different parameter scales.

Table 4: Comparison between existing benchmark objectives and the proposed SRRM benchmark. SRRM extends previous evaluations by jointly measuring targeted retrieval, global information reconstruction, and computational efficiency under progressively increasing factual contexts.

Table 13: reports the exact retrieval accuracy obtained by each model at every evaluated context size. Presenting the numerical results in tabular form complements the graphical representation in Figure 7 by providing precise values for each experimental condition, enabling direct comparison across both models and context levels.

Table 14: summarizes the overall retrieval characteristics of each evaluated model. Mean Accuracy represents the average retrieval accuracy across all five context sizes, Max Accuracy and Min Accuracy denote the highest and lowest recorded retrieval performance, respectively, while Accuracy Drop measures the absolute decrease in retrieval accuracy between the evaluations conducted with 10 and 100 information items.

Table 16 : Summarizes the overall reconstruction characteristics of each evaluated model. Mean CIR represents the average reconstruction score across all five context sizes, Max CIR and Min CIR indicate the highest and lowest reconstruction scores observed during the benchmark, respectively, while CIR Drop denotes the absolute decrease in reconstruction performance between the evaluations conducted using 10 and 100 information items.

Table 18 summarizes the benchmark-level ranking derived from the retrieval and reconstruction evaluations presented in the preceding sections. The ranking provides a consolidated comparison of overall memory performance across the evaluated models while preserving the detailed retrieval, reconstruction, and category-level analyses reported previously. As such, it serves as a concise reference for comparing the relative benchmark performance of the evaluated Qwen2.5 model family.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a benchmark for evaluating long-context memory preservation in small language models, directly relevant to long-context processing and memory evaluation.
papers.title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
papers.tldr: SRRM shows that retrieval accuracy alone overestimates long-context memory in small language models, as reconstruction degrades much faster with increasing context.

papers.abstract: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) demands more than empathic validation, requiring instead a structured formulation of the interplay among situations, automatic thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Therapists formalize this interplay through a Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram, where maintaining longitudinal coherence necessitates continuous evidential adjudication to separate tentative hypotheses from established findings. Current dialogue systems track conversational history via retrieval or static profiles but lack the representational capacity to encode epistemic status. Consequently, provisional interpretations are often prematurely reified as established facts, inadvertently biasing downstream interventions. Addressing this limitation, CCDWiki is introduced as a plug-and-play advisor conceptualizing longitudinal therapy as evidence-grounded hypothesis adjudication. The approach encodes each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to corroborating and contradicting evidence. Across sessions, accumulating data strengthens supported entries, preserves provisional ones, and retracts contradicted assumptions. The resulting formulation distills into concise guidance for unmodified therapeutic language models. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in both conceptualization and intervention quality without requiring backbone retraining.
authors: Mingwen Zhang, Ruiyang Song, Qinying Wang, Yuchen Wang, Changsheng Ma, Minqiang Yang
bullets: Addresses the problem of therapy systems prematurely treating tentative interpretations as established facts.
Represents each CBT hypothesis as a mutable entry linked to supporting and contradicting evidence.
Updates formulations across sessions by strengthening supported hypotheses, preserving provisional ones, and retracting contradicted assumptions.
Distills the evolving formulation into concise guidance for an unchanged therapeutic language model.
Experiments show substantial gains in conceptualization and intervention quality without backbone retraining.

papers.abstract: Visual autoregressive generation spans two dominant paradigms: next-scale prediction for images and video, and next-frame prediction for video. Both decode block-by-block rather than token-by-token, yielding KV caches whose statistics diverge from those of language models. At scale, KV memory exceeds the weights and limits large-scale deployment caused by a large amount of visual tokens. Our analysis of these caches reveals three findings. First, a small set of massive-value channels carries the functional load: ablating these outlier channels collapses generation, whereas ablating a matched set of inlier channels leaves quality intact. Second, the outliers organize along two axes, feature and block, with magnitudes persistent within each cell and shifting across cells. Third, this structure arises from two independent mechanisms: projection bias and RoPE-induced scattering. Guided by these findings, we propose VAR-Q, a tuning-free KV-cache quantization framework that groups along the same two axes. The generation loop provides block boundaries for free, removing the need for outlier detection or calibration. Paired with bit-packing kernels for runtime memory reduction, VAR-Q delivers low-bit quantization across nine models spanning both paradigms, cutting KV memory by up to 78.5% with negligible quality degradation and enabling 6x larger inference batches.
authors: Boxun Xu, Jiaji Lu, Yuxuan Yin, Zihu Wang, Ziyue Liu, Yu Wang, Zirui Liu, Peng Li
bullets: Visual autoregressive models decode in blocks, creating KV-cache statistics that differ from language models and can make KV memory exceed model weights.
A small set of persistent outlier channels is functionally critical, with outliers structured across feature and block axes.
VAR-Q groups cache values along these two axes and uses naturally available block boundaries, avoiding outlier detection and calibration.
Bit-packing kernels reduce KV memory by up to 78.5% across nine models and enable inference batches up to 6× larger.
The approach targets next-scale and next-frame image/video generation; the abstract does not report broader settings beyond these paradigms.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces VAR-Q, a tuning-free KV cache quantization framework for visual autoregressive models that reduces memory usage by grouping outliers along feature and block axes.
papers.title: VAR-Q: Tuning-free KV Cache Quantization for Visual Autoregressive Image and Video Generation

papers.abstract: Under expert parallelism, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers pay all-to-all token dispatch, grouped GEMMs, and a combine step in every layer. In decode each rank holds only 1-256 tokens: dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate while tensor-core utilization is inherently low. In fused operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation overlap only by sharing every SM: dispatch warps compete with TMA/MMA and epilogue warps for registers, shared memory, and issue slots; every phase shares one CTA resource budget, synchronization spans the whole SM array, and every replay ends with a workspace-clean pass and a cross-rank barrier. We present GC-MoE, an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the device into a small communication partition and a large compute partition. Each role gets its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain, so dispatch and GEMM tune independently. A three-node CUDA Graph (four on Hopper with fused shared experts) launches the dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots; a token-ring handshake starts computation on the first filled ring blocks, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier between replays. The compute partition runs operand-swapped tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts. On 8 H20 GPUs GC-MoE accelerates DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x); on 8 B300 GPUs it accelerates GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), beating Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy. GC-MoE reserves only 20 of 148 SMs on B300 for dispatch.
authors: Yong Li, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Targets decode-time MoE bottlenecks where all-to-all dispatch and weight traffic dominate and tensor-core utilization is low.
Uses CUDA Green Contexts to assign dispatch and grouped GEMM separate SM partitions, resource budgets, kernels, and synchronization domains.
Overlaps work through CUDA Graph roots, token-ring handshaking, and double-buffered receive counters that eliminate trailing cross-rank barriers.
Supports FP8/FP4 inference on Hopper and Blackwell, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts.
Reports 1.188× average speedup on 8 H20s and 1.106× on 8 B300s, outperforming Mega MoE at all 54 matched-accuracy test points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of one GC-MoE layer replay. The child CUDA Graph holds three nodes: role1 (dispatch) and role2 (grouped GEMM) have no dependency edge and are concurrent roots, whereas role3 (finalize/combine) depends on both (solid arrows). Dashed arrows map each role to the green context that launches it—role1 to the 20-SM communication context, role2 and role3 to the 128-SM compute context—each with its own balanced workqueue so that the driver co-schedules them on disjoint SM sets. All cross-rank state lives in one symmetric-memory workspace whose boxes name the buffers exchanged over NVLink (double arrows): activations and scales, routing metadata, the role1→role2 token ring, the role2→role3 combine buffer, and the counters and parity signals. Every synchronization object is device-persistent and replay-aware, so a replay needs no host-side reset.

Figure 1: Execution timelines. (a) On B300 the baseline is DeepGEMM’s Mega MoE, one persistent fused kernel on all 148 SMs: after routing counts and a tag-1 cross-rank barrier, the dispatch warps stream tokens, scales, and routing metadata into a per-block token ring while the GEMM consumes each ring block as soon as it is full. The phases overlap, but on the same SMs, with the dispatch warps and their staging buffers carved out of every SM’s register file and shared memory; the tail is max(Tcombine, tclean + ttag2)—the workspace clean overlaps the combine, but the tag-2 barrier is still a cross-rank round trip on every replay. (b) GC-MoE runs role1 (dispatch) on the 20-SM communication context and role2 (grouped GEMM) plus role3 (combine) on the 128-SM compute context. Role2 starts when the first ring block is filled (dashed trigger), and parity-double-buffered receive counters remove the tag-2 barrier, so the next replay can start as soon as role3 completes (green band). Each role is an ordinary kernel with its own register, shared-memory, and synchronization budget, so the dispatch and GEMM paths can be optimized independently. Bars are illustrative; measured end-to-end speedups span 1.03–1.30× across the routed-expert sweeps and 1.01–1.35× including shared experts (Section 6.2). Partitions are the B300 values.

papers.selection_reason: CUDA-level MoE inference optimization that reduces latency and improves tensor-core utilization; transferable to efficient LLM serving.
papers.title: GC-MoE: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with FP8/FP4 Grouped GEMM via CUDA Green Contexts
papers.tldr: GC-MoE speeds up low-token MoE decoding by isolating communication and computation on separate GPU partitions and overlapping them efficiently.

papers.abstract: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. We show that, for retrieval, length is cheap and competition is not. On five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families), neutral filler costs nothing: accuracy stays at 0.97 to 1.00, up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Statements in the format of the evidence, placed at the same positions, drop it to 0.16 to 0.33. A single statement that gives the queried key a rival value multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and every additional rival adds to it. Inside the model, one quantity tracks the failure: the attention mass left on the evidence. Across 126,473 trials it explains up to 58% of the variance in loss; log length explains at most 8%. The masked-filler protocol behind the claim that length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU (11 to 18 points lost at 30K tokens), but fails a visible control in retrieval: masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K tokens, while the same filler left visible costs none. In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention. We release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.
bullets: Neutral filler preserves retrieval accuracy—even up to 32K tokens—while same-format statements sharply reduce it.
A single rival value for the queried key increases loss 9–110×, with additional rivals worsening performance.
Attention remaining on the evidence explains up to 58% of loss variance; log context length explains at most 8%.
A masked-filler protocol can make length appear harmful, but visible filler has no effect in the retrieval control.
The study evaluates five open models across 126,473 trials and releases the probe and measurements.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes why retrieval fails on long inputs, attributing context rot to attention competition rather than length; relevant to long-context understanding.
papers.title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval
papers.tldr: Retrieval failures in long contexts are driven mainly by competing evidence that steals attention, not by context length alone.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.
authors: Lixuan He, Jihyeon Je, Yang You, Leonidas Guibas
bullets: Frames or segments shown to the decoder are treated as an explicit test-time selection decision.
The training-free method uses internal representations to select globally relevant, nonredundant context.
It preserves temporal boundary coverage and increases the diversity of visible spatial layouts.
Selected context units are placed on a compact causal axis before generating the next video block.
Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, ReCR improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the ReCR framework. Instead of exposing the full generated history or a fixed recent window, ReCR scores context units with unit-level representations and selects a compact visible context. The selection objective favors high representation utility, preserves boundary coverage over early and recent context, and discourages redundant selected units. At most one spatial-range exchange, not drawn here, then refines the selection (Sec. 3.2). The selected context is then temporally reindexed onto a compact causal axis before being passed to the causal video decoder.

Figure 1: Qualitative overview of ReCR across backbones. ReCR is applied as a training-free context rewriting module on top of different autoregressive video backbones. On 60-second rollouts, ReCR reduces common long-horizon failures such as scene drift, visual artifacts, and oversaturation. On 300-second ultra-long rollouts, ReCR further extends backbones with stable visual continuity.

Figure 3: ReCR further strengthens training-free decoding methods. Qualitative comparisons on two 60-second prompts. For both methods, ReCR improves temporal consistency and visual fidelity over time: it reduces drift and artifacts in Deep Forcing, and further improves the stability and text-alignment ability of Infinity-RoPE. These results show that ReCR is a complementary context-rewriting module that can be added on top of strong training-free methods.
Figure 5: Qualitative transition examples. ReCR improves cross-segment consistency of persistent visual anchors and requested local actions under the same directive-switch schedules.

papers.tldr: ReCR improves long-horizon autoregressive video generation by explicitly rewriting which past content remains visible to the decoder.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support construction hazard monitoring, yet their frequent false alarms remain poorly understood. This study investigates whether false struck-by hazard warnings arise from failures in object recognition, spatial relation encoding, or hazard decisions dominated by learned co-occurrence priors. We evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B using 355 counterfactual worker-excavator scene pairs with controlled spatial proximity and worker-removal variants, combining behavioral analysis, internal representation probing, causal interventions, and decision correction. Both models recognized the entities and encoded their spatial relations (out-of-fold AUROC: 0.82 and 0.91), assigning higher hazard scores to near than far scenes in 79% and 73% of pairs. Nevertheless, 74% and 100% of far scenes were falsely classified as hazardous. Removing the worker reduced Qwen's hazard rate to 11%, while worker presence exerted 2.4- and 3.2-times greater influence on hazard scores than spatial proximity in the respective models. Attention-head interventions, neuron-level interventions, and activation steering failed to eliminate this co-occurrence bias. However, conditioning hazard decisions on the model's own spatial-relation representation improved Qwen's specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity, outperforming threshold recalibration. These findings reveal that VLM struck-by false alarms stem primarily from decision-making failures rather than deficiencies in object recognition or spatial encoding, suggesting that future efforts should prioritize conditioning hazard decisions on encoded spatial evidence rather than further improving visual recognition alone.
bullets: Evaluated Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B on 355 counterfactual worker–excavator scene pairs.
Both models encoded spatial relations, but falsely classified 74% and 100% of far scenes as hazardous.
Worker presence influenced hazard scores 2.4× and 3.2× more than spatial proximity, indicating co-occurrence bias.
Attention, neuron, and activation interventions did not eliminate the bias.
Conditioning decisions on encoded spatial relations improved Qwen’s specificity from 0.36 to 0.58 at matched sensitivity.

papers.abstract: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, and arithmetic methods have emerged as a simple yet effective way to merge models without data. However, existing arithmetic methods treat task vectors in parameter space and apply a single element-wise rule to directions that can differ in mergeability. In a shared directional basis, we find a consistent two-regime structure: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion task-dominated tail that carries disproportionate energy. These findings motivate Common--Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that separates task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with a downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately. Experiments across $11$ base models, four model families, and four arithmetic-based merging operators show that CUSD improves 42 of 44 model--operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/stwang666/CUSD
authors: Shiting Wang, Yingjie Zou, Ke Li
bullets: Existing arithmetic merging methods apply one element-wise rule to task vectors despite differences in directional mergeability.
Task vectors exhibit a common, low-dispersion bulk and a high-dispersion, task-dominated tail with disproportionate energy.
CUSD decomposes task vectors into common and unique components, merges the common part, and preserves unique residuals separately.
Across 11 base models, four model families, and four operators, CUSD improves 42 of 44 model–operator combinations, with up to 22.5% improvement over baselines.
The method is data-free and requires no additional training; scope is limited to the evaluated model families and arithmetic operators.

papers.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.
bullets: Uses a normalized Transformer with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, divided into input, recurrent, and output blocks.
Variable loop counts provide elastic inference compute, with harder prompts routed to deeper loops during post-training.
More loops yield the largest accuracy gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks.
With at least two loops, it outperforms several larger models across 12 benchmarks, according to the abstract.
Caching only the final loop’s keys and values keeps KV-cache memory comparable to a non-looped model; quantized checkpoints are released.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Overview of the post-training pipeline for Dory1.0-4B. The base context window is 262,144 tokens (256K). SFT trains on packed sequences of 262,144 tokens, and samples loop counts for each microbatch randomly, while RLVR routes harder prompts to deeper loops with higher probability.

Figure 2 | Dory1.0-4B’s looped nGPT architecture. A 16-layer input block produces a fixed representation 𝑢. A 40-layer recurrent block refines the state over 𝑘 passes (up to four), sharing all of its weights and learned scales across each loop. Each loop adds 𝑢 to the current state, initialized as 𝑠0 = 𝑢, and applies L2 normalization before and after the recurrent block. A 16-layer output block processes the final state before the LM head. Within each block, an eight-layer pattern contains three SWA–SwiGLU pairs followed by one full-attention–SwiGLU pair, giving a 3:1 ratio of sliding-window attention (SWA) to full attention. SWA uses a window of 𝑊 =1024 tokens with RoPE base 𝜃S = 104; full attention uses 𝜃F = 107. RoPE acts on all Q/K dimensions. Each sublayer updates the residual stream by blending its normalized output with the normalized residual using learned per-channel weights, then normalizing the result.

papers.title: Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT

papers.abstract: With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. Manual memory strategies further limit adaptation to diverse and evolving shared contexts. To this end, we propose \textbf{EvoGroup (EvoG)}, a self-evolving harness for group agents that starts from a minimal six-tool cold start and adapts through interaction with shared context. EvoG uses confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories, while also eliciting self-reflections on uncertainty in low-confidence cases. The analysis agent then examines selected trajectories through adaptive progressive disclosure, followed by bucketed analysis to synthesize high-level findings that guide the evolve agent in revising the Harness. Empirically, pass@1 on held-out split of EverMemBench improves from 71.07\% to 89.58\%, surpassing both self-evolving memory and human-designed harnesses, including Claude Code (85.83\%). To evaluate generalization, we freeze the evolved harness and evaluate it on the unseen GroupMemBench, where, with GPT-5.5, it demonstrates effective generalization and outperforms both memory baselines and human-designed harnesses.
bullets: Targets the gap between individual-user memory systems and the relationship- and collaboration-aware knowledge needed by group agents.
Starts with six tools and evolves through interaction, using confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories.
Uses self-reflection for uncertain cases, adaptive progressive disclosure, and bucketed analysis to guide harness revisions.
Improves EverMemBench held-out pass@1 from 71.07% to 89.58%, exceeding reported self-evolving and human-designed baselines.
A frozen evolved harness also generalizes effectively to the unseen GroupMemBench, outperforming memory and human-designed baselines.

papers.title: EvoGroup: A Self-Evolving Harness for Group Agents in Shared Contexts
papers.tldr: EvoGroup is a self-evolving harness that learns to manage group-level knowledge in shared contexts, substantially improving group-agent memory performance and generalizing to an unseen benchmark.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.
bullets: Continuous learning under finite memory causes unchecked plasticity and accumulating memory problems.
The selectionist RRR account of sleep—ringing, resonance, and renormalization—can be mapped to operations in digital memory systems.
The framework addresses when and what an agent should forget during persistent operation.
It predicts that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores become large.
The claim is theoretical and presents a falsifiable prediction rather than reported experimental results.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes sleep-inspired consolidation for continuous learning and memory management in stateful LLM-based agents.
papers.title: Do agents need to sleep?
papers.tldr: Persistent LLM agents may need sleep-like memory consolidation to prevent drift, retrieval degradation, stored errors, and capacity saturation.

papers.abstract: Data flywheels promise continuous improvement via insights from deployment data. Understanding how the deployed model succeeds and fails can steer subsequent data collection towards patching failures and reinforcing successes. However, robot deployments create large volumes of high-dimensional rollout data, which is challenging to understand and confidently ground data collection decisions in. To make deployment data easier to analyze and act on, we propose behavior graphs, which compress policy rollouts into a single interpretable, directed graph. We construct the graphs by learning to identify similar behavior modes across rollouts, connecting the behaviors temporally, and finally linking them to outcomes. In a user study on three real-world tasks, where participants analyzed rollouts to choose a data collection strategy, 16 of 18 preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, reaching comparable conclusions with 40.3% lower perceived temporal demand and 37.6% lower effort. Beyond interpretability for deployment data, behavior graphs are capable progress predictors: across 43 datasets, they improve the rank correlation between predicted progress and true temporal order by 22.9% and reduce mean absolute error by 53.5% relative to the strongest baseline. As the number of deployed robots grows, behavior graphs lend structure to high-dimensional policy rollouts and make deployment data easier to interpret and reason about.
authors: Erik Bauer, Jakob Thumm, Christopher Agia, Rohan Sinha, Chen Xu, Haruki Nishimura, Jeannette Bohg, Marco Pavone, Masha Itkina
bullets: Robot deployments generate high-dimensional rollout data that is difficult to interpret and use for data-collection decisions.
The method discovers similar behavior modes, connects them over time, and links them to outcomes in a directed graph.
In a user study across three real-world tasks, 16 of 18 participants preferred behavior graphs to rollout videos, with lower perceived time demand and effort.
Across 43 datasets, behavior graphs improved progress-order rank correlation and reduced prediction error relative to the strongest baseline.
The approach is evaluated for deployment-data interpretation and progress prediction; its scope is limited to the studied tasks and datasets.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Behavior graph construction. Left: Each trajectory’s state-action pairs are embedded, mean-pooled over temporal windows, and assigned to behavior modes by dimensionality reduction and clustering fit on all trajectories. Consecutive windows with the same mode are collapsed into segments, and a VLM captions each mode. Right: The resulting behavior sequences from all trajectories are merged into a single directed graph from a start node to success and failure outcomes, with edges weighted by empirical transition probabilities.

Fig. 4: Tasks for the user study, in which participants analyze policy rollouts to choose which demonstrations to collect next. Keyframes of a successful rollout from left to right. (a) Set table: places a pumpkin, then a milk carton from the shelf; the training data omits the carton’s leftmost position. (b) Prepare tray: slides out a tray, places a bowl from the top or bottom shelf onto it, and grasps a fork, requiring precise grasps. (c) Cooking: a long-horizon task that clears a ladle, adds a corn, carrot, and chili to the pot, and closes the lid.

Fig. 5: Targeted data helps only when it addresses the policy’s most frequent failure mode. Estimated success rates [27] of the baseline policy and of policies retrained with 30 additional demonstrations for each candidate data-collection strategy, on three real-world DROID tasks. In Set table, only demonstrations with the milk carton on the left (the position missing from the baseline training data) improve performance. In Prepare tray, bottom-shelf bowl demonstrations improve over the baseline. In Cooking, no single-subtask strategy makes a significant difference. Violins show the Bayesian posterior over each policy’s success rate (uniform Beta prior). Dots and bars mark the posterior mean and 95% credible interval. Letters above each column [28] summarize pairwise significance tests within a task [29]: two policies that share a letter are not significantly different; policies with no letter in common are. Tests follow [29] with family-wise error rate controlled at 5%, and 60 policy rollouts to estimate each posterior. Below, histograms show the strategies participants chose with the graph and with the video browser, which are similar.

Fig. 3: Behavior graph for the cooking task of our user study (Sec. IV-A). The larger the node, the higher the visitation count. Node colors indicate success likelihood (increasing from red to green), while all terminal nodes are annotated with their likelihoods. Fig. 6: Behavior graphs make rollout analysis less demanding without changing the decisions users reach. Responses from 18 participants. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of language models keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer and serves rollouts from a bf16 copy produced by round-to-nearest conversion. At the learning rates in common use, most per-step updates are smaller than half a bf16 spacing and the conversion discards them: on Qwen3-1.7B only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per step, and the policy that generates the training data lags the optimizer by 50-150 steps. Existing mismatch corrections cannot see this lag because they compare two copies downstream of the same rounding. We propose Fair Cast: export the master with an unbiased rounding rule (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and compute the training loss on the served copy. The change is one line at the export call, adds no hyperparameters and costs 22-38 ms per export of 1.7B parameters. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on Qwen3-0.6B to 4B with AdamW and Muon, Fair Cast is ahead on 18, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points; on zebra puzzles it reaches 0.57 +/- 0.16 over four runs where round-to-nearest collapses to 0.33 +/- 0.10. It also makes the saved fp32 checkpoint agree with the served model, and it exposes the implicit lag of round-to-nearest as a regularizer that can be restored explicitly when a task needs it.
bullets: In common RL post-training, only 0.4–0.5% of served Qwen3-1.7B weights change per step, creating a 50–150-step policy lag.
Existing mismatch corrections miss this lag because they compare copies affected by the same rounding.
Fair Cast applies stochastic rounding or error feedback when exporting weights and computes loss on the served copy.
Across 25 matched seed-pairs, it was ahead in 18, tied in 6, and behind in 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points.
The method adds no hyperparameters but costs 22–38 ms per 1.7B-parameter export; round-to-nearest’s lag may still be useful as an explicit regularizer.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses a training-inference mismatch in RL post-training of language models, a meaningful methodological contribution to LLM training.
papers.title: bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates: A Hidden Training-Inference Mismatch and an Unbiased One-Line Fix
papers.tldr: bf16 round-to-nearest silently drops most RL policy updates, while Fair Cast uses unbiased rounding to align training with the served model and improves results.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon consistency is essential for video world models, yet it becomes difficult to maintain once observed content falls outside the context window. Existing memory mechanisms either retrieve history as implicit context, which remains constrained by context capacity and entangles static and dynamic information or consolidate history into explicit global representations, which struggle to model evolving dynamics and accumulate geometric errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce GROME, a novel factorized memory framework that augments video world models for long-horizon coherence across both static scenes and dynamic entities. GROME operates via three synergistic components: 1) Static-Dynamic Factorization decouples historical evidence into static and dynamic components, preserving static scene geometry and dynamic entity states separately; 2) Local Memory Retrieval selects spatially aligned static history to eliminate geometric drift alongside the latest dynamic entity states to ensure temporal continuity; 3) Training-Free Memory Injection seamlessly grounds the factorized memory into video world models via their native conditioning pathways. Experiments on long-horizon revisit scenarios demonstrate that GROME substantially enhances scene persistence and dynamic entity fidelity over existing methods, all while preserving the visual quality and controllability of the frozen backbone without additional training. Beyond self-rollouts, GROME readily accommodates external observations as plug-and-play memory, unlocking flexible and controllable video continuation and scene exploration.
bullets: Addresses context-window limitations and errors from mixing static and evolving information in video-model memory.
Factorizes history into static scene components and dynamic entity states.
Retrieves spatially aligned static memories and the latest dynamic states to reduce geometric drift and preserve temporal continuity.
Uses training-free injection through the world model’s native conditioning pathways.

Long-horizon revisit experiments show improved scene persistence and dynamic-entity fidelity while preserving visual quality and controllability; it also supports external observations for video continuation and exploration.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GROME. GROME factorizes historical evidence into static scene and dynamic entity components. Both are retained over extended rollouts as local spatial memories, with the dynamic component further organized by explicit temporal indexing. Given a target camera trajectory, relevant historical evidence is separately retrieved from the static and dynamic components to render references. These static-dynamic references are then injected into the model’s native history-conditioning pathway through a set of training-free injection strategies, conditioning generation together with the local context and user actions. This allows GROME to better preserve consistency over long rollouts while maintaining generation quality and controllability.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. GROME better preserves revisit scene structure and entity consistency simultaneously across diverse revisit trajectories compared with existing world models.

Figure 12: Static complex-memory revisit-case 2. The L-shaped explore–return trajectory distributes pose and scene evidence across several views, causing context-based methods to drift or omit content. GROME retrieves complementary static scene evidence through max-coverage retrieval, preserving the revisit scene structure. Red boxes mark representative failures.

Figure 11: Static complex-memory revisit-case 1. When exploring both sides of the kitchen, the visual evidence required for the return view is distributed across multiple historical frames, exceeding the model’s finite context window. GROME retrieves and consolidates local memories to reconstruct comprehensive, high-fidelity static scene references. Red boxes highlight representative inconsistencies in the baselines.

Figure 20: Robustness to imperfect geometric projection. Although rendered historical memories often exhibit geometric artifacts such as disocclusion holes and blur, GROME leverages them as soft spatial guidance rather than rigid pixel-level targets via timestep-aware memory routing. Guided by pretrained world priors, the frozen model corrects moderate rendered distortions and plausibly synthesizes unobserved regions during finer denoising steps while maintaining scene consistency.
Figure 6: Local retrieval vs. Global consolidation.
Figure 7: Applications of GROME.

Figure 8: Evaluation set and trajectory design. The top panels show representative static and dynamic scene categories and their proportions. The bottom panels illustrate exploration-and-revisit camera trajectories; dashed arrows mark returns to previously observed regions.

Figure 13: Static complex-memory revisit-case 3. Complex camera trajectories create multi-view spatial configurations where different parts of the target view are scattered across disparate historical references, exposing the limits of single-frame retrieval. While maintaining a monolithic global cache often suffers from accumulated drift and high overhead, GROME retains historical evidence as local point clouds and selectively retrieves them under target poses. This strategy synthesizes complementary scene evidence to generate the target view with high-fidelity revisit consistency. Red boxes mark representative baseline failures.
Figure 15: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 2.

Figure 14: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 1. Explicit-memory baselines overlook dynamic entities during memory construction, freezing them at outdated historical states, whereas context-only generation inevitably loses long-range environmental evidence. By factorizing static structure from dynamic entities, GROME simultaneously preserves background consistency and enables dynamic states to evolve. Red boxes mark representative failures.
Figure 16: Dynamic complex-memory revisit-case 3.

Figure 19: Spatially Grounded Exploration. Additional spatially grounded exploration cases. Each row shows the source evidence, the memory transformation or composition, and the resulting rollout under a novel camera trajectory. This arrangement exposes which visual content originates from each memory region.

Figure 21: Representative failure cases of GROME. (a) At long rollout horizons, appearance and color drift inherited from the frozen backbone can still accumulate despite Reference Value Adaptation. (b) Severe local geometry errors can produce sparse or corrupted warped evidence. Although the pretrained VWM usually tolerates moderate projection imperfections, extreme artifacts may be interpreted as plausible scene content and propagate into the generated frame.

Figure 2: Comparison of memory paradigms. Implicit memory suffers from substantial scenecontent overlap and ambiguous in dynamic states, while explicit memory consolidates historical frames into a global 3D scene but struggles with evolving dynamic entities and accumulated geometric drift. GROME instead factorizes historical frames into static-dynamic memory, preserving both persistent static scene structure and evolving dynamic entities over long-horizon generation.
Figure 5: Qualitative ablation of GROME. Static-dynamic factorization and three injection strategies demonstrate their complementary roles in maintaining static scene and evolving entity states.

Figure 17: Long-horizon qualitative comparison. When historical views leave the finite context, implicit memory and explicit memory-based baselines drift from the scene, while GROME preserves static structure beyond 1,400 frames. On dynamic scenes, factorized memory retains evolving dynamic entities without forcing them to remain in a stale state.

Figure 18: Video-to-Memory Continuation. Additional real-world video-continuation cases. Each row pairs an observed video with a GROME rollout generated along a new camera trajectory. Revisit frames assess retention of previously observed scene content, while novel-view frames show the continuation beyond the input.

Figure 9: DA3 inference scaling with input-frame count. Geometry-estimation cost increases with the active input-window size during initialization. GROME subsequently maintains a fixed sliding window instead of expanding the geometry input with rollout length.

Table 3: Comparison of historical memory access patterns in long-horizon world models. Implicit memory methods rely on temporally indexed 2D frames, whereas explicit memory methods maintain global 3D reconstructions. In contrast, GROME introduces a unified, factorized memory: both static and dynamic components are grounded as local pointmaps, with the dynamic stream retaining source timestamps for temporal indexing.

papers.tldr: GROME improves long-horizon video world-model consistency by separately remembering static scene geometry and dynamic entities, then injecting retrieved memories without retraining the backbone.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings. For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know. Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries. We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know. Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly. Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras. Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers' coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab.
bullets: Covers 30 quantitative science experiments across five disciplines and 14 simulated laboratory apparatuses.
Agents receive a goal and apparatus, choose experimental procedures, and use camera-based instrument readings to investigate resampled systems.
Evaluation scores both the knowledge acquired from recorded observations and the required resulting physical state; all tasks are verified solvable.
Six frontier models are tested with native control, enhanced perception and planning, and distilled manipulation skills.
With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; apparatus interaction causes most failures, while manipulation skills particularly help weaker agents.

papers.abstract: Cascade world-action models (WAMs) use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, but inherit costly iterative inference from diffusion-pretrained experts. We ask what a single-step predicted future must preserve to support accurate single-step action prediction. In the evaluated WAM, resampling video noise has little effect on downstream actions, yet naively truncating both streams to one step substantially reduces task success. Video-space supervision only partially closes this gap, and a local sensitivity analysis shows that vision prediction errors have highly unequal consequences for action accuracy. These findings motivate DirectWAM, which converts pretrained video and action experts into single-step predictors without stochastic sampling through action-sufficient distillation, while retaining the explicit future-to-action cascade. After learning a one-step action model, we train the future predictor by decoding actions from its own predicted futures and backpropagating demonstration action error through the expert, with an optional future-latent reconstruction loss. The resulting objective evaluates the student-generated future through its downstream control consequences rather than relying on representation matching alone. DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success across four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same one-evaluation-per-stream budget. This advantage has also extended to three real-world tasks that we designed. Compared with the full iterative teacher, it reduces inference latency by $28.0\times$.
bullets: WAMs can lose task success when diffusion inference is naively reduced to one step, even though video-noise resampling has little effect on actions.
Vision prediction errors have unequal impacts on action accuracy, motivating action-sufficient rather than purely representation-matching distillation.
DirectWAM retains the future-to-action cascade and trains the future predictor through downstream demonstration-action error, with optional future-latent reconstruction.
It achieves 97.1% average success on four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same inference budget.
The method also extends to three designed real-world tasks and reduces latency 28.0× versus the full iterative teacher.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for AI-generated image (AIGI) detection, providing natural-language explanations for authenticity judgments. However, their ability to interpret text within images may also expose these judgments to misleading semantic cues. We systematically evaluate typographic attack strategies across detection-oriented, open-weight, and commercial VLMs, considering both real-to-fake and fake-to-real attacks. Our results show that reasoning modes generally exhibit greater vulnerability than direct modes and that attack effectiveness exhibits pronounced directional asymmetry. Moreover, larger models tend to exhibit higher clean detection accuracy but also higher attack success rates. We further examine attack robustness under image and text transformations and investigate whether overlays indicating the correct class can aid error correction. Together, these analyses characterize how typographic attacks influence authenticity judgments and expose limitations of current VLM-based AIGI detection systems.
bullets: Evaluates typographic attacks against detection-oriented, open-weight, and commercial VLMs.
Studies attacks that flip judgments from real to fake and from fake to real, revealing strong directional asymmetry.
Finds reasoning modes are generally more vulnerable than direct modes.
Larger models tend to achieve higher clean accuracy but also higher attack success rates.
Examines robustness to image/text transformations and whether correct-class overlays help correct errors.

papers.abstract: Effective human-AI collaboration requires partners to establish references through interaction, which becomes fragile when descriptions are ambiguous, similar referents compete, or partners see different things. We study referential uncertainty - uncertainty over which candidate object a description refers to - in a collaborative puzzle task where a human Helper instructs an AI Worker to place pieces. The Worker must identify and communicate its uncertainty, and the Helper must recognize and act on it. We show that a separately elicited belief distribution over candidate pieces is better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and better discriminates correct from incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) than raw action-token probabilities, which are severely overconfident (0.97 mean confidence, ECE 0.44). Across three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5), this elicited uncertainty rises predictably with instruction vagueness, but not with competing referents in context, even when those increase errors. The models seldom externalize it, asking for clarification on only 3.5-16.7% of turns. In a controlled human study (N=210), participants given only the Worker's default message accept 78% of wrong placements and cannot tell right from wrong (AUC 0.50). Precise descriptions and, especially, well-targeted hedges cut wrong-move acceptance to 36% while largely preserving correct-move acceptance, compensating for missing shared awareness such as not seeing the Worker's action. But this benefit depends on targeting: a deployable hedge derived from the model's own belief entropy inherits that signal's weakness and can do more harm than good. Externalized uncertainty helps a human partner only when it is accurately targeted.
bullets: Studies referential uncertainty in a collaborative puzzle task where an AI places pieces based on human instructions.
Elicited belief distributions over candidate pieces are better calibrated and discriminative than raw action-token probabilities, which are overconfident.
Across GPT-4.1, GPT-5, and GPT-5.5, uncertainty increases with vague instructions but often misses competing referents that cause errors.
Models ask for clarification infrequently, and humans given default messages accept many incorrect placements without distinguishing them from correct ones.
Precise descriptions and targeted hedges reduce wrong-move acceptance, but entropy-based hedges can be counterproductive when uncertainty is misaligned.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The collaborative puzzle task and the human study conditions. The partners hold asymmetric information: the Worker (AI) sees the current board and all 24 available pieces but not the target, whereas theHelper (human) sees the target pattern but neither the pieces nor—by default—the Worker’s board. The Helper gives a referring instruction and the Worker selects, places a piece, and replies with a message (here, a blue spiral placed in the target slot). Each condition changes exactly one element of this same turn. Four vary only the Worker’s message while the board stays hidden: Generic (A) is the original message; Described (C) appends a precise description of the placed piece; and Hedged (D) and Self-hedged (E) additionally append an expression of uncertainty—inserted by an oracle on the objectively wrong turns (D) or, in the deployable variant, from the Worker’s own belief entropy (E). The fifth condition, Visible board, keeps the Generic message but reveals the Worker’s board to the Helper—the shared-view control (A/shared). Holding the turn fixed and varying only the message or the board’s visibility isolates how each externalized signal shapes the Helper’s perceived confidence, error detection, and willingness to act.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on memory to generalize beyond their training environments. However, agents are bounded by what they have seen and believed, and leveraging such memories in unseen environments can introduce biases into their internal beliefs. We formalize this phenomenon as \textit{false memory}, which can arise from spurious correlations, environment shifts, and knowledge conflicts. Despite its importance, false memory is difficult to evaluate because it stems from agent internal beliefs and is easily confounded with ordinary generalization failures. Therefore, we propose FAME, a training-free framework that evaluates false memory through the evolution of agent beliefs under counterfactual reasoning. Specifically, counterfactual scenarios reveal how beliefs change as the latent concept of memory shifts under hypothetical interventions; thus, measuring the resulting concept drift provides a signal for distinguishing faithful versus false memory. Such concepts can be estimated from agent hidden states before answer generation, avoiding the need for reward design or answer sampling. Empirical experiments reveal that simply monitoring answers often fails to detect false memory, while FAME achieves AUROCs of 76.2% - 96.7% across false-memory settings, and outperforms the best baseline by 3.4% - 23.3% across realistic benchmarks, spanning math reasoning (GSM-Symbolic), code generation (GitChameleon), and complex reasoning (BigBench-Hard). We further release corresponding counterfactual templates and facilitate future research on false memory.
bullets: False memory can arise from spurious correlations, environment shifts, and knowledge conflicts, but is difficult to distinguish from ordinary generalization failures.
FAME evaluates how an agent’s latent memory concepts change across counterfactual scenarios, using hidden states before answer generation.
The approach avoids reward design and answer sampling, and shows that answer monitoring alone often misses false memory.
Across math, code-generation, and complex-reasoning benchmarks, FAME achieves AUROCs of 76.2%–96.7% and improves over the strongest baseline by 3.4–23.3%.
The authors release counterfactual templates to support further research.

papers.abstract: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? To answer this question, we first conduct preliminary experiments showing that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To understand these effects, we use controlled replay to isolate internal state changes specific to each problem-history pairing. Across different histories, these changes preserve similar relationships among current problems. To improve reasoning under retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). STAIR captures keys and values from earlier response generation in a fixed bank. It learns to redirect current queries when they read this bank during prompt processing. The base model remains frozen; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history.
bullets: Retained conversation history changes later-turn accuracy even for problems in the same domain.
Controlled replay shows that history induces problem-specific internal state changes with consistent relationships across histories.
STAIR stores earlier-generation keys and values in a fixed bank and redirects current queries to reuse them.
The base model stays frozen; only 12,288 parameters are trained.
Across three Qwen models and four benchmarks, STAIR raises average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history.
